species.name: Hoary Bat
species.description: North America's largest vespertilionid and most widespread. Low-frequency QCF calls ~20–25 kHz. Long-distance migrant. Solitary tree-roosting. Formerly Lasiurus cinereus. Major wind-turbine collision casualty.

species.name: Big Red Bat
species.description: Large South American lasiurine. FM-QCF calls ~30–35 kHz. Solitary tree-roosting migratory bat. Formerly Lasiurus egregius. Rarely captured; known mainly from southern Brazil.

species.name: Banana Bat
species.description: Sub-Saharan Africa. Peak about 70 kHz. FM-QCF calls about 3 ms long. Named for roosting in furled banana leaves. Small (3–5 g).

species.name: Smoky Bat
species.description: Rare, endemic to western South America (Ecuador, Peru, Chile). High-frequency FM sweeps ~80–100 kHz. Cave-dwelling. IUCN Vulnerable.

species.name: Tailed Tailless Bat
species.description: Nectarivore with short tail (unlike tailless A. geoffroyi). Peak ~72 kHz. Low-intensity FM. Atlantic Forest and lower Andean slopes. Important pollinator.

species.name: Handley's Tailless Bat
species.description: Highland nectarivore. Peak ~68 kHz. Low-intensity FM. Andean cloud forests 1000–2600 m. Uniquely keeled lower incisors.

species.name: Geoffroy's Tailless Bat
species.description: High-altitude nectarivore. Peak ~70 kHz. Low-intensity multiharmonic FM. Found in cloud forests and highlands.

species.name: Pallid Bat
species.description: Unique dual foraging strategy: echolocates for aerial prey and uses passive listening to glean scorpions and large insects from the ground. FM calls ~30 kHz characteristic. Large ears, pale fur. Immune to scorpion venom.

species.name: Aztec Fruit-eating Bat
species.description: Small frugivorous phyllostomid endemic to montane cloud forests of Mexico and Central America. Low-intensity whispering FM. Feeds primarily on figs.

species.name: Jamaican Fruit Bat
species.description: Very common frugivore. Peak ~56 kHz. Variable intensity (mean ~96 dB SPL); not always a quiet "whisperer". Important seed disperser.

species.name: Great Fruit-eating Bat
species.description: Large frugivore. Peak about 61 to 65 kHz. Prominent facial stripes. Important pollinator.

species.name: Dark Fruit-eating Bat
species.description: Common Amazonian frugivore. Peak ~55 kHz. Intermediate size between A. jamaicensis and A. lituratus. Low-intensity FM. Indistinct facial stripes.

species.name: Flat-faced Fruit Bat
species.description: Very common South American frugivore, replaces A. jamaicensis in many mainland habitats. Peak ~54 kHz. Low-intensity multiharmonic FM. Important seed disperser.

species.name: Trident Leaf-nosed Bat
species.description: CF about 115 to 120 kHz; resting bats 111 to 124 kHz. Most widespread hipposiderid in the Middle East and North Africa. Trident-shaped noseleaf. Highly colonial; desert-adapted. Morocco to Pakistan.

species.name: Stoliczka's Trident Bat
species.description: CF ~119–120 kHz with terminal FM sweep. Distinctive trident nose-leaf. Southeast China (Yunnan, Guizhou, Guangxi) in karst limestone. Cave-roosting.

species.name: White-striped Free-tailed Bat
species.description: Australia's largest insectivorous bat. Loud, low-frequency calls audible to some humans. Fast, high-flying open-air forager.

species.name: Antarctic Minke Whale
species.description: No echolocation. The most abundant baleen whale in Antarctic waters. Produces a distinctive "bio-duck" sound — a repetitive, quacking pulse train — that puzzled researchers for decades before being attributed to this species. Small for a rorqual; frequently seen in pack ice.

species.name: Blue Whale
species.description: No echolocation. The largest animal ever to have lived. Produces infrasonic calls (10–40 Hz) detectable across ocean basins. Antarctic blue whales (B. m. intermedia) feed on enormous quantities of krill in the Southern Ocean during austral summer. Critically endangered; slowly recovering from whaling.

species.name: Fin Whale
species.description: No echolocation. Second-largest animal on Earth. Produces powerful 20 Hz pulses that carry across ocean basins — among the loudest sustained biological sounds. Asymmetric colouration: white right lower jaw, dark left. Fast swimmer, nicknamed the 'greyhound of the sea'. Regular summer visitor to Antarctic waters.

species.name: Gray Sac-winged Bat
species.description: Open-area forager. Long narrowband QCF (about 9 to 14 ms) peaking near 41 kHz (2nd harmonic), ending in a short steep downward sweep. Bats flying in groups shift their peak frequency.

species.name: Barbastelle
species.description: Distinctive flat face with upturned nose. Alternating call frequencies (~32 and ~34 kHz). Specialist moth-hunter; forest dependent. Rare across most of its range.

species.name: Asian Barbastelle
species.description: FM calls in two alternating types: type A at 32–37 kHz, type B at 38–45 kHz. Similar to European B. barbastellus. Rare in Japan (Honshu). Forest-dwelling, very elusive.

species.name: Van Gelder's Bat
species.description: Very quiet calls. Related to long-eared bats (Plecotus-like). Gleaning insectivore. Peak ~35 kHz. Rare, poorly known.

species.name: Arnoux's Beaked Whale
species.description: Largest beaked whale in the Southern Hemisphere (up to 10 m). Produces FM echolocation clicks during deep foraging dives. Two teeth erupt at the tip of the lower jaw in both sexes. Circumpolar in cold southern waters, occasionally sighted near the ice edge. Closely related to Baird's Beaked Whale of the North Pacific.

species.name: Heart-nosed Bat
species.description: Large sit-and-wait predator of East African savannas. Heart-shaped nose leaf. Low-intensity broadband FM calls. Hunts from perches, taking large insects, scorpions, and small vertebrates.

species.name: Silky Short-tailed Bat
species.description: Calls much like C. perspicillata (peak about 69 kHz on the 2nd harmonic, 86 kHz when the 3rd is loudest). Frugivore. Low-intensity FM.

species.name: Chestnut Short-tailed Bat
species.description: Higher peak (~78 kHz) than C. perspicillata, consistent with smaller body. Frugivore. Low-intensity FM. Documented from Costa Rica.

species.name: Seba's Short-tailed Bat
species.description: One of the most abundant Neotropical bats. Peak ~71 kHz. Frugivore that also takes insects. Low-intensity whispering calls.

species.name: Sowell's Short-tailed Bat
species.description: Lowland forest frugivore, closely related to C. brevicauda. Multi-harmonic FM calls. Important seed disperser of Piper plants. Central America to NW South America.

species.name: Thomas's Shaggy Bat
species.description: Rare canopy-dwelling emballonurid. QCF calls ~40–45 kHz. Shaggy fur. Roosts singly on tree trunks and in leaf clusters. Southern Mexico to Ecuador.

species.name: Shaggy Bat
species.description: Rare canopy-level forager. Steep FM sweeps ~45–55 kHz. Long shaggy fur. One of the least-known Neotropical emballonurids. Amazonian forests.

species.name: Wrinkle-faced Bat
species.description: Bizarre wrinkled face with skin fold that can cover it like a mask. Peak ~65 kHz. Relatively long calls for a stenodermatine (1–3 ms). Frugivore.

species.name: Ansorge's Free-tailed Bat
species.description: West, Central, and East Africa forests. Peak ~28–32 kHz. Forest edge and canopy forager.

species.name: Chapin's Free-tailed Bat
species.description: Central and East Africa. Peak ~25–28 kHz. Forest and forest edge. Similar to C. pumilus but forest-associated.

species.name: Greater Northern Free-tailed Bat
species.description: Very loud, low-frequency QCF calls (16–23 kHz) often audible to humans. Large free-tailed bat of tropical northern Australia. Fast, high-altitude forager over woodland and open habitats.

species.name: Wrinkle-lipped Free-tailed Bat
species.description: Narrowband FM sweeps, about 17 to 40 kHz with a peak near 23 to 28 kHz. Forms some of the world’s largest bat colonies (millions). Fast high-altitude open-air forager. Widespread across South and SE Asia. Spectacular synchronous dusk emergence columns.

species.name: Large-eared Pied Bat
species.description: Broadband FM calls. Distinctive black and white fur pattern. Roosts in sandstone cliff overhangs and caves near fertile areas. Restricted to eastern Australia. Vulnerable (EPBC Act).

species.name: Gould's Wattled Bat
species.description: Widespread and abundant across Australia. Roosts in tree hollows, buildings, and bat boxes. Alternating call frequencies are distinctive.

species.name: Chocolate Wattled Bat
species.description: Common across southern Australia. Small, dark bat roosting in tree hollows and buildings. Higher frequency calls than Gould's Wattled Bat.

species.name: Hoary Wattled Bat
species.description: Curved FM calls with a characteristic frequency of about 36 to 41 kHz. Found across northern and eastern Australia and Papua New Guinea. Roosts in tree hollows. Medium-sized wattled bat of open woodland and forest edges.

species.name: New Zealand Long-tailed Bat
species.description: One of only two native land mammals of New Zealand. FM calls ~37–45 kHz. Nationally Critical. Forest-dwelling; roosts in tree hollows. Rapid decline from predation by introduced mammals.

species.name: Hairy Big-eyed Bat
species.description: Canopy frugivore with large eyes. Peak ~62 kHz. Low-intensity FM. Widespread in Neotropical lowlands. White dorsal stripe.

species.name: Mexican Long-tongued Bat
species.description: Nectar-feeding bat with elongated snout and long tongue. Very quiet FM calls, about 125 to 75 kHz on the 2nd harmonic. Seasonal migrant to southern AZ. Pollinates agave and columnar cacti. Low-intensity echolocation typical of phyllostomids.

species.name: Big-eared Woolly Bat
species.description: Carnivorous gleaner. Peak ~77 kHz, higher than predicted for body size. Short FM sweeps (0.8–1.4 ms). Low-intensity; hard to detect beyond a few meters.

species.name: Percival's Short-eared Trident Bat
species.description: Highest known bat echolocation frequency (~212 kHz). Southern and East Africa caves and mines. Tiny bat (3–5 g). Requires >400 kHz sample rate detectors.

species.name: Tail-less Roundleaf Bat
species.description: Tiny tail-less roundleaf bat. CF ~110–120 kHz. Mainland SE Asia and Sundaland. Unusual for foraging in open grass habitats rather than forest interior.

species.name: African Sheath-tailed Bat
species.description: East Africa coast, caves and rock shelters. Low-duty-cycle QCF calls peaking at ~33 kHz. Near Threatened. Colonial in coastal caves.

species.name: Wagner's Sac-winged Bat
species.description: Unusual: most energy in 5th harmonic (~68 kHz). Forest-interior forager. Multiharmonic calls with shallow FM sweeps.

species.name: Rafinesque's Big-eared Bat
species.description: Southeastern counterpart of Townsend's Big-eared Bat. Very quiet gleaning calls, sweeps ~45 to 22 kHz, characteristic frequency ~23–25 kHz, second harmonic sometimes louder. Roosts in abandoned buildings, hollow trees, and under bridges. White belly fur distinctive.

species.name: Townsend's Big-eared Bat
species.description: Enormous ears (~35 mm). Very quiet, short FM calls for gleaning moths from foliage. Characteristic frequency ~23–28 kHz, peak ~31–34 kHz. Highly sensitive to roost disturbance. Several subspecies are endangered.

species.name: Cinnamon Dog-faced Bat
species.description: Medium molossid. Alternating low-frequency QCF calls with peaks near 22 and 30 kHz (French Guiana). Open-space forager. Brazilian cerrado and Atlantic Forest edge.

species.name: Greenhall's Dog-faced Bat
species.description: Low frequency (~22 kHz) open-space forager. Flat-faced with forward-pointing nostrils. Roosts in buildings and hollow trees.

species.name: Mexican Dog-faced Bat
species.description: Small molossid endemic to western Mexico. Tropical dry forest and thorn scrub. Roosts in tree hollows and buildings, foraging above the canopy.

species.name: Southern Dog-faced Bat
species.description: Small to medium molossid. QCF at ~25 kHz. Flat face with forward-pointing nostrils. Open habitats across South American lowlands.

species.name: Lesser Short-nosed Fruit Bat
species.description: Produces primitive tongue-click echolocation for crude orientation but relies mainly on vision and smell. Common small fruit bat across SE Asia. Modifies palm fronds into tent roosts. Important pollinator.

species.name: Greater Short-nosed Fruit Bat
species.description: No echolocation; navigates by vision and smell. Tent-roosting in modified palm and screwpine leaves. Important pollinator and seed disperser across South and SE Asia.

species.name: Southern Yellow Bat
species.description: Medium-sized tree bat, characteristic frequency ~35–40 kHz. Roosts in dead palm fronds. Southern USA to South America. Formerly Lasiurus ega.

species.name: Pygmy Fruit-eating Bat
species.description: Small frugivore (formerly Artibeus phaeotis). Peak ~75 kHz. Low-intensity multiharmonic FM. Common in lowland forests.

species.name: Thomas's Fruit-eating Bat
species.description: Small frugivorous phyllostomid of lowland forests. Multi-harmonic FM. Roosts in modified leaves (tent-making). Southern Mexico to NW Colombia.

species.name: Common Vampire Bat
species.description: Short calls (about 2 ms). Peak about 57 to 61 kHz; the loudest harmonic varies. Obligate blood-feeder. Emits single pulses or groups of 2–3.

species.name: White-winged Vampire Bat
species.description: Feeds on bird blood. Peak ~70 kHz. White wing tips distinctive in flight. Low-intensity FM. Rarer than D. rotundus. Lowland forests.

species.name: Northern Ghost Bat
species.description: Large emballonurid with distinctive white fur. Narrowband QCF at ~24 kHz. Long inter-pulse intervals. Rarely encountered.

species.name: Hairy-legged Vampire Bat
species.description: Bird blood specialist (unlike the mammal-feeding D. rotundus). Peak ~80 kHz. Higher frequency than common vampire. Short multiharmonic FM. Low-intensity.

species.name: Cyclops Leaf-nosed Bat
species.description: Large hipposiderid of West and Central African forests. CF about 58 to 61 kHz in West Africa and about 51 kHz in Uganda. Formerly Hipposideros cyclops. Massive noseleaf. Gleans large insects from foliage.

species.name: Honduran White Bat
species.description: Tiny, iconic white tent-roosting bat. Peak ~75 kHz. Low-intensity FM. Endemic to Central America (Honduras to Panama). Frugivore specializing on one fig species.

species.name: Straw-coloured Fruit Bat
species.description: Most widespread African megabat. Massive colonies (up to 1 million). Important seed disperser. Uses vision and smell only.

species.name: Small Asian Sheath-tailed Bat
species.description: Small emballonurid of Indonesia, Philippines, and New Guinea. QCF calls ~45–55 kHz. Cave and rock-shelter roosting. Forages in forest understory.

species.name: Lesser Sheath-tailed Bat
species.description: Search calls sweep up, hold about 46 to 51 kHz, then sweep down, over 6 to 8 ms. Small sheath-tailed bat. Lowland forest of Sundaland (Malaysia, Indonesia, Brunei). Small groups on cave walls; forest interior forager.

species.name: Sheath-tailed bats
species.description: Quasi-constant-frequency calls; some species sweep 40–100 kHz

species.name: Velvety Fruit-eating Bat
species.description: Montane frugivore found from Mexico to Bolivia. Prefers cloud forest and premontane elevations. Quiet multi-harmonic FM calls. Distinctive velvety brown fur.

species.name: Cave Nectar Bat
species.description: No echolocation. Key pollinator of durian, banana, and petai in SE Asia. Cave-roosting; large colonies. Long tongue for probing flowers. India to the Philippines.

species.name: Gambian Epauletted Fruit Bat
species.description: No echolocation. Common fruit bat of West African savannas. Males have white shoulder epaulettes used in courtship displays. Loud honking calls. Important pollinator of baobab trees.

species.name: Wahlberg's Epauletted Fruit Bat
species.description: East and southern Africa savannas. Males produce loud honking display calls (audible). No echolocation. Common in gardens.

species.name: Franquet's Epauletted Fruit Bat
species.description: Central and West Africa tropical forests. Males produce repetitive metallic calls during display. Important pollinator and seed disperser.

species.name: Botta's Serotine
species.description: FM-QCF, peak ~30–35 kHz. Arid Middle Eastern and Central Asian habitats. Arabian Peninsula through Iran and Afghanistan. Rocky desert; buildings and rock crevices.

species.name: Brazilian Brown Bat
species.description: Peak about 41 to 45 kHz in Brazil, Trinidad and Ecuador, 37 kHz in Costa Rica. Source level ~101–106 dB SPL. Frequency decreases with temperature. FM-QCF structure.

species.name: Diminutive Serotine
species.description: Small Eptesicus of southern Brazil, Paraguay, Argentina. Peak ~50 kHz. FM-QCF. Forest edges and open areas.

species.name: Argentine Brown Bat
species.description: Lower frequency than E. brasiliensis (~43 kHz peak). More FM in cluttered habitats. FM-QCF structure.

species.name: Big Brown Bat
species.description: One of the best-studied bat species globally. Large vespertilionid. Peak ~30 kHz. FM-QCF. Open-space forager. Common in buildings.

species.name: Long-tailed House Bat
species.description: Southern Africa rocky areas. Peak ~30–35 kHz. Distinctive long free tail. Roosts in rock crevices.

species.name: Isabelline Serotine
species.description: FM-QCF, peak about 25 to 29 kHz. Pale sandy serotine of arid North Africa and the Middle East; recently separated from E. serotinus by molecular work. Open landscapes and towns.

species.name: Japanese Short-tailed Bat
species.description: FM-QCF calls similar to E. nilssonii. Endemic to Japan (Honshu, Shikoku, Kyushu). Forest-dwelling, roosts in tree hollows and buildings.

species.name: Northern Bat
species.description: The world's northernmost bat, found above the Arctic Circle. Tolerates cold climates. Common in Scandinavia and mountain regions of central Europe.

species.name: Northern Bat
species.description: FM-QCF calls, peak ~30.5 kHz, duration ~6 ms, bandwidth ~32 kHz. Hokkaido and northern Honshu. The most northerly-ranging bat in the world.

species.name: Serotine
species.description: Large bat with broad FM sweeps. One of the last to emerge, often foraging along tree lines and around street lights. Roosts almost exclusively in buildings.

species.name: Southern Right Whale
species.description: No echolocation. Slow, rotund baleen whale with distinctive callosities (rough skin patches colonised by cyamid whale lice). Produces low-frequency moans and up-calls for contact. Once hunted to near-extinction — the 'right' whale to hunt because it floated when dead. Sub-Antarctic; calves in sheltered bays.

species.name: Spotted Bat
species.description: Lowest echolocation frequency of any North American bat (~10–12 kHz), audible to humans. Unmistakable: three large white spots on black dorsal fur, enormous pink ears. Rare but widespread in western arid lands.

species.name: Black Bonneted Bat
species.description: Large molossid. Alternating calls that sweep down from about 32 to 36 kHz and end near 18 and 22 kHz. High, fast flight. Long-duration narrowband calls.

species.name: Peters' Mastiff Bat
species.description: Medium-sized bonneted bat. QCF at ~26–30 kHz. Open-area forager. Southern South America (Argentina, Uruguay, Brazil). Roosts in buildings.

species.name: Big Bonneted Bat
species.description: Very large molossid. Low-frequency QCF at ~18–20 kHz, sometimes audible. Open-space forager over savanna and cerrado. Northern Argentina to Colombia.

species.name: Florida Bonneted Bat
species.description: Federally endangered, restricted to southern Florida. Low-frequency QCF calls ~14–16 kHz. One of the rarest bats in North America. Roosts in tree cavities and bat houses. Occasionally audible to humans.

species.name: Wagner's Bonneted Bat
species.description: Among the lowest-frequency calling molossids (~22–25 kHz). Large bat with long, narrow wings. High-altitude open-space forager.

species.name: Sanborn's Bonneted Bat
species.description: Medium molossid. QCF at ~28–32 kHz. Amazonian and Atlantic Forest lowlands. Roosts in tree hollows. Uncommonly recorded.

species.name: Patagonian Bonneted Bat
species.description: Medium bonneted bat of the southern cone (Argentina, Paraguay, southern Brazil). QCF at ~28 kHz. Open and semi-open habitat forager. Roosts in buildings and tree hollows.

species.name: Western Mastiff Bat
species.description: Largest bat in North America (wingspan ~56 cm). Very low-frequency QCF calls ~10–12 kHz, easily audible to humans. Needs vertical drop to launch into flight. Roosts in tall cliff faces and buildings.

species.name: Trumbull's Bonneted Bat
species.description: Large bonneted bat of Central and South America. Very low-frequency QCF ~12–20 kHz, partially audible to humans. Fast high-altitude forager with long narrow wings.

species.name: Underwood's Bonneted Bat
species.description: Large molossid of arid and semiarid habitats from the southwestern US through western Mexico to Central America. Loud low-frequency calls, often audible to humans.

species.name: Eastern Falsistrelle
species.description: Large vesper bat of south-eastern forests. Roosts in tree hollows. Vulnerable (IUCN). Distinctive mid-range frequency calls.

species.name: Thumbless Bat
species.description: Tiny (3–5 g) insectivore with vestigial thumb. Very high frequency FM sweeps peaking ~130–150 kHz. One of the highest-frequency New World bats. Caves and mines.

species.name: Common Butterfly Bat
species.description: Central and East African forest bat with distinctive silvery reticulated wing pattern. FM calls ~40–50 kHz. Roosts in small groups under banana leaves and in buildings.

species.name: Variegated Butterfly Bat
species.description: Sub-Saharan Africa savanna and woodland. Broadband FM sweeps 70–30 kHz. Distinctive wing markings. Slow fluttery flight.

species.name: Long-finned Pilot Whale
species.description: Large, gregarious dolphin with a bulbous melon and sickle-shaped flippers. Echolocates with broadband clicks; also produces complex social calls and buzzes during deep squid-hunting dives. Found throughout sub-Antarctic waters in large, tightly bonded pods. Prone to mass strandings.

species.name: Commissaris's Long-tongued Bat
species.description: Similar call structure to G. soricina but slightly lower peak (~75 kHz). Nectarivore. Low-intensity multiharmonic FM.

species.name: Pallas's Long-tongued Bat
species.description: Nectarivore that uses echolocation to find flowers (some have evolved acoustic reflectors). Peak ~80 kHz. Multiharmonic FM. Low intensity.

species.name: Tricolored Big-eared Bat
species.description: Rare gleaning insectivore. Peak ~85 kHz. Very short broadband FM calls (0.3–1 ms). Ultra-low intensity.

species.name: Blanford's Bat
species.description: FM-QCF, peak ~32–40 kHz. Mainland SE Asia (Myanmar, Thailand, Vietnam). Open forest and over water. Poorly studied acoustically.

species.name: Roundleaf bats
species.description: CF calls; Cleotis percivalis reaches 212 kHz, the highest known bat frequency

species.name: Great Roundleaf Bat
species.description: Largest Hipposideros in Asia (~35 g). CF ~60–75 kHz. Widespread from India through China to SE Asia. Cave-roosting, often in large colonies. Doppler-shift compensation.

species.name: Dusky Leaf-nosed Bat
species.description: Very high-frequency CF calls, about 147 to 162 kHz in Australia and higher in India. Small hipposiderid of tropical woodlands and monsoon forests in northern Australia. Roosts in caves, mines, and tree hollows.

species.name: Bicolored Roundleaf Bat
species.description: Small roundleaf bat. High CF about 127 to 135 kHz in Malaysia and Borneo, and reported at about 147 to 161 kHz in South Asia. Species complex: a second group calling near 140 kHz occurs in Malaysia and Borneo too. Widespread from India to the Philippines. Caves and forest edge.

species.name: Sundevall's Roundleaf Bat
species.description: Most widespread African hipposiderid. High CF calls; frequency varies geographically. Caves, mines, buildings.

species.name: Diadem Roundleaf Bat
species.description: Large roundleaf bat with striking pale shoulder markings. CF varies by region: about 58 to 62 kHz in the Malay Peninsula, 64 to 69 kHz in Borneo and Java. Mainland SE Asia to Indonesia and the Philippines. Large cave colonies; long-distance forager.

species.name: Diadem Leaf-nosed Bat
species.description: Largest Australian hipposiderid with striking pale shoulder markings. CF ~58–63 kHz. Cave-roosting in tropical rainforest of far north Queensland. Long-distance forager.

species.name: Durgadas's Leaf-nosed Bat
species.description: CF ~163–176 kHz; among the highest-frequency bats in South Asia. Endemic to peninsular India cave systems. Poorly studied; IUCN Vulnerable.

species.name: Cantor's Roundleaf Bat
species.description: CF about 99 to 117 kHz in Indochina and Borneo, but about 81 to 92 kHz on the Thai-Malay Peninsula. Lowland forest from Indochina to Sundaland. Small caves and rock shelters.

species.name: Giant Roundleaf Bat
species.description: West and Central Africa forests. Largest hipposiderid; CF ~60–63 kHz. Caves near forest.

species.name: Indian Leaf-nosed Bat
species.description: CF about 73 to 84 kHz in India and about 69 to 71 kHz in Myanmar; low for a leaf-nosed bat because of its large size. Peninsular and north-east India, Sri Lanka, Bangladesh and Myanmar. Caves, tunnels, temples and old forts.

species.name: Intermediate Roundleaf Bat
species.description: Very common medium-sized roundleaf bat. CF ~77–98 kHz (cryptic species complex with two phonic types). Throughout SE Asia and southern China. Caves, gardens, and forest.

species.name: Pomona Roundleaf Bat
species.description: CF about 120 to 130 kHz (113 to 141 kHz in Vietnam). Southern India, southern China and mainland SE Asia; SE Asian bats are now often called H. gentilis. Small cave groups in dense forest.

species.name: Pratt's Leaf-nosed Bat
species.description: CF 2nd harmonic ~59–60 kHz; 1st harmonic ~29 kHz. Large species endemic to China. Cave-roosting in central and southern China (Hubei, Sichuan, Guizhou). Well-studied for auditory neuroscience.

species.name: Noack's Roundleaf Bat
species.description: West, Central and East Africa. CF about 128 to 148 kHz, varying by region, lineage and sex (females higher). Overlaps H. caffer slightly near 145 kHz. Cryptic species pair.

species.name: Schneider's Leaf-nosed Bat
species.description: CF about 125 to 139 kHz, varying by region. One of the most studied South Asian hipposiderids. Widespread across peninsular India and Sri Lanka; caves, temples, and old buildings.

species.name: Temminck's Leaf-nosed Bat
species.description: CF calls at ~77–84 kHz (about 82 kHz on Iriomote). Southern Ryukyu Islands (Ishigaki, Iriomote, Miyako). Roosts in limestone caves. Feeds mainly on beetles.

species.name: Striped Roundleaf Bat
species.description: East and southern Africa. Large species; low CF ~60 kHz for a hipposiderid. Caves and large rock overhangs.

species.name: Big-eared Brown Bat
species.description: Largest-eared Histiotus. Very low-frequency peak ~25 kHz. FM sweeps. Chile and western Argentina. Arid and semi-arid open habitats. Gleans insects from foliage.

species.name: Small Big-eared Brown Bat
species.description: Distinctive very large ears (Plecotus-like). Peak about 32 to 35 kHz. FM sweeps. Open habitats in southern South America (Patagonia to southern Brazil). Slow, maneuverable flight.

species.name: Tropical Big-eared Brown Bat
species.description: Large-eared vespertilionid. Peak ~32 kHz. FM sweeps. Brazilian cerrado and Atlantic Forest. Slightly higher frequency than H. montanus, consistent with smaller ears.

species.name: Leopard Seal
species.description: Not echolocation. Apex predator of the Antarctic pack ice. Males produce haunting, pulsing underwater trills and low-frequency broadcast calls during the breeding season — audible over great distances beneath the ice. Feeds on penguins, seals, krill, and fish. Solitary; sinuous and powerful.

species.name: Underwood's Long-tongued Bat
species.description: Very small nectarivore. High frequency calls (~90 kHz peak). Low-intensity FM. Found in montane forests.

species.name: Southern Bottlenose Whale
species.description: Deep-diving beaked whale of the circumpolar Southern Ocean. Produces frequency-modulated echolocation clicks during foraging dives exceeding 1,000 m. One of the most commonly sighted beaked whales in Antarctic waters. Bulbous forehead; males develop a pronounced melon with age.

species.name: Hammer-headed Fruit Bat
species.description: Central and West Africa forests. Largest African bat (wingspan to 90 cm). Males have enlarged larynx for loud lek-display calls. No echolocation.

species.name: Alashanian Pipistrelle
species.description: FM-QCF, peak ~34–37 kHz. Previously a subspecies of Savi’s Pipistrelle (H. savii). Northern and central China, Korea, Mongolia, Russia. Crevices and buildings.

species.name: Savi's Pipistrelle
species.description: Medium pipistrelle with shallow FM sweep ending in a quasi-constant-frequency tail around 32–34 kHz. Primarily Mediterranean; increasingly recorded as a vagrant in southern England.

species.name: Great Evening Bat
species.description: Low FM calls sweeping from ~40 kHz down to ~16 kHz, peak ~25 kHz, often with harmonics. One of the world’s largest vespertilionids (~60 g). Carnivorous aerial hawker preying on large moths and occasionally small birds. South and central China, extending into montane SE Asia.

species.name: Allen's Big-eared Bat
species.description: Short FM search calls sweeping from ~26–30 kHz down to ~12–14 kHz, often audible to humans; long trills at ~20–27 kHz are social calls. Large lappets projecting from base of ears. Southwestern pine and oak forests. Calls unlike any other NA Myotis-sized bat.

species.name: Damara Woolly Bat
species.description: East and southern Africa. Very high frequency, low-intensity FM calls (~90–118 kHz). Clutter specialist in dense vegetation. Difficult to detect.

species.name: Hardwicke's Woolly Bat
species.description: Very high-frequency FM, peak ~120–140 kHz. Tiny orange-furred bat foraging in dense forest understory. One of the highest-frequency vespertilionids. Sundaland; often roosts in pitcher plants.

species.name: Lesser Woolly Bat
species.description: Sub-Saharan Africa forests. Very high frequency broadband FM. Forest interior specialist. Similar to K. argentata but slightly different peak.

species.name: Clear-winged Woolly Bat
species.description: Very high-frequency FM, peak ~115–130 kHz. Partially transparent wing membranes. Lowland forest of Sundaland. Gleans insects from foliage.

species.name: Painted Bat
species.description: Steep broadband FM ~157–41 kHz; very low-intensity whisper echolocator. Striking orange-and-black wing membranes. South and SE Asian lowland forests. Roosts in dead bamboo and banana flowers.

species.name: Botswana Long-eared Bat
species.description: Central and southern Africa. Peak ~37 kHz. Broadband FM. Large ears suggest some gleaning behavior. Poorly known species.

species.name: Hourglass Dolphin
species.description: The only small dolphin found exclusively in cold Antarctic and sub-Antarctic waters. Named for its striking black-and-white hourglass flank pattern. Produces broadband echolocation clicks. One of the least-studied cetaceans due to its remote pelagic habitat; rarely approaches vessels.

species.name: Yellow-throated Big-eared Bat
species.description: Rare gleaning insectivore. Peak ~75 kHz. Low-intensity multiharmonic FM. Poorly documented acoustically.

species.name: Silver-haired Bat
species.description: Medium-sized bat with distinctive silver-tipped dark fur. Low-frequency QCF calls ~25–27 kHz characteristic frequency. Slow, maneuverable flight. Solitary tree-roosting migrant. One of the most frequently killed bats at wind turbines.

species.name: Desert Red Bat
species.description: Open-air forager. Maximum energy ~42 kHz. FM-QCF. Migratory. Roosts solitarily in foliage. Distinctive reddish fur.

species.name: Eastern Red Bat
species.description: Distinctive reddish fur. Solitary foliage-roosting tree bat. FM sweep with characteristic frequency ~40 kHz. Long-distance migrant. One of the most common bats in eastern North America.

species.name: Northern Yellow Bat
species.description: Large yellowish tree bat of the southeastern coastal plain. FM-QCF calls with characteristic frequency ~30 kHz. Roosts in dead palm fronds and Spanish moss.

species.name: Seminole Bat
species.description: Southeastern counterpart of the Eastern Red Bat with deep mahogany fur. FM sweep with characteristic frequency ~40 kHz. Roosts in Spanish moss and pine foliage.

species.name: South American Hoary Bat
species.description: Large vespertilionid, recently split from L. cinereus. Low-frequency FM-QCF at ~22–25 kHz. Long narrow wings for fast open-air flight. Migratory. Frosted fur.

species.name: Western Yellow Bat
species.description: Southwestern desert species. FM-QCF calls with characteristic frequency ~34 kHz. Roosts in palm fronds. Range expanding northward with ornamental palm plantings.

species.name: Weddell Seal
species.description: Not echolocation. Southernmost breeding mammal in the world. Produces an extraordinary repertoire of underwater sounds: eerie descending trills, chirps, and otherworldly whistles audible through the ice. Dives to 600+ m and maintains breathing holes by grinding ice with its teeth. Lives on fast ice year-round.

species.name: Mexican Long-nosed Bat
species.description: Federally endangered nectar bat. Migrates to Big Bend region of Texas in summer. Pollinates agave plants. Quiet FM calls ~75 kHz. Only known US roost in a single cave in the Chisos Mountains.

species.name: Lesser Long-nosed Bat
species.description: Nectar bat, major pollinator of saguaro and organ pipe cacti. Quiet FM calls sweeping from about 85 to 50 kHz. Migrates to southern AZ in summer. Formerly endangered, delisted in 2018 — a conservation success story.

species.name: Dark Long-tongued Bat
species.description: Rare nectarivore with elongated muzzle and long tongue. Very quiet FM calls. Lowland tropical forests from southern Mexico to Brazil. Poorly known ecology.

species.name: Southern Right Whale Dolphin
species.description: Slender, finless dolphin of the Southern Ocean — the only dolphin in the Southern Hemisphere lacking a dorsal fin. Jet black above, bright white below. Fast, graceful swimmer found in large schools. Produces broadband clicks for echolocation. Circumpolar in cool temperate to sub-Antarctic waters.

species.name: Goldman's Nectar Bat
species.description: Small nectarivore of Central American lowland forests. Broadband multi-harmonic FM calls. Visits Heliconia and other tubular flowers. Costa Rica to NW Ecuador.

species.name: Orange Nectar Bat
species.description: Largest Lonchophylla species. Distinctive orange fur. Broadband multi-harmonic FM calls. Nectarivore of premontane and montane forests. Nicaragua to NW Ecuador.

species.name: Thomas's Nectar Bat
species.description: Small nectarivore. Peak ~80 kHz. Low-intensity multiharmonic FM. Important pollinator of understory plants. Amazonian forests.

species.name: Tomes's Sword-nosed Bat
species.description: UNIQUE among phyllostomids: uses CF-FM calls like mormoopids. Long CF at ~45 kHz (3rd harmonic dominant). Longest calls of any phyllostomid (up to 8.7 ms).

species.name: Pygmy Round-eared Bat
species.description: Smallest Lophostoma. Gleaning insectivore in forest understory. Multi-harmonic FM. Roosts in termite nests and hollow trees. S. Mexico to S. Brazil.

species.name: White-throated Round-eared Bat
species.description: Large gleaning insectivore. Distinctive white throat patch. Roosts in termite nests, which it excavates. Multi-harmonic FM. Honduras to Bolivia.

species.name: Ghost Bat
species.description: Australia's only megadermatid and largest carnivorous bat. Very quiet, broadband FM calls (20–56 kHz). Hunts vertebrate prey including other bats, lizards, and frogs. Cave-roosting. Vulnerable (EPBC Act).

species.name: Long-legged Bat
species.description: Unusual phyllostomid: trawls insects from water surfaces. Louder than most phyllostomids (~101 dB SPL). Adjusts intensity by habitat openness. Peak ~85 kHz.

species.name: California Leaf-nosed Bat
species.description: Low-intensity gleaning calls (peak about 60 kHz), difficult to detect with bat detectors. Large ears and prominent nose leaf. Non-migratory desert species of AZ and southern CA. Cannot hibernate; relies on warm roost sites year-round.

species.name: Greater False Vampire Bat
species.description: Low-intensity multiharmonic FM calls (about 19 to 120 kHz). Large carnivorous bat preying on frogs, lizards, and other bats. Locates prey mainly by passive listening. South and mainland SE Asia; caves, ruins, and culverts.

species.name: Lesser False Vampire Bat
species.description: Low-intensity broadband FM calls. Smaller than M. lyra. Primarily insectivorous. Mainland SE Asia through Sundaland to the Philippines. Caves, hollow trees, and buildings.

species.name: False vampires
species.description: Low-intensity broadband FM; large carnivorous bats

species.name: Humpback Whale
species.description: No echolocation. Famous for complex, evolving songs lasting up to 30 minutes. Migrates from tropical breeding grounds to Antarctic feeding waters each summer, using bubble-net feeding to corral krill. Songs propagate hundreds of kilometres and shift culturally across populations.

species.name: MacConnell's Bat
species.description: Very small (5–7 g) with the highest peak frequency recorded among phyllostomids (~100–118 kHz). Ultra-low intensity. Tent-roosting frugivore.

species.name: Strap-toothed Whale
species.description: Remarkable beaked whale whose males grow long strap-like teeth that curl over the upper jaw, eventually preventing it from opening fully — yet they still catch squid using suction feeding. Produces FM echolocation clicks for deep-water prey detection. Circumpolar in southern temperate and sub-Antarctic seas.

species.name: East Coast Free-tailed Bat
species.description: QCF search calls at ~32–35 kHz. Small free-tailed bat of coastal eastern Australia from SE Queensland to southern NSW. Roosts in tree hollows and under bark. Vulnerable (EPBC Act).

species.name: Hairy Big-eared Bat
species.description: Lower peak frequency (~52 kHz) than M. microtis. Gleaning insectivore. Low-intensity multiharmonic FM. Documented from Costa Rica.

species.name: Common Big-eared Bat
species.description: Gleaning insectivore in dense understory. Can detect silent, motionless prey. Very short broadband calls (about 0.35 ms, peak near 80 kHz) that can reach 140 kHz. Ultra-low intensity.

species.name: Tiny Big-eared Bat
species.description: Very small gleaning insectivore. Broadband multi-harmonic FM, very quiet. Picks prey from foliage and surfaces. Forest-dependent. Honduras to Brazil.

species.name: Striped Hairy-nosed Bat
species.description: Gleaning insectivore. Peak ~75 kHz. Low-intensity multiharmonic FM. Now placed in genus Gardnerycteris by some authorities.

species.name: Bent-winged bats
species.description: FM-dominated calls; formerly classified within Vespertilionidae

species.name: African Long-fingered Bat
species.description: East African bent-winged bat. FM calls ~50–55 kHz. Cave-roosting; fast agile flight. Recently split from M. natalensis complex. Kenya, Tanzania, and adjacent regions.

species.name: Little Bent-winged Bat
species.description: High-frequency FM calls (57–64 kHz). Smaller than the Eastern Bent-winged Bat. Cave-roosting in eastern Australia from Cape York to northern NSW. Often found in mixed-species colonies with Miniopterus orianae.

species.name: Lesser Long-fingered Bat
species.description: Southern Africa. Peak about 60 to 66 kHz, about 12 kHz higher than M. natalensis. Smaller species. Cave-roosting.

species.name: Eastern Bent-wing Bat
species.description: FM sweep into a short shallow tail, end ~45–50 kHz, peak ~48–52 kHz. Fast agile flier. Cave-roosting, forms large maternity colonies. Widespread from Honshu to the Ryukyus.

species.name: Ryukyu Bent-wing Bat
species.description: FM calls slightly higher frequency than M. fuliginosus due to smaller body size. Ryukyu Islands and southern Kyushu. Cave-roosting.

species.name: Greater Long-fingered Bat
species.description: Central and East Africa. Larger species; lower peak ~52–55 kHz than M. natalensis. Caves in forested areas.

species.name: Greater Bent-wing Bat
species.description: FM sweeps, terminal frequency ~44–55 kHz. Largest Miniopterus in South and SE Asia. Large cave colonies. Fast agile flight. Previously misidentified as M. schreibersii.

species.name: Natal Long-fingered Bat
species.description: Southern and East Africa. Peak about 48 to 54 kHz, varying by region. Large cave colonies (thousands). FM-QCF hockey-stick calls. Key cave-roosting species.

species.name: Southern Bent-wing Bat
species.description: Critically Endangered (EPBC Act). Dependent on a single maternity cave. Population critically low.

species.name: Eastern Bent-wing Bat
species.description: Cave-roosting bat found along eastern Australia. Fast, agile flier.

species.name: Pale Bent-wing Bat
species.description: FM ~47–62 kHz, acoustically indistinguishable from M. schreibersii. Central Asian and Middle Eastern distribution (Kazakhstan, Uzbekistan, Iran, Afghanistan). Recently split from M. schreibersii. Large cave colonies; migratory.

species.name: Small Bent-wing Bat
species.description: FM calls, terminal frequency ~52–58 kHz (higher than M. magnater). Widespread in SE Asia. Often co-roosts with M. magnater in large limestone caves.

species.name: Common Bent-wing Bat
species.description: Fast, agile cave-dweller found across southern Europe. Long, narrow wings for sustained flight. Large colonies; sensitive to cave disturbance.

species.name: Free-tailed bats
species.description: Narrowband, long-duration QCF calls; 16–44 kHz peak typical

species.name: Rufous Dog-faced Bat
species.description: Small Amazonian molossid. QCF at ~40 kHz. Poorly known. Forest edge and gap forager.

species.name: Dwarf Dog-faced Bat
species.description: Small molossid that forages close to vegetation. Search calls sweep upward from about 43 to 54 kHz, unusual among molossids, with occasional downward calls. Open cerrado and forest edge forager.

species.name: Alvarez's Mastiff Bat
species.description: Recently described molossid from Mexico and Central America. Alternating QCF calls near 31 and 34 kHz, with a third tone near 37 kHz. Fast open-air forager. Similar to M. molossus but acoustically and genetically distinct.

species.name: Bonda Mastiff Bat
species.description: Similar to M. molossus but slightly lower frequency (~33 kHz). Open-space forager. Roosts in buildings.

species.name: Coiban Mastiff Bat
species.description: Similar to M. molossus (~35 kHz). Originally described from Coiba Island, Panama. Open-space forager.

species.name: Velvety Free-tailed Bat
species.description: Alternates between ~34.5 and ~39.6 kHz when foraging. Narrowband QCF. Common in buildings and urban areas. Open-space aerial hawker.

species.name: Black Mastiff Bat
species.description: Widespread Mesoamerican molossid, split from M. rufus (M. ater) in 2020. Alternating QCF calls peaking near 29 and 33 kHz. Roosts in buildings and tree hollows. Fast open-air forager.

species.name: Black Mastiff Bat
species.description: Large molossid. Alternating QCF calls: lower call peaking ~25–27 kHz, higher call ~29–31 kHz. Open-space forager. Formerly M. ater. Roosts in buildings and hollow trees.

species.name: Sinaloan Mastiff Bat
species.description: QCF at ~34 kHz in natural habitat; shifts up ~6 kHz in urban noise (Lombard effect). Open-space forager. Larger than M. molossus.

species.name: Angolan Free-tailed Bat
species.description: Sub-Saharan Africa savannas. Peak ~25–28 kHz. Roosts in buildings and tree hollows. Often in mixed colonies with Chaerephon pumilus.

species.name: Lappet-eared Free-tailed Bat
species.description: One of the largest Mops species. QCF calls ~22–26 kHz. West and Central African forests. Fast open-air forager above the canopy.

species.name: Midas Free-tailed Bat
species.description: Sub-Saharan Africa. Very low frequency QCF, peak ~13–16 kHz. Large molossid (40–60 g). Calls partially audible to humans. High, fast flight.

species.name: Malayan Free-tailed Bat
species.description: QCF ~22–28 kHz. Sundaland (Malaysia, Indonesia, Brunei, Singapore). Hollow trees and buildings. Forages high above canopy.

species.name: Little Free-tailed Bat
species.description: Small molossid widespread across sub-Saharan Africa. QCF at ~21–25 kHz. Roosts in buildings, roof spaces, and tree hollows. Common in urban areas. Geographic frequency variation noted.

species.name: Sulawesi Free-tailed Bat
species.description: Molossid endemic to Sulawesi and nearby islands. Low-frequency QCF at ~20–24 kHz. Roosts in caves and buildings. Fast open-air forager.

species.name: Ghost-faced bats
species.description: P. parnellii CF at ~63 kHz with FM sweep to ~54 kHz

species.name: Ghost-faced Bat
species.description: Bizarre facial leaf. Short calls (about 5 to 7 ms) with most energy in the 2nd harmonic: peak ~52 kHz, ending in a steep sweep to ~42 kHz. Cave-roosting; large colonies.

species.name: Reunion Free-tailed Bat
species.description: Endemic to Réunion Island in the Indian Ocean. QCF calls with most energy at about 31 to 51 kHz. One of only two bat species on Réunion. Roosts in buildings and lava tubes.

species.name: Round-eared Tube-nosed Bat
species.description: Very broadband FM, on average about 165 down to 62 kHz. Tubular nostrils; extreme-clutter specialist. Widespread across South and SE Asia in forests. Slow-flying gleaner; roosts in leaves and dead fronds.

species.name: Hilgendorf's Tube-nosed Bat
species.description: Very short broadband FM sweeps from ~105–125 kHz down to ~27–44 kHz, peak ~50–55 kHz. Forest gleaner. Throughout Japan (Hokkaido to Kyushu). Roosts in tree hollows and dead curled leaves.

species.name: Greater Tube-nosed Bat
species.description: Broadband FM, peak ~45–68 kHz. Forest gleaner. Widespread in northern and central China, Korea, Russia, and Japan. Tree hollows and bark.

species.name: Ryukyu Tube-nosed Bat
species.description: Broadband FM calls typical of Murina. Endemic to the Ryukyu Islands. Recently described species from Okinawa. Forest-dwelling.

species.name: Ognev's Tube-nosed Bat
species.description: Broadband FM calls typical of Murina. Distribution spans ~2000 km north–south across the Japanese archipelago. Forest bat roosting in dead curled leaves.

species.name: Gloomy Tube-nosed Bat
species.description: FM calls presumed similar to other Murina. Known only from a single holotype on Tsushima Island (1962). Possibly extinct. Alliance for Zero Extinction species.

species.name: Ussuri Tube-nosed Bat
species.description: Very short broadband FM sweeps from ~90–135 kHz down to ~42–55 kHz. Peak higher than M. hilgendorfi: ~62–65 kHz in Kyushu and Shikoku, ~86 kHz in Hokkaido. Tiny bat (4–8 g). Remarkably hibernates under snow. Roosts in curled dead leaves. Hokkaido and Honshu.

species.name: Silver-tipped Myotis
species.description: Common South American Myotis. Peak about 64 to 80 kHz in South American recordings, 42 to 52 kHz in Panama. FM sweeps. Silver-tipped dorsal fur distinctive. Forages over water and in forest clearings.

species.name: Alcathoe Bat
species.description: Tiny Myotis first described in 2001, confirmed breeding in the UK in 2010. FM calls sweep from ~100 kHz down to ~40 kHz with peak energy around 50–55 kHz. Closely resembles whiskered and Brandt's bats but smaller with shorter ears.

species.name: Southeastern Myotis
species.description: Southeastern US cave bat, often found near water. FM sweep with characteristic frequency ~44–45 kHz. Forms large maternity colonies in caves, sometimes with thousands of individuals.

species.name: Bechstein's Bat
species.description: Rare woodland specialist with very quiet, broadband calls. Indicator species for old-growth forest. Roosts in tree holes; rarely found in buildings.

species.name: Lesser Mouse-eared Bat
species.description: Steep FM sweep from about 100 to 120 kHz down to about 25 kHz, very similar to M. myotis. Widespread from Europe through Turkey, the Levant, Iran, and Central Asia. Key cave bat of the Middle East.

species.name: Rufous Myotis
species.description: Sub-Saharan African Myotis with reddish-brown fur. FM sweeps. Forages over water and along forest edges. Also called Bocage's Mouse-eared Bat.

species.name: Far Eastern Natterer's Bat
species.description: Very broadband FM calls from ~70–135 kHz down to ~20–30 kHz, peak ~36–57 kHz. Gleaning insectivore, hawks near vegetation. Forests of Kyushu and other regions.

species.name: Brandt's Bat
species.description: Closely related to whiskered bat; prefers mature woodland. Slightly lower frequency calls. Identified reliably only by dentition or genetics.

species.name: California Myotis
species.description: Small western Myotis, highly adaptable. FM sweep with characteristic frequency ~50 kHz. Difficult to distinguish acoustically from Western Small-footed Myotis. Often the most common bat at western sites.

species.name: Long-fingered Bat
species.description: Trawling bat of Mediterranean rivers and lakes. Long toes and large feet for gaffing prey from water surfaces. FM sweep ~90–38 kHz. Vulnerable across its range due to water pollution and cave disturbance.

species.name: Chilean Myotis
species.description: Southern South American Myotis (Chile, Argentina, Patagonia). Short calls (about 2 to 4 ms) sweeping down from about 89 kHz to 39 to 43 kHz, peak about 47 kHz. One of the southernmost-ranging bats in the Americas.

species.name: Large Myotis
species.description: Broadband FM ~98–28 kHz, ending as low as ~14 kHz in Beijing, peak ~38–54 kHz. Largest Myotis in China (forearm ~65–70 mm). Cave-roosting, large maternity colonies in southern and central China.

species.name: Western Small-footed Myotis
species.description: Tiny bat (~5 g) of western arid lands. FM sweep with characteristic frequency ~44 kHz. Calls nearly identical to California Myotis. Roosts in rock crevices, cliff faces, and badlands.

species.name: Cryptic Myotis
species.description: Split from M. nattereri in 2019. Iberian Peninsula and SW France. Broadband FM calls very similar to Natterer's bat; separated by genetics and subtle morphology.

species.name: Pond Bat
species.description: Larger relative of Daubenton's bat. Trawls over broad lakes and slow rivers. Vulnerable across most of its range in NW Europe.

species.name: Daubenton's Bat
species.description: Forages low over calm water, trawling insects from the surface. Steep FM sweeps. Often seen along canals and rivers at dusk.

species.name: David's Myotis
species.description: FM sweeps from ~80–110 kHz down to ~27–35 kHz, peak ~42–55 kHz with geographic variation. Endemic to China. Forest bat. Well-studied for genome analysis of bat-specific adaptations.

species.name: Elegant Myotis
species.description: High-frequency calls typical of small Myotis. Peak ~55 kHz. Difficult to distinguish from M. nigricans acoustically.

species.name: Geoffroy's Bat
species.description: Short, steep FM sweep from about 110 to 140 kHz down to about 35 to 38 kHz. Distinctive notched ear margin. Gleaner specialist. Europe across Turkey, the Levant, Iran, and into Central Asia. Cave-roosting.

species.name: Escalera's Bat
species.description: Iberian endemic from the Natterer's bat complex. Broadband FM gleaners. Distinguished from M. nattereri and M. crypticus by genetics; morphological differences subtle.

species.name: Long-eared Myotis
species.description: Very quiet, short FM calls typical of a gleaning forager. Characteristic frequency ~34 kHz. Large ears extend well beyond nose when laid forward. Western forests and woodlands.

species.name: Fringed Long-footed Myotis
species.description: East Asian Myotis found in China, Japan, and Vietnam. FM sweeps. Trawling forager over rivers and lakes. Large feet for gaffing prey from water surfaces.

species.name: Hodgson's Bat
species.description: Steep downward FM calls ~110–30 kHz, peak ~44–50 kHz. Distinctive orange-brown coloring. Tsushima Island and western Japan. Forest-dwelling insectivore. Korean and Tsushima bats are now often placed in M. rufoniger.

species.name: Fraternal Bat
species.description: Brief FM pulses ~110–50 kHz, duration ~3.5 ms. Edge-space forager. Honshu and Kyushu in forested areas near cliffs and caves.

species.name: Gracile Myotis
species.description: FM calls typical of small Myotis. Endemic to Japan (Honshu). Forest-dwelling. Limited published acoustic data.

species.name: Gray Myotis
species.description: Largest eastern Myotis. FM sweep ~80–42 kHz, characteristic frequency ~46 kHz. Obligate cave bat year-round. Federally endangered but populations recovering.

species.name: Lesser Large-footed Myotis
species.description: FM, peak ~50–60 kHz. Large-footed trawling bat capturing prey from water surfaces. Sundaland and mainland SE Asia; almost always near still or slow-moving water.

species.name: Horsfield's Myotis
species.description: Broadband FM, peak about 54 to 65 kHz. Trawling insectivore catching prey from water surfaces using large hind feet. Widespread across South and SE Asia in forested lowlands near streams.

species.name: Hosono's Myotis
species.description: FM calls typical of Myotis. Endemic to Japan (Honshu). Cave-dwelling. Poorly studied.

species.name: Ikonnikov's Bat
species.description: Steep FM sweeps, start ~90–120 kHz, end ~38–44 kHz, peak ~50–57 kHz, duration ~2–3 ms. Small forest bat. Hokkaido and northern Honshu.

species.name: Hairy-legged Myotis
species.description: High variable repetition rates (15–20 calls/s). Short, high-intensity calls (~2.5 ms). Peak ~55 kHz. Recorded from colonies in Costa Rica.

species.name: Keen's Myotis
species.description: Rare Pacific Northwest endemic restricted to temperate rainforests from SE Alaska to Washington. Broad FM sweep. Roosts in tree and rock crevices.

species.name: LaVal's Myotis
species.description: Small Myotis endemic to eastern Brazil (Cerrado, Caatinga). Peak ~52 kHz. Steep FM sweeps. Recently described. Associated with rock outcrops.

species.name: Eastern Small-footed Myotis
species.description: One of North America's smallest bats (~5 g). FM sweep with characteristic frequency ~50–55 kHz. Roosts in rock crevices and talus slopes. Appears somewhat resistant to White-nose Syndrome.

species.name: Yellowish Myotis
species.description: South American Myotis. Peak ~46 kHz. FM sweeps. Southern Brazil, Uruguay, Argentina. Open areas and forest edges.

species.name: Little Brown Myotis
species.description: Historically North America's most common bat, now severely impacted by White-nose Syndrome. FM sweep ~80–40 kHz, characteristic frequency ~40 kHz. Forages over water and forest edges.

species.name: Large-footed Bat
species.description: Steep FM sweeps ~80–35 kHz, peak ~49–52 kHz. Trawling insectivore, hunts over water using large feet to gaff prey. Rivers and streams throughout Japan.

species.name: Large-footed Myotis
species.description: Australia's only fishing bat. Trawls water surfaces with large feet. Found near rivers, lakes, and dams. Very quiet calls.

species.name: Burmese Whiskered Bat
species.description: Broadband FM sweeps, peak ~40–55 kHz. Southern Western Ghats and northeastern India. Clutter-adapted gleaning forager of forested hill slopes.

species.name: Wall-roosting Myotis
species.description: Broadband FM, peak about 55 to 82 kHz. Very widespread and commonly recorded in SE Asia. Roosts in rolled leaves and on vertical surfaces. Forest understory and edge forager.

species.name: Greater Mouse-eared Bat
species.description: One of Europe's largest vespertilionids. Ground-gleaning specialist hunting beetles in short grass and forest floors. Large nursery colonies in roofs and caves.

species.name: Whiskered Bat
species.description: Small Myotis often found in villages and woodland edges. Very similar in call and appearance to Brandt's bat; confirmed by handling or genetics.

species.name: Natterer's Bat
species.description: Very broadband FM calls with prominent harmonics. Gleaning specialist, picks prey from foliage and walls. Roosts in old buildings and tree holes.

species.name: Black Myotis
species.description: Highly plastic call structure. Narrowband ~7 ms in open space; adds broadband FM in clutter. Convergent with European pipistrelles. Peak ~54 to 55 kHz.

species.name: Montane Myotis
species.description: High-altitude Andean Myotis (1500–3800 m). Peak ~50 kHz. FM sweeps. Cloud forests and paramo edges. Colombia to Bolivia.

species.name: Ozensis Myotis
species.description: FM calls typical of Myotis. Endemic to Japan (central Honshu mountains). Cave-dwelling. Limited distribution.

species.name: Northern Hairy-legged Myotis
species.description: Small Myotis of Mexico and Central America, recently split from M. keaysi. Steep FM sweeps from ~90–110 kHz to a tail near 59 kHz (most energy 59–63 kHz). Forest and forest-edge forager. Characteristic hairy tibia.

species.name: Rickett's Big-footed Bat
species.description: FM ~70–28 kHz (start up to ~84, end down to ~23), peak ~37–41 kHz. East Asia’s only confirmed piscivorous bat; trawls rivers using large feet. Endemic to China, also recorded in Korea. Cave roosts near rivers.

species.name: Frosted Myotis
species.description: FM sweeps typical of Myotis. Endemic to Japan (Honshu, Shikoku, Kyushu). Forest-dwelling, roosts in tree hollows and buildings. Named for frosted fur.

species.name: Maghreb Mouse-eared Bat
species.description: Large Myotis of North Africa and Mediterranean islands (Corsica, Sardinia, Malta). Formerly a subspecies of M. myotis. Ground-gleaning beetle specialist.

species.name: Riparian Myotis
species.description: Steep FM sweep from about 100 kHz to about 60 kHz, ending in a short flatter part. Calls about 4 to 5 ms. No harmonics observed. Recorded in Costa Rica.

species.name: Northern Long-eared Myotis
species.description: Steep broadband FM sweeps, short duration. Characteristic frequency ~43 kHz. Gleaning forager in forest understory. Federally endangered due to White-nose Syndrome.

species.name: Indiana Bat
species.description: Calls very similar to Little Brown Myotis; characteristic frequency ~41 kHz. Hibernates in dense clusters in limestone caves. Federally endangered.

species.name: Fringed Myotis
species.description: Named for the fringe of stiff hairs along the tail membrane. Steep FM sweep with characteristic frequency ~21–26 kHz. Roosts in caves, mines, and buildings in western mountains.

species.name: Temminck's Myotis
species.description: Southern and East Africa. Broadband FM sweep. Peak ~48 kHz. Caves and mines. Distinctive tricolored fur.

species.name: Cave Myotis
species.description: Large Myotis of the south-central US and Mexico. FM sweep with characteristic frequency ~42 kHz. Forms large cave colonies. Bare patches on back between shoulder blades diagnostic.

species.name: Long-legged Myotis
species.description: Western species found in coniferous forests. FM sweep with characteristic frequency ~40 kHz. Keeled calcar and furred underwing membrane diagnostic. Fast, direct flight.

species.name: Welwitsch's Myotis
species.description: Sub-Saharan Africa woodlands. Lower peak ~34 kHz than M. tricolor. Short broadband FM calls. Roosts in foliage.

species.name: Yanbaru Whiskered Bat
species.description: FM calls above 40 kHz. Endemic to northern Okinawa (Yanbaru forest). Described in 1997. One of the rarest bats in Japan.

species.name: Yuma Myotis
species.description: Western water-foraging specialist. FM sweep with characteristic frequency ~50 kHz. Trawls insects from water surfaces with large feet. Common near rivers and lakes.

species.name: Brazilian Funnel-eared Bat
species.description: Very high frequency echolocator, peak ~100–120 kHz. Extremely low intensity. Cave-roosting. Endemic to eastern Brazil (Cerrado/Caatinga). IUCN Vulnerable.

species.name: Mexican Funnel-eared Bat
species.description: Among the highest frequency echolocating bats. Peak ~100–130 kHz (2nd harmonic). Very low intensity; barely detectable beyond 50 cm. Cave-roosting.

species.name: Trinidadian Funnel-eared Bat
species.description: Very high frequency FM, peak ~100–130 kHz. Cave-roosting. Northern South America (Venezuela, Colombia, Trinidad). Low-intensity calls barely detectable beyond 1 m.

species.name: Cape Serotine
species.description: Ubiquitous across southern Africa. Peak ~38 kHz. Hockey-stick FM-QCF calls. Roosts in buildings. One of the most frequently recorded species.

species.name: Lesser Bulldog Bat
species.description: Smaller than N. leporinus with higher calls: a CF part at about 70 to 75 kHz, then an FM sweep down to about 40 to 45 kHz. Trawls insects from water surfaces.

species.name: Greater Bulldog Bat
species.description: Large fishing bat. Long CF component at 53–56 kHz followed by FM sweep. Forages over water; one of few New World bats with long CF calls.

species.name: Japanese Noctule
species.description: FM-QCF calls, peak ~19–21 kHz, search calls ~16–21 ms long. Japan's largest open-space insectivorous bat. Forages up to 300 m altitude. Occasionally preys on migrating birds. Roosts in tree cavities.

species.name: Greater Noctule
species.description: Europe's largest bat. Occasionally catches small birds in flight during nocturnal migration. Very low-frequency calls. Rare across its range.

species.name: Leisler's Bat
species.description: Smaller noctule with slightly higher frequency calls. Fast open-air forager. Migratory in parts of its range. Common in Ireland.

species.name: Common Noctule
species.description: Large, fast-flying bat. Loud, narrowband calls audible on bat detectors at distance. Roosts in tree holes; one of the first species to emerge at dusk.

species.name: Chinese Noctule
species.description: FM-QCF, peak ~25 kHz in open space; short close-range calls sweep from ~60–80 kHz down to ~23 kHz. Fast high-altitude aerial forager. Endemic to China and Taiwan. Tree hollows. Closely related to N. aviator and N. noctula.

species.name: Slit-faced bats
species.description: Low-intensity, multi-harmonic FM calls emitted through nostrils

species.name: Large Slit-faced Bat
species.description: Central and West Africa forests. Largest nycterid. Very low intensity broadband FM. Hunts vertebrate prey (fish, frogs, smaller bats).

species.name: Large-eared Slit-faced Bat
species.description: West and Central Africa forests. Low-intensity broadband FM similar to N. thebaica but larger. Gleaner in forest understory.

species.name: Egyptian Slit-faced Bat
species.description: Most widespread African nycterid. Very low intensity broadband FM calls (“whispering bat”). Gleaner; uses passive listening. Very difficult to detect on bat detectors.

species.name: Schlieffen's Twilight Bat
species.description: Sub-Saharan Africa savannas. Peak ~42 kHz. Often one of the first bats to emerge at dusk. Roosts in buildings and tree bark.

species.name: Evening Bat
species.description: Medium-sized bat of the eastern US. FM-QCF calls with characteristic frequency ~38 kHz. Resembles Big Brown Bat but smaller. Roosts in tree cavities and buildings. Does not use caves.

species.name: Queensland Tube-nosed Fruit Bat
species.description: No echolocation. Small fruit bat of NE Australian rainforests. Distinctive tubular nostrils and spotted wings. Solitary roosting in dense foliage. Feeds on figs and other fruit.

species.name: Pocketed Free-tailed Bat
species.description: Medium-sized free-tailed bat of the southwestern deserts. QCF calls ~22 kHz characteristic frequency. Named for the pocket-like fold on the tail membrane. Roosts in rock crevices.

species.name: Broad-eared Free-tailed Bat
species.description: Three-frequency alternation pattern (~26.7, 28.7, 32.4 kHz). Downward-modulated QCF. Open-space forager.

species.name: Big Free-tailed Bat
species.description: Large molossid with low QCF calls: peak frequency about 20–22 kHz, sweeping down to about 14–18 kHz, often audible. Roosts in high cliff crevices. Southwestern US. Loud, piercing social calls can be heard from considerable distance.

species.name: Northern Long-eared Bat
species.description: Very quiet broadband FM gleaning calls, similar to other Nyctophilus. Found in tropical woodlands and monsoon forests of northern Australia (Arnhem Land, Kimberley, Cape York).

species.name: South-eastern Long-eared Bat
species.description: Vulnerable (EPBC Act). Extremely rare; restricted to northwest woodlands.

species.name: Lesser Long-eared Bat
species.description: Australia's most widespread bat. Very quiet, broadband FM calls; often difficult to detect acoustically. Gleaning insectivore with large ears.

species.name: Gould's Long-eared Bat
species.description: Common in forests of eastern Australia. Very quiet calls, similar to Lesser Long-eared Bat. Distinguished by larger size and habitat preference.

species.name: Greater Long-eared Bat
species.description: Formerly N. timoriensis. Restricted to drier woodlands. Very quiet gleaning calls. Vulnerable.

species.name: Pygmy Long-eared Bat
species.description: Very quiet broadband FM calls. Australia's smallest long-eared bat (~4 g). Found in sandstone escarpments and monsoon forests of the Top End and Kimberley. Gleaning insectivore.

species.name: Orca
species.description: Apex predator of the Southern Ocean. Produces broadband echolocation clicks (peak ~20 kHz, energy to 80+ kHz) plus complex pulsed calls and whistles for communication. Antarctic populations include fish-eating Type C, mammal-hunting Type A, and pack-ice specialist Type B. Highly social; pods use distinct vocal dialects.

species.name: Javan Mastiff Bat
species.description: Very large molossid with long ears. Very low QCF ~12–16 kHz. Rare; primarily Java and Borneo. High-altitude open-air forager.

species.name: Harrison's Giant Mastiff Bat
species.description: Large free-tailed bat recently split from O. martiensseni. East Africa and Arabian Peninsula. Very low QCF calls, often audible to humans. Cave and building rooster.

species.name: Large-eared Free-tailed Bat
species.description: East and southern Africa. Very low frequency calls (~11–14 kHz), audible to humans. Very large molossid. Caves and buildings. Individual call signatures documented.

species.name: Wroughton's Free-tailed Bat
species.description: Very low frequency QCF ~14–17 kHz; among the lowest of any bat. Rare; known from a few cave sites in peninsular India (Karnataka, Goa) and Meghalaya, and recorded acoustically in Sri Lanka. IUCN Data Deficient.

species.name: Desert Long-eared Bat
species.description: Short broadband FM sweeps with a strong second harmonic, peak about 23 to 27 kHz. Calls quietly when gleaning, so often missed on detectors, but can call loudly when hawking insects. Scorpion predator that also listens for prey. Enormous ears (38–45 mm). Sahara through Arabia to Central Asia.

species.name: Northern Free-tailed Bat
species.description: Shallow FM calls at about 24 to 28 kHz. Largest Ozimops species. Formerly Mormopterus beccarii (in part). Widespread across tropical and subtropical northern Australia. Tree-hollow roosting.

species.name: Southern Free-tailed Bat
species.description: Small free-tailed bat of south-eastern Australia. Roosts in tree hollows and buildings. Rapid, direct flight.

species.name: Ride's Free-tailed Bat
species.description: Widespread across eastern Australian coasts. Similar to Southern Free-tailed Bat but slightly higher frequency calls.

species.name: Canyon Bat
species.description: Smallest bat in North America (~3.5 g), formerly called Western Pipistrelle. FM sweep with characteristic frequency ~46 kHz (peak ~47–48 kHz). Common in desert canyons and rock outcrops. Often the first bat seen at dusk.

species.name: Tricolored Bat
species.description: Tiny bat (~6 g) formerly called Eastern Pipistrelle. FM sweep with characteristic frequency ~42–43 kHz. Distinctive tricolored fur bands. Severely affected by White-nose Syndrome; proposed for ESA listing.

species.name: Greater Dog-like Bat
species.description: Lower frequency (~32 kHz) than P. macrotis, consistent with larger body size. Open-space forager. Most energy in 2nd harmonic.

species.name: White-winged Dog-like Bat
species.description: Distinctive white wing membrane patches. QCF at ~42 kHz. Amazonian lowland forests.

species.name: Lesser Dog-like Bat
species.description: Multiharmonic QCF with most energy in 2nd harmonic at ~40 kHz. Higher frequency than P. kappleri.

species.name: Trinidad Dog-like Bat
species.description: Northern South America. QCF at ~43 kHz. Open-area forager near rock shelters and caves.

species.name: Spectacled Porpoise
species.description: Elusive sub-Antarctic porpoise with distinctive dark eye patches. Uses narrow-band high-frequency (NBHF) clicks around 128–130 kHz — a stealth sonar strategy thought to evade orca predation, as orcas hear poorly above ~100 kHz. Rarely seen alive; mostly known from strandings on Tierra del Fuego and the Falklands.

species.name: Golden-tipped Bat
species.description: Extremely broadband FM calls (60–155 kHz) for detecting stationary prey. Specialist predator of orb-weaving spiders. Roosts in abandoned bird nests. Rare along eastern Australia from Cape York to southern NSW.

species.name: Pale-faced Bat
species.description: Large omnivorous phyllostomid. Peak ~55 kHz. Low-intensity FM. Pale face distinctive. Roosts in hollow trees. Amazonian forests.

species.name: Leaf-nosed bats
species.description: Low-intensity "whispering" bats; multi-harmonic FM calls

species.name: Pale Spear-nosed Bat
species.description: Omnivore with lower frequency than most phyllostomids (~55 kHz peak). Best hearing sensitivity at 20 kHz. Low-intensity whispering calls.

species.name: Greater Spear-nosed Bat
species.description: Large omnivore. One of the lowest-frequency phyllostomids (~47 kHz peak). Multiharmonic FM. Forms harem groups in caves and hollow trees.

species.name: Sperm Whale
species.description: The loudest animal on Earth — produces echolocation clicks exceeding 230 dB re 1µPa. The enormous spermaceti organ acts as an acoustic lens, focusing powerful, directional clicks for hunting giant squid at depths beyond 1,000 m. Also produces codas: rhythmic click patterns used for social communication between matrilineal clans. Males range into Antarctic waters seasonally.

species.name: Japanese Pipistrelle
species.description: FM sweep into a long shallow tail ending near 41–45 kHz, peak ~45–48 kHz. Japan's most common urban bat. Roosts in buildings and under bridges. Forages around streetlights.

species.name: Mount Gargues Pipistrelle
species.description: Rare pipistrelle from montane forests of Cameroon. FM calls ~45–50 kHz. Known from very few specimens. Highland forest specialist.

species.name: Kelaart's Pipistrelle
species.description: FM-QCF, peak ~36–38 kHz. One of the most commonly detected bat species acoustically in South Asian surveys. Widespread across the Indian subcontinent and Sri Lanka. Water and forest edges.

species.name: Indian Pipistrelle
species.description: FM-QCF, end frequency ~40–42 kHz. Very common and widespread across South Asia. Closely associated with human settlements. Often the first bat to emerge at dusk.

species.name: Desert Pipistrelle
species.description: FM-QCF, peak ~44–48 kHz. Small pale pipistrelle of Saharan and Arabian desert margins. Separated from P. kuhlii by slightly higher frequency. Egypt, Israel, Jordan, Saudi Arabia, Yemen.

species.name: Endo's Pipistrelle
species.description: FM-QCF calls similar to P. abramus but slightly lower frequency. Endemic to Japan (Honshu). Temperate forests at 100–1500 m. IUCN Near Threatened.

species.name: Hanak's Pipistrelle
species.description: Endemic to Crete and possibly nearby Greek islands. Characteristic frequency ~47–48 kHz, intermediate between common and soprano pipistrelles. Recently described cryptic species.

species.name: Dusky Pipistrelle
species.description: Sub-Saharan Africa. Peak ~45–48 kHz. Small bat frequently detected around human habitation and streetlights.

species.name: Javan Pipistrelle
species.description: FM-QCF, peak ~50–55 kHz. Common urban pipistrelle. South Asia through mainland SE Asia to the Greater Sundas. Buildings; gardens, parks, and agricultural areas.

species.name: Kuhl's Pipistrelle
species.description: Expanding northward across Europe. Characteristic frequency ~40 kHz. Common around buildings and street lights in Mediterranean regions.

species.name: Madeira Pipistrelle
species.description: Macaronesian island endemic found on Madeira, Canary Islands, and Azores. Characteristic frequency ~43 kHz. Forages around street lights and vegetation edges.

species.name: Nathusius' Pipistrelle
species.description: Long-distance migrant; travels up to 2,000 km. Characteristic frequency ~38 kHz. Favours wetlands and riparian woodland.

species.name: Common Pipistrelle
species.description: Europe's most abundant bat. Characteristic frequency ~45 kHz separates it from soprano pipistrelle. Roosts in buildings; forages along edges and over water.

species.name: Soprano Pipistrelle
species.description: Cryptic species split from common pipistrelle in 1999. Characteristic frequency ~55 kHz. Strongly associated with riparian habitats.

species.name: Rüppell's Pipistrelle
species.description: North Africa, Sahel, East Africa, Middle East. Calls end at about 46 to 48 kHz in much of Africa but higher, about 49 to 57 kHz, in Israel and Morocco. Associated with arid habitats and waterways.

species.name: Rusty Pipistrelle
species.description: Small pipistrelle of southern and eastern African woodlands and savannas. FM-QCF calls ending at about 53 to 57 kHz, peak about 56 to 62 kHz. Roosts in tree hollows and buildings.

species.name: Sturdee's Pipistrelle
species.description: Presumed FM-QCF calls. Known only from a specimen on the Bonin Islands (Ogasawara). Not seen since 1915—possibly extinct.

species.name: Northern Pipistrelle
species.description: FM calls peaking ~45–50 kHz. One of Australia's smallest bats (~3 g). Found along northern coasts from WA through NT to Queensland. Roosts in mangroves, tree hollows, and buildings.

species.name: Heller's Broad-nosed Bat
species.description: Small frugivore. Peak ~68 kHz. Low-intensity FM. Widespread in Neotropical lowland forests. Important seed disperser.

species.name: White-lined Broad-nosed Bat
species.description: Common frugivore of open habitats and forest edges. Peak ~62 kHz. Prominent white facial and dorsal stripes. Low-intensity FM. Cerrado and Atlantic Forest.

species.name: Brown Long-eared Bat
species.description: Iconic enormous ears. Very quiet, broadband calls; often called a "whispering bat". Gleaning specialist in woodland. Roosts in buildings and tree holes.

species.name: Grey Long-eared Bat
species.description: Prefers warmer lowland areas. Quieter and slightly lower frequency than brown long-eared. Difficult to distinguish visually; confirmed by tragus shape.

species.name: Christie's Long-eared Bat
species.description: Very quiet broadband FM, similar to other Plecotus. Gleaning specialist replacing P. auritus in arid Middle Eastern and North African habitats. Ruins and rock crevices in desert environments.

species.name: Kolombatovic's Long-eared Bat
species.description: Mediterranean long-eared bat found along the Adriatic coast and eastern Mediterranean. Very quiet broadband FM calls. Gleaning insectivore.

species.name: Alpine Long-eared Bat
species.description: Montane species of the Alps, Pyrenees, and mountains of the eastern Mediterranean. Broadband FM calls, very quiet. Roosts in buildings and rock crevices at altitude.

species.name: Ognev's Long-eared Bat
species.description: Eastern European and Caucasus long-eared bat. Very quiet broadband FM, similar to other Plecotus. Forests and rocky habitats in mountainous terrain.

species.name: Japanese Long-eared Bat
species.description: Low-intensity FM calls, start ~46 kHz, peak ~41 kHz, end ~23 kHz. Gleaning forager specialising in fluttering moths. Endemic to Japan (Honshu, Hokkaido, Shikoku, Kyushu).

species.name: Big-crested Mastiff Bat
species.description: Distinctive upward-modulated calls (unusual for molossids). Alternating pulse pairs at ~30 and ~35 kHz. Most energy in 1st harmonic. Easily recognizable.

species.name: Brown Mastiff Bat
species.description: Long, nearly flat search calls rising slightly from about 33 to 35 kHz, with occasional higher calls sweeping down from about 44 to 47 kHz. Higher than P. centralis. Open-space forager. South American drylands and forest edges.

species.name: Davy's Naked-backed Bat
species.description: CF-FM with short CF at ~68 kHz, a sweep down, then a short QCF near 58 kHz. Shorter calls than P. mesoamericanus. Most energy in 2nd harmonic. Wing membranes fused across back.

species.name: Thomas's Naked-backed Bat
species.description: Mexican mormoopid split from P. davyi. Z-shaped calls: short CF at ~73 kHz, a sweep down, then a short QCF near 60 to 62 kHz (2nd harmonic). Wing membranes fused across back. Cave-roosting; large colonies.

species.name: Big Naked-backed Bat
species.description: CF component at ~54–57 kHz. Similar structure to P. davyi but lower frequency, consistent with larger body size.

species.name: Mesoamerican Mustached Bat
species.description: The ONLY New World high-duty-cycle echolocator. Long CF at ~61 kHz (2nd harmonic) with Doppler compensation. 4–5 harmonics. Formerly P. parnellii.

species.name: Parnell's Mustached Bat
species.description: High-duty-cycle echolocator with Doppler compensation. Long CF-FM calls (about 15 to 21 ms); the CF part (2nd harmonic) is at about 53 kHz or about 59 kHz depending on the cryptic form (the 53 kHz form is P. rubiginosus). Split from P. mesoamericanus. Huge cave colonies.

species.name: Wagner's Mustached Bat
species.description: Highest frequency Pteronotus in Costa Rica (excl. P. mesoamericanus harmonics). Initial CF ~83 kHz, terminal CF ~68 kHz. Shows Doppler-shift compensation.

species.name: Dobson's Lesser Mustached Bat
species.description: Recently split from P. personatus. Z-shaped calls: short CF at ~82 kHz, a sweep down, then a short QCF near 65 kHz (2nd harmonic). Smaller body and higher calls than P. mesoamericanus. Mexico to western Honduras; cave-dwelling.

species.name: Sooty Mustached Bat
species.description: Caribbean endemic mormoopid (Cuba, Jamaica, Puerto Rico, Hispaniola). QCF of 2nd harmonic at ~81–84 kHz followed by FM sweep. Smallest Pteronotus. Cave-dwelling; large mixed-species colonies.

species.name: Fruit bats
species.description: Most don't echolocate; Rousettus uses tongue clicks for cave navigation

species.name: Black Flying-fox
species.description: Does not echolocate. Large flying-fox of tropical and subtropical northern Australia. Roosts in large colonies in mangroves, rainforest, and paperbark swamps.

species.name: Spectacled Flying-fox
