species.description: Does not echolocate. Endangered (EPBC Act). Restricted to Wet Tropics and Cape York in far north Queensland. Key rainforest pollinator and seed disperser.

species.name: Ryukyu Flying Fox
species.description: Large fruit bat of the Ryukyu Islands (4 subspecies in Japan). Does not echolocate. Feeds on fruit, flowers, and leaves. Endangered due to habitat loss and hunting.

species.name: Indian Flying Fox
species.description: No echolocation. Largest bat in South Asia (wingspan up to 1.5 m). Large noisy roost camps in tall trees. Pakistan, India, Nepal, Bangladesh, Sri Lanka. Important pollinator and seed disperser.

species.name: Island Flying Fox
species.description: No echolocation. Medium-sized flying fox of small tropical islands from Myanmar to Melanesia. Roosts in coastal mangroves. Important long-distance seed disperser between islands.

species.name: Marianas Flying Fox
species.description: No echolocation. Endemic to the Mariana Islands (Guam, Rota, Saipan). Endangered due to hunting and habitat loss; nearly extinct on Guam due to brown tree snake impacts on forest.

species.name: Indian Flying Fox
species.description: No echolocation. Large flying fox of the Indian subcontinent. Forms enormous noisy roost camps in banyan and other tall trees. Key pollinator and seed disperser. Formerly P. giganteus.

species.name: Grey-headed Flying-fox
species.description: Australia's largest bat (wingspan ~1 m). Does not echolocate. Camps in colonies along waterways. Vulnerable (EPBC Act). Pollinator and seed disperser.

species.name: Malagasy Flying Fox
species.description: No echolocation. Madagascar's largest bat. Endemic; Vulnerable. Essential seed disperser and pollinator for Malagasy forests. Large communal roosts in tall trees. Hunted for bushmeat.

species.name: Little Red Flying-fox
species.description: Does not echolocate. Nomadic, following eucalypt flowering. Seasonal visitor to southern regions.

species.name: Large Flying Fox
species.description: No echolocation. One of the world's largest bats (wingspan up to 1.7 m). Mainland SE Asia and the Malay Archipelago. Flies long distances nightly to fruit trees. Near Threatened.

species.name: Horseshoe bats
species.description: Constant-frequency calls; species range ~30 kHz (large) to ~112 kHz (lesser horseshoe)

species.name: Acuminate Horseshoe Bat
species.description: CF2 ~73 kHz (72–76 kHz across range). Philippines and Sunda shelf islands (Indonesia, Malaysia). Forest interior species. Closely related to R. stheno.

species.name: Intermediate Horseshoe Bat
species.description: CF about 67 to 90 kHz, varying by region. One of the most widespread horseshoe bats from South Asia through China and SE Asia. Common in forests, caves, and forest edges.

species.name: Halcyon Horseshoe Bat
species.description: West and Central African forest horseshoe bat. CF peak ~88–92 kHz. Forest-interior species; sensitive to deforestation.

species.name: Andaman Horseshoe Bat
species.description: Horseshoe bat of the Andaman Islands and parts of mainland SE Asia. CF peak ~63–68 kHz. Forest-dwelling; roosts in caves and buildings.

species.name: Lesser Woolly Horseshoe Bat
species.description: CF about 38 to 44 kHz in India and about 53 kHz in Sri Lanka. Endemic to peninsular India and Sri Lanka; Western and Eastern Ghats moist forests. Cave-roosting.

species.name: Blasius's Horseshoe Bat
species.description: CF about 92 to 95 kHz in Europe, North Africa and the Middle East; about 86 kHz in southern Africa. Mediterranean-type habitats and caves.

species.name: Bornean Horseshoe Bat
species.description: CF ~80–83 kHz. Endemic to Borneo and Palawan (Philippines). Similar frequency to R. affinis; distinguished by morphology. Forest-dependent.

species.name: Cape Horseshoe Bat
species.description: Endemic to South Africa (Western, Eastern, Northern Cape). CF about 76 to 87 kHz, lower in the west of its range. Coastal caves and rocky outcrops.

species.name: Geoffroy's Horseshoe Bat
species.description: Widespread in caves across southern and eastern Africa. CF about 90 to 92 kHz in South Africa, but about 80 to 84 kHz in Mozambique and Malawi. Often roosts with Miniopterus.

species.name: Andaman Horseshoe Bat
species.description: Endemic to the Andaman Islands. CF peak ~85–92 kHz (mean ~90 kHz). Cave-roosting.

species.name: Japanese Lesser Horseshoe Bat
species.description: CF-FM calls with peak CF ~103–111 kHz, increasing from north to south. Endemic to Japan (Honshu, Shikoku, Kyushu). Roosts in caves and buildings.

species.name: Darling's Horseshoe Bat
species.description: Southern Africa woodlands (Zimbabwe, Mozambique, South Africa). Small species; CF peak ~86–88 kHz. Rocky habitats and caves.

species.name: Decken's Horseshoe Bat
species.description: East African cave-dwelling horseshoe bat found in Kenya, Tanzania, and Mozambique. CF peak ~86 kHz. Roosts in caves and mines in coastal and lowland habitats.

species.name: Eloquent Horseshoe Bat
species.description: Large horseshoe bat endemic to East African highlands of Kenya, Tanzania, and Ethiopia. CF peak ~50–52 kHz. Montane forest and woodland caves.

species.name: Mediterranean Horseshoe Bat
species.description: Medium-sized horseshoe bat. CF call at about 102 to 105 kHz. Restricted to Mediterranean and warm-temperate zones. Cave-dwelling; large colony roosts.

species.name: Greater Horseshoe Bat
species.description: Europe's largest horseshoe bat. Constant-frequency call at ~83 kHz. Hunts large beetles and moths in flight. Roosts in caves, mines, and old buildings.

species.name: Japanese Greater Horseshoe Bat
species.description: CF-FM calls with CF ~65–70 kHz in Japan (about 65 kHz in Hokkaido, 67–70 kHz further south) and 66–72 kHz in Korea. FM/CF/FM structure. Widespread from Hokkaido to Kyushu. Roosts in caves, mines, and tunnels.

species.name: Rüppell's Horseshoe Bat
species.description: Sub-Saharan Africa woodlands and savanna. CF peak geographically variable: ~53–59 kHz (southern), ~62–66 kHz (Cameroon).

species.name: Hildebrandt's Horseshoe Bat
species.description: Large horseshoe bat of east and southern Africa. CF peak varies 32–46 kHz (species complex). Low frequency for a rhinolophid due to large body size.

species.name: Lesser Horseshoe Bat
species.description: One of Europe's smallest bats (~5 g). CF call at ~110 kHz. Forages close to vegetation in sheltered valleys. Very sensitive to disturbance at roost sites.

species.name: Imaizumi's Horseshoe Bat
species.description: CF-FM calls with CF ~92–93 kHz on Iriomote. Endemic to the Yaeyama Islands (Iriomote and Kohama). Often treated as part of R. perditus.

species.name: Indian Rufous Horseshoe Bat
species.description: CF about 87 to 95 kHz (mean about 92 kHz). The higher-frequency form of the rufous horseshoe bat in Tamil Nadu and Kerala; the name is not formally valid and many lists keep it in R. rouxii. Caves and tunnels in humid forests.

species.name: Lander's Horseshoe Bat
species.description: Small horseshoe bat widespread across sub-Saharan Africa. CF peak ~102–108 kHz. Cave and hollow-tree rooster. Forages in forest and woodland.

species.name: Blyth's Horseshoe Bat
species.description: CF about 100 to 110 kHz; bats in Kudremukh, Karnataka call near 95 kHz. One of the most widespread horseshoe bats in South Asia, from Pakistan through India to Nepal. Caves, rock crevices, and buildings.

species.name: Woolly Horseshoe Bat
species.description: Largest horseshoe bat in Asia (~35 g). Unusually low CF, about 32 to 35 kHz on the mainland and 38 to 43 kHz in Borneo, Malaysia and Singapore. Dense woolly fur. Primary forests from Nepal through China to Borneo. Mainland bats are now often called R. perniger.

species.name: Big-eared Horseshoe Bat
species.description: CF ~42–58 kHz (large and small cryptic forms). Distinctive very large ears. Widespread in southern and central China in karst terrain. May represent distinct species.

species.name: Malayan Horseshoe Bat
species.description: CF about 72 to 96 kHz, lower in the north and higher in the south. Widespread in mainland SE Asia (Thailand, Vietnam, Myanmar, Laos, Cambodia). Roosts in caves and tunnels; forages in and near forest.

species.name: Eastern Horseshoe Bat
species.description: Constant-frequency echolocation using distinctive horseshoe-shaped noseleaf. Cave-roosting. Found in forests of eastern Australia.

species.name: Mehely's Horseshoe Bat
species.description: CF ~107–111 kHz; closely overlaps R. euryale in frequency. Mediterranean and Middle East (Turkey, Israel, Jordan, Iran). Cave-roosting, often with R. euryale and R. blasii.

species.name: Formosan Lesser Horseshoe Bat
species.description: CF ~106–117 kHz (females ~2 kHz higher than males). Endemic to Taiwan. Geographic variation up to 6 kHz across populations. Cave-roosting; widespread in forested mountains.

species.name: Pearson's Horseshoe Bat
species.description: CF ~51–70 kHz, varying across the range: about 51–56 kHz in Vietnam and Cambodia, 58–62 in south China, 64–70 in eastern China. Hilly and montane forests of mainland SE Asia and south China. Distinctive large ears. Often found alongside R. affinis.

species.name: Yaeyama Horseshoe Bat
species.description: CF-FM calls with peak CF ~92–98 kHz (92–93 on Iriomote, 96–98 on Ishigaki). Endemic to the Yaeyama Islands. Forest-dwelling, cave-roosting.

species.name: Okinawa Least Horseshoe Bat
species.description: CF-FM calls with CF ~105–120 kHz, higher in southern than in northern Okinawa (5–8 kHz dialect difference). Endemic to the central and southern Ryukyus.

species.name: Least Horseshoe Bat
species.description: Very small horseshoe bat (~3 g). High CF about 92 to 115 kHz, lowest in Peninsular Malaysia. Widespread across southern China, Taiwan, and SE Asia in forest and scrub habitats.

species.name: Large-eared Horseshoe Bat
species.description: Lowest echolocation frequency of any rhinolophid bat (~28–34 kHz CF). Cave-roosting in warm humid caves and old mines. Restricted to tropical north Queensland. Vulnerable (EPBC Act).

species.name: Rufous Horseshoe Bat
species.description: CF about 78 to 85 kHz in India and 73 to 79 kHz in Sri Lanka. Widespread across the Indian subcontinent and Sri Lanka. Common in forests and caves.

species.name: Bushveld Horseshoe Bat
species.description: Southern and eastern Africa savannas. CF peak about 80 kHz in South Africa, up to 86 kHz in Malawi. Often sympatric with R. swinnyi.

species.name: Chinese Rufous Horseshoe Bat
species.description: CF ~69–89 kHz (about 80–88 kHz in China, ~77.5 kHz in Vietnam; females higher). Widespread in southern and central China. Cave-roosting, often sympatric with R. affinis. Important SARS-CoV host species.

species.name: Swinny's Horseshoe Bat
species.description: Eastern South Africa, Eswatini, Zimbabwe. High CF peak ~107 kHz. Clutter forager in dense vegetation.

species.name: Trefoil Horseshoe Bat
species.description: Distinctive three-leafed noseleaf. CF about 50 to 53.5 kHz. Sundaic lowland forest (Malaysia, Indonesia, Brunei). Found in both primary and disturbed forest.

species.name: Yellow-faced Horseshoe Bat
species.description: Philippine endemic horseshoe bat. CF peak ~58–62 kHz. Forest-dependent; roosts in caves. Named for the distinctive yellowish facial skin around the noseleaf.

species.name: Orange Leaf-nosed Bat
species.description: High-frequency CF calls at about 107 to 128 kHz. Pilbara bats call higher (mean 120 kHz) than Kimberley and Top End bats (about 116 kHz). Obligate cave-dweller requiring hot humid roosts. Vulnerable (EPBC Act).

species.name: Dwarf Little Fruit Bat
species.description: Small Amazonian frugivore. Peak ~80 kHz. Low-intensity FM. Related to Carollia. Important disperser of understory fruits. Common in terra firme forest.

species.name: Small Mouse-tailed Bat
species.description: Smallest Rhinopoma; QCF calls with the loudest (second) harmonic at about 33 to 35 kHz. Northeast Africa (Egypt, Sudan) and the Levant (Israel, Jordan, Syria). Rocky desert habitats.

species.name: Lesser Mouse-tailed Bat
species.description: QCF calls with several harmonics; the loudest (second) harmonic is at about 34 to 36 kHz in Iran and 30 to 40 kHz in India. Iran and Pakistan to India; Levantine and North African bats once listed under this name are now R. cystops. Often roosts with R. microphyllum, which calls lower.

species.name: Greater Mouse-tailed Bat
species.description: QCF calls with several harmonics; the loudest (second) harmonic is at about 27 to 29 kHz. The largest Rhinopoma. Widespread from Morocco to South Asia. Desert-adapted; roosts in ruins, caves, and rock crevices. Family Rhinopomatidae is endemic to the Old World arid zone.

species.name: Yucatan Yellow Bat
species.description: Small vespertilionid of the Yucatan Peninsula (SE Mexico, N Guatemala, N Belize). Steep FM sweeps ending in a short tail near 45–50 kHz. Forest edges and secondary growth. Closely related to R. tumida.

species.name: Black-winged Little Yellow Bat
species.description: Small vespertilionid. Broadband steep FM with small QCF termination. Peak ~48 kHz. Bandwidth >15 kHz.

species.name: Proboscis Bat
species.description: Tiny bat roosting along rivers. Short calls (about 4 to 5 ms), narrowband near 95 to 100 kHz (2nd harmonic) with a downward sweep at the end. Detectors may pick up the 1st harmonic, near 40 to 51 kHz.

species.name: Egyptian Rousette
species.description: Only African fruit bat with true echolocation (tongue clicks). Broadband clicks ~50–100 µs duration. Caves and mines. Very large colonies.

species.name: Geoffroy's Rousette
species.description: Tongue-click echolocation for cave navigation. Enormous cave colonies (millions). Widespread across SE Asia. Important seed disperser.

species.name: Leschenault's Rousette
species.description: Tongue clicks of ~1–2 ms with most energy at ~18–32 kHz (peak ~23 kHz), often in pairs. The only South Asian pteropodid with confirmed echolocation. Cave-roosting across India, Sri Lanka, and southern China. Large colonies.

species.name: Yellow-bellied Sheathtail Bat
species.description: Large, fast-flying bat with glossy black fur and yellow belly. Migratory. High-altitude forager.

species.name: Bare-rumped Sheathtail Bat
species.description: Narrow-band QCF search calls averaging ~20 kHz. Large sheathtail bat of tropical woodlands in far north Queensland and Top End. Tree-hollow roosting. Critically Endangered (EPBC Act).

species.name: Greater Sac-winged Bat
species.description: Alternates between ~45 and ~48 kHz when foraging. Most energy in 2nd harmonic. Well-studied species with vocal learning. Distinctive white dorsal stripes.

species.name: Frosted Sac-winged Bat
species.description: Amazonian endemic. Highest frequency Saccopteryx (~52 kHz). Similar QCF structure to congeners. Smaller than S. bilineata. Roosts on tree trunks in terra firme forest.

species.name: Lesser Sac-winged Bat
species.description: Higher frequency than S. bilineata. Similar multiharmonic QCF structure. Most energy in 2nd harmonic. Thinner dorsal stripes.

species.name: Roberts's Flat-headed Bat
species.description: Southern Africa. Peak ~30 kHz. Narrow bandwidth QCF. Roosts in rock crevices. Flattened skull for squeezing into narrow cracks.

species.name: Greater Broad-nosed Bat
species.description: Large, robust bat of eastern coastal forests. Aggressive predator of large insects and small vertebrates.

species.name: White-bellied Lesser House Bat
species.description: East African vespertilionid associated with buildings and dry woodland. FM calls ~35–45 kHz. Often roosts in roof spaces.

species.name: Dark-winged Lesser House Bat
species.description: Small vespertilionid of sub-Saharan savannas. Shallow FM search calls ending at about 30 to 34 kHz and about 5 to 6 ms long; steeper calls starting up to 70 kHz near clutter. Roosts in buildings and under bark.

species.name: Harlequin Bat
species.description: FM calls starting ~45–68 kHz, ending ~18–23 kHz, peak ~25–36 kHz. Large, strikingly patterned bat (black, white, chestnut). Southern and central China. Forested hillsides; rarely encountered.

species.name: Yellow-bellied House Bat
species.description: Most common vespertilionid in sub-Saharan Africa. Peak about 34 to 38 kHz. The similar S. mhlanganii, which roosts in trees, calls about 10 kHz higher. Roosts in buildings. Hockey-stick call shape.

species.name: Greater Asiatic Yellow Bat
species.description: FM-QCF, peak about 35 to 43 kHz. One of the most common bats across the Indian subcontinent. Buildings, hollow trees, and roof spaces. Open and edge habitat forager.

species.name: Lesser Asiatic Yellow Bat
species.description: QCF, peak ~40–47 kHz. One of the most commonly recorded bats in SE Asian urban and agricultural areas. Bright yellow-orange undersides. Buildings and palm crowns. Highly synanthropic.

species.name: White-bellied House Bat
species.description: Sahel and West Africa savannas. Peak ~32–35 kHz. Larger than S. dinganii. Roosts in buildings and palm trees.

species.name: Nut-colored Yellow Bat
species.description: Medium-large yellow bat of West and Central African forests. FM-QCF calls ~28–35 kHz. Roosts in buildings and tree hollows. Larger than S. dinganii.

species.name: Green House Bat
species.description: East and southern African savannas. Peak ~40–47 kHz. Smaller than S. dinganii. Roosts in buildings and tree hollows.

species.name: Inland Broad-nosed Bat
species.description: Widespread across inland Australia. Found in drier regions. Similar frequency to Gould's Wattled Bat.

species.name: Eastern Broad-nosed Bat
species.description: Robust bat of south-eastern coastal forests. Narrow frequency range distinctive. Roosts in tree hollows.

species.name: Bogota Yellow-shouldered Bat
species.description: High-altitude Andean frugivore (2000–3400 m). Peak ~68 kHz. Low-intensity FM. One of the few bat species found above 3000 m.

species.name: Hairy Yellow-shouldered Bat
species.description: Andean frugivore of montane forests (1000–3200 m). Peak ~70 kHz. Low-intensity FM. Key seed disperser in cloud forest ecosystems.

species.name: Little Yellow-shouldered Bat
species.description: Frugivore. Peak ~66.5 kHz (well documented). Low-intensity multiharmonic FM. Common in forest and edge habitats.

species.name: Highland Yellow-shouldered Bat
species.description: Montane frugivore of cloud forests from Mexico to Bolivia. Multi-harmonic FM. Important seed disperser at higher elevations. Males have yellow shoulder epaulettes.

species.name: Little Yellow-shouldered Bat
species.description: Common frugivore of Mesoamerican lowlands. Whispering FM calls. Recently split from S. lilium. Important seed disperser in tropical forests.

species.name: Egyptian Free-tailed Bat
species.description: Throughout Africa and into the Middle East. Long narrowband QCF calls, peak ~18–23 kHz. High-flying open-air forager. Very loud calls detectable at long range.

species.name: Mexican Free-tailed Bat
species.description: Search calls are long, shallow QCF with a characteristic frequency of about 25–29 kHz; calls vary from flat to FM, and some start above 40 kHz. Broadband FM during approach. Forms massive colonies.

species.name: Madagascan Large Free-tailed Bat
species.description: East Africa and Madagascar. Low frequency QCF, peak ~16–18 kHz. Large species. Long narrow wings for fast open-air flight.

species.name: East Asian Free-tailed Bat
species.description: Low FM-QCF search calls ~19–11 kHz, peak ~13–14 kHz, about 14–18 ms long. Fast, high-flying open-air forager. Western Japan. Roosts in rock crevices and buildings.

species.name: La Touche's Free-tailed Bat
species.description: Echolocation ~20 kHz. High-altitude flier, very difficult to capture. Known in Japan from a single specimen on Amami-Oshima (1985). IUCN Data Deficient.

species.name: European Free-tailed Bat
species.description: Europe's only free-tailed bat. Loud, low-frequency calls audible to humans. Fast, high-altitude forager. Roosts in cliff crevices and tall buildings.

species.name: Coastal Sheathtail Bat
species.description: Flat to slightly sloped QCF calls at 23–27 kHz. Restricted to coastal caves and boulder piles along the Queensland and Northern Territory coasts. Rare and poorly known.

species.name: Common Sheathtail Bat
species.description: QCF search calls peaking ~25 kHz. Widespread across northern and western Australia. Roosts in caves, rock crevices, and abandoned mines. Fast, direct flight in open habitats.

species.name: Long-winged Tomb Bat
species.description: QCF calls ~28–35 kHz. Fast direct flight in open areas. South and SE Asia from India to Indonesia. Roosts on exposed surfaces of buildings and rock faces.

species.name: Mauritian Tomb Bat
species.description: Sub-Saharan Africa and Madagascar. Multiharmonic CF search calls with FM approach calls. Fundamental at 11–13 kHz. Roosts on walls and tree trunks.

species.name: Black-bearded Tomb Bat
species.description: Low-intensity FM calls, dominant frequency ~29–33 kHz with four harmonics and most energy in the second. Ryukyu Islands. Roosts on rock walls and in caves.

species.name: Naked-rumped Tomb Bat
species.description: QCF, peak about 22 to 25 kHz. Bare rump patch. Most commonly encountered tomb bat in the Middle East. Egypt, Levant, Iraq, Iran, Saudi Arabia, Yemen. Ruins, tombs, and rock fissures; often large colonies.

species.name: Egyptian Tomb Bat
species.description: North and East Africa, arid regions. QCF calls peaking at about 27 to 31 kHz in the Middle East. Roosts in tombs, ruins, rock faces.

species.name: Theobald's Tomb Bat
species.description: Large tomb bat. QCF ~25–30 kHz. Mainland SE Asia (Myanmar, Thailand, Vietnam, Cambodia). Obligate cave-roosting, often in large limestone cave colonies.

species.name: Troughton's Sheathtail Bat
species.description: Low-frequency QCF calls below 25 kHz. Roosts in sandstone caves and rocky escarpments in inland Queensland and western NSW. Rarely recorded; poorly known ecology.

species.name: Peters' Disk-winged Bat
species.description: Similar to T. tricolor but slightly larger suction disks. Peak ~50 kHz. Roosts in furled Heliconia leaves. Amazonian lowland forests. Extremely low-intensity echolocation.

species.name: LaVal's Disk-winged Bat
species.description: Rare Amazonian disk-winged bat. Roosts in curled leaves. Poorly known acoustically. Low-intensity FM calls.

species.name: Spix's Disk-winged Bat
species.description: Suction-cup disks on wrists and ankles for roosting in rolled Heliconia leaves. Extremely low intensity; barely detectable at <1 m. Distinctive social calls for roost-finding.

species.name: Blunt-eared Bat
species.description: Enigmatic Peruvian bat; monotypic genus sometimes placed in its own family Tomopeatidae. Roosts in desert cliffs along the arid Pacific coast. QCF calls. One of South America's rarest bats.

species.name: Baker's Round-eared Bat
species.description: Forest gleaning insectivore split from T. saurophila. Multi-harmonic FM calls. Forest understory specialist. Central America.

species.name: Stripe-headed Round-eared Bat
species.description: Gleaning insectivore/carnivore. Peak ~65 kHz. Low-intensity multiharmonic FM. Forest interior species.

species.name: Fringe-lipped Bat
species.description: Famous frog-eating bat. Listens for frog mating calls to locate prey. Low-intensity multiharmonic FM (~70 kHz peak). Hard to detect acoustically.

species.name: Niceforo's Big-eared Bat
species.description: Low-intensity gleaner. Peak ~80 kHz. Multiharmonic FM. Forest understory specialist.

species.name: Lesser Bamboo Bat
species.description: FM, peak ~65–75 kHz. One of the world’s smallest bats (~2 g). Flattened skull and adhesive pads for roosting inside bamboo internodes. Widespread in bamboo forests across SE Asia.

species.name: Greater Bamboo Bat
species.description: FM, peak ~55–65 kHz (lower than T. pachypus). Same bamboo-roosting ecology. Widespread in SE Asian bamboo forests. Often co-roosts with T. pachypus.

species.name: Tent-making Bat
species.description: Tent-roosting frugivore. Modifies large leaves into tents. Peak about 68 or 90 kHz, depending on which harmonic is loudest. Low-intensity nasal FM. Found in lowland forests.

species.name: Pacific Tent-making Bat
species.description: Split from U. bilobatum. Pacific slope frugivore that modifies large leaves into tent-like day roosts. Multi-harmonic FM calls. Central America to Ecuador.

species.name: Northern Little Yellow-eared Bat
species.description: Small frugivore. Peak ~78 kHz. Low-intensity FM. Tent-roosting. Yellow ear margins. Northern South American lowlands.

species.name: Great Stripe-faced Bat
species.description: Large stenodermatine frugivore. Peak ~58 kHz. Prominent white facial stripes. Low-intensity FM. Forages in canopy.

species.name: Spectral Bat
species.description: Largest bat in the Americas (wingspan ~1 m). Low-intensity multiharmonic FM. Carnivorous: preys on birds and other bats. Very difficult to detect acoustically.

species.name: Inland Forest Bat
species.description: Small bat of inland Australia. Restricted to semi-arid regions.

species.name: Large Forest Bat
species.description: Largest Vespadelus species. Found in wet and dry forests of south-eastern Australia including Tasmania.

species.name: Finlayson's Cave Bat
species.description: Steep FM calls with a characteristic frequency near 53 to 56 kHz. Small bat of arid and semi-arid inland Australia. Roosts in caves, mines, rock crevices, and buildings. Tolerates very hot, dry conditions.

species.name: Southern Forest Bat
species.description: Small forest bat found across southern Australia. Roosts in tree hollows. Call frequency overlaps with Little Forest Bat.

species.name: Eastern Cave Bat
species.description: FM/QCF calls at ~49–53 kHz. Cave-roosting bat of eastern Australia from Cape York to central NSW. Found in sandstone overhangs, caves, and mine tunnels in woodland and dry forest.

species.name: Little Forest Bat
species.description: One of Australia's smallest bats (~4 g). Common in forests and urban areas. High-frequency calls.

species.name: Parti-coloured Bat
species.description: Striking frosted fur. Calls do not alternate in a regular pattern, unlike the noctule. Migratory; roosts in high-rise buildings. Males produce audible courtship calls from roost entrances.

species.name: Asian Parti-coloured Bat
species.description: FM-QCF calls, peak ~24–25 kHz, end ~22 kHz, start ~48 kHz (up to ~56). Steep FM into shallow QCF tail. Migratory. Hokkaido to Kyushu. Roosts in tree hollows and buildings.

species.name: Vesper bats
species.description: Broadest family; FM sweeps; most species 20–60 kHz peak

africa.description: Most common vespertilionid in sub-Saharan Africa. Peak ~34–38 kHz; the similar S. mhlanganii (tree roosts) calls at ~43 kHz. Hockey-stick FM-QCF call shape. Roosts in roofs and buildings across a wide range of habitats.
Ubiquitous across southern Africa. Peak frequency ~38 kHz. FM-QCF hockey-stick calls. Roosts in buildings. One of the most frequently recorded species on bat detectors in South Africa.
Extremely common across sub-Saharan Africa. Narrowband QCF calls peaking ~25 kHz. Forms large colonies in roofs of buildings. Geographic variation in call frequency documented.
Throughout Africa and into the Middle East. Long narrowband QCF calls peaking ~18–23 kHz. High-flying open-air forager. Very loud calls detectable at long range.

Most widespread African hipposiderid. High CF calls (about 142 kHz in southern Africa, 143–156 kHz in Kenya). Frequency varies geographically; East/Central Africa populations ~10 kHz higher than southern. Caves, mines, buildings.

Most widespread African slit-faced bat. Very low intensity broadband FM calls (“whispering bat”). Multi-harmonic with peaks at 50, 73, 90, 113 kHz. Gleaner that uses passive listening. Very difficult to detect on bat detectors.

Southern and East Africa. Peak about 48–54 kHz. FM-QCF hockey-stick calls. FM-QCF hockey-stick calls. Forms large cave colonies of thousands. Key cave-roosting species, often sympatric with Rhinolophus.
Only African fruit bat with true echolocation—using tongue clicks (broadband, ~50–100 µs duration, 12–70 kHz). Caves and mines across sub-Saharan Africa and Egypt. Very large colonies.
Most widespread African megabat. Massive migratory colonies of up to 1 million individuals (Kasanka, Zambia). Critical seed disperser for tropical forests. Uses vision and smell only.
East and southern Africa savannas. Males produce loud honking display calls audible at considerable distance. Common in gardens and fruit orchards. No echolocation.
Widespread in caves across southern and eastern Africa. CF peak varies geographically (~90–92 kHz in southern Africa, ~80–100 kHz across full range). Often roosts alongside Miniopterus colonies.
Southern and eastern Africa savannas. CF peak ~80 kHz. Often sympatric with R. swinnyi and R. clivosus. Savanna woodland specialist.
Large horseshoe bat of east and southern Africa. CF peak varies 32–46 kHz across a species complex (Taylor et al. 2012). Unusually low frequency for a rhinolophid due to large body size.
Sub-Saharan Africa woodlands and savanna. CF peak shows strong geographic variation: ~53–59 kHz (southern), ~62–66 kHz (Cameroon), ~45–50 kHz (Uganda). Multiple cryptic species likely.
Endemic to South Africa (Western, Eastern, Northern Cape). CF peak ~83–86 kHz. Inhabits coastal caves and rocky outcrops. Well-studied acoustically.
West, Central and East Africa. CF about 128–148 kHz, varying by region, lineage and sex. Cryptic species pair with H. caffer—distinguishable by lower call frequency. Often sympatric.
East and southern African savannas. Peak ~40–47 kHz (geographically variable). Smaller than S. dinganii. Roosts in buildings and tree hollows.
Sahel and West Africa savannas. Peak ~32–35 kHz. Largest Scotophilus in Africa. Roosts in buildings and palm trees.
Sub-Saharan Africa. Peak ~45–48 kHz. Small bat frequently detected around human habitation and streetlights. Similar call to P. kuhlii.
Sub-Saharan Africa. Peak about 70 kHz. FM-QCF calls about 3 ms long. Named for roosting in furled banana leaves. One of Africa's smallest bats (3–5 g).
North Africa, Sahel, East Africa, and into the Middle East. FM-QCF ending about 46–48 kHz in much of Africa, higher (49–57 kHz) in Morocco and Israel. Associated with arid habitats and waterways.
Southern and East Africa. Broadband FM sweep peaking ~48 kHz. Cave- and mine-roosting. Distinctive tricolored fur pattern.
North Africa and Mediterranean margin. Peak ~38–42 kHz. Common around streetlights in urban areas. Range expanding.
Sub-Saharan Africa savannas. FM-QCF calls peaking ~25–28 kHz. Roosts in buildings and tree hollows. Often in mixed colonies with Chaerephon pumilus.
Southern Africa. Narrowband QCF calls peaking ~30 kHz. Roosts in rock crevices. Distinctively flattened skull for squeezing into narrow cracks.
Sub-Saharan Africa and Madagascar. Multiharmonic CF search calls with FM approach calls. Fundamental at 11–13 kHz (often audible to humans). Roosts on exposed walls and tree trunks.
North and East Africa, arid regions. QCF calls peaking about 27–31 kHz. Roosts in tombs, ancient ruins, and rock faces.
Southern Africa. Peak about 60–66 kHz, about 12 kHz higher than M. natalensis. Smaller species. Cave-roosting. Distinguished from M. natalensis by higher call frequency.
Central and West Africa forests. Largest African bat (wingspan to 90 cm). Males have enlarged larynx and rostrum for loud lek-display calls. No echolocation.
Central and West Africa tropical forests. Males produce repetitive metallic calls during display. Important pollinator and seed disperser. No echolocation.
Eastern South Africa, Eswatini, Zimbabwe. High CF peak ~107 kHz. Clutter forager in dense vegetation. Less common than sympatric R. simulator.
North Africa and East Africa. CF about 92–95 kHz in North Africa; about 86 kHz in southern Africa. Mediterranean-type habitats and caves.
Southern Africa woodlands (Zimbabwe, Mozambique, South Africa). Small species with CF peak ~86–88 kHz. Rocky habitats and caves.
East and southern Africa. Large species with unusually low CF ~60 kHz for a hipposiderid. Caves and large rock overhangs.
Sub-Saharan Africa woodlands. Lower peak ~34 kHz than M. tricolor. Short broadband FM calls. Unusual among African Myotis for roosting in foliage.
Southern Africa rocky areas. Peak ~30–35 kHz. FM-QCF calls. Distinctive long free tail. Roosts in rock crevices.
Sub-Saharan Africa savanna and woodland. Broadband FM sweeps 70–30 kHz. Distinctive reticulated wing markings. Slow, fluttery flight.
Sub-Saharan Africa savannas. Peak ~42 kHz. FM-QCF calls. Often one of the first bats to emerge at dusk. Roosts in buildings and under tree bark.
Sub-Saharan Africa. Very low frequency QCF peaking ~13–16 kHz. Large molossid (40–60 g). Calls partially audible to humans. High, fast flight above the canopy.
East and southern Africa. Very low frequency calls (~11–14 kHz), audible to humans. Very large molossid. Caves and buildings. Individual call signatures documented.
West, Central, and East Africa forests. QCF calls peaking ~28–32 kHz. Forest edge and canopy forager.
East Africa and Madagascar. Low frequency QCF peaking ~16–18 kHz. Large species with long narrow wings for fast open-air flight.
Central and East Africa. QCF calls peaking ~25–28 kHz. Forest and forest edge habitat. Similar call to C. pumilus but more forest-associated.
East Africa coast. Low-duty-cycle QCF calls peaking at ~33 kHz. Near Threatened. Colonial in coastal caves and rock shelters.
Central and West Africa forests. Largest nycterid. Very low intensity broadband FM. Remarkable predator—hunts fish, frogs, and smaller bats.
West and Central Africa forests. Low-intensity broadband FM similar to N. thebaica but larger. Gleaner in forest understory.
Central and East Africa. Larger species with lower peak ~52–55 kHz than M. natalensis. Caves in forested areas.
West and Central Africa forests. Largest hipposiderid; CF ~60–63 kHz. Caves near forest. Rarely encountered.

Holds the record for the highest known bat echolocation frequency (~212 kHz). Southern and East Africa caves and mines. Tiny bat (3–5 g). Requires very high sample rate detectors (>400 kHz) to record.
Central and southern Africa. Peak ~37 kHz. Broadband FM. Large ears suggest some gleaning behavior. One of Africa's least-known bat species.
East and southern Africa. Very high frequency, low-intensity FM calls (~90–118 kHz). Clutter specialist in dense vegetation. Very difficult to detect on standard bat detectors.
Sub-Saharan Africa forests. Very high frequency broadband FM (~95–105 kHz peak). Forest interior specialist. Rarely captured or recorded.
West and Central African forest horseshoe bat. CF peak ~88–92 kHz. Forest-interior species.
Small horseshoe bat widespread across sub-Saharan Africa. CF peak ~102–108 kHz. Caves and hollow trees.
Large hipposiderid of West and Central African forests. CF about 58–61 kHz in West Africa and about 51 kHz in Uganda. Formerly Hipposideros cyclops. Massive noseleaf.
Large Mops of West and Central African forests. QCF calls ~22–26 kHz. Fast open-air forager above the canopy.
Sub-Saharan African Myotis with reddish-brown fur. FM sweeps. Forages over water and along forest edges.
Small pipistrelle of southern and eastern African woodlands. FM-QCF calls ending ~53–57 kHz, peak ~56–62 kHz. Tree hollows and buildings.
Montane forest pipistrelle from Cameroon highlands. FM calls ~45–50 kHz. Known from very few specimens.
Central and East African forest bat with distinctive silvery wing pattern. FM calls ~40–50 kHz. Roosts under banana leaves.
Medium-large yellow bat of West and Central African forests. FM-QCF ~28–35 kHz. Roosts in buildings and tree hollows.
East African vespertilionid. FM calls ~35–45 kHz. Often roosts in roof spaces. Dry woodland and savanna.
East African bent-winged bat. FM calls ~50–55 kHz. Cave-roosting. Recently split from M. natalensis complex.
Large sit-and-wait predator. Heart-shaped noseleaf. Low-intensity broadband FM. Hunts from perches, taking large insects and small vertebrates.
Endemic to Réunion Island. QCF calls with most energy at ~31–51 kHz. One of only two bat species on the island. Roosts in buildings and lava tubes.
No echolocation. Common fruit bat of West African savannas. Males have white shoulder epaulettes. Loud honking calls. Pollinates baobab trees.

antarctica.description: Abundant throughout Antarctic waters year-round. Type A (large, open-water, hunts minke whales), Type B (pack-ice specialist, hunts seals using wave-washing), and smaller Type C (found in dense pack ice near Ross Sea, hunts fish). All types echolocate with broadband clicks.

Males migrate to rich Antarctic feeding grounds in summer, diving deep for squid. Produces the most powerful biosonar on Earth — clicks exceeding 230 dB. The massive spermaceti organ focuses sound into a directional beam for hunting at abyssal depths. Females and calves stay in warmer waters.

The only small dolphin endemic to Antarctic and sub-Antarctic waters. Distinctive black-and-white hourglass pattern. Echolocates with broadband clicks. Among the least-studied dolphins on Earth — almost everything known comes from at-sea sightings and strandings. Often bow-rides with vessels.

Common in sub-Antarctic and Southern Ocean waters. Highly social; travels in large, tight pods. Echolocates with broadband clicks during deep squid-hunting dives. Also produces complex pulsed social calls. Known for mass strandings, particularly in New Zealand and Tasmania.

Graceful, finless dolphin of the Southern Ocean — unique among southern dolphins in lacking a dorsal fin. Travels in large schools, sometimes thousands strong. Echolocates with broadband clicks. Circumpolar in cool to sub-Antarctic waters. Swift and acrobatic.

The most frequently sighted beaked whale in Antarctic waters. Deep-diving; forages with frequency-modulated echolocation clicks. Males develop a prominent, bulging forehead with age. Circumpolar south of 30°S. Curious and approachable; sometimes spy-hops near ships.

Largest beaked whale in the Southern Hemisphere. Echolocates with FM clicks during deep dives. Two teeth at the tip of the lower jaw erupt in both sexes. Occasionally sighted near the Antarctic ice edge. Very poorly known; much of its biology is inferred from its northern relative, Baird's Beaked Whale.

A bizarre beaked whale: males grow long, strap-shaped teeth that curve over the upper jaw, eventually preventing it from opening more than a few centimetres. Despite this, they catch squid by suction feeding. Uses FM echolocation clicks. Circumpolar in sub-Antarctic waters; rarely seen alive.

Cryptic sub-Antarctic porpoise with dark eye rings. Uses narrow-band high-frequency (NBHF) clicks at ~130 kHz — acoustic camouflage against orca predation, exploiting the orca's poor high-frequency hearing. Among the least-known cetaceans; almost all records are from strandings on Tierra del Fuego and the Falkland Islands.

No echolocation. Migrates thousands of kilometres from tropical breeding grounds to Antarctic krill-rich feeding waters each summer. Males sing haunting, complex songs lasting up to 30 minutes. Uses bubble-net feeding — spiralling underwater while blowing bubbles to corral krill into dense columns.

No echolocation. The most abundant baleen whale in Antarctic waters, commonly seen in pack ice. Source of the mysterious 'bio-duck' signal — a repetitive quacking sound recorded for decades before being attributed to this species via acoustic tags. Small for a rorqual but plays a huge role in the krill ecosystem.

No echolocation. The largest animal that has ever lived — up to 30 m and 180 tonnes. Produces infrasonic calls (10–40 Hz) audible across entire ocean basins. Antarctic blue whales (B. m. intermedia) were hunted to near-extinction; fewer than 3,000 may remain. A single blue whale can consume 4 tonnes of krill per day.

No echolocation. Second-largest animal on Earth. Produces powerful 20 Hz pulses — among the loudest sustained biological sounds. Distinctive asymmetric colouration: white right lower jaw, dark left. Nicknamed the 'greyhound of the sea' for its speed. Summers in Antarctic waters feeding on krill and small fish.

No echolocation. Slow, rotund whale with callosities — rough white skin patches unique to each individual, used for photo-ID. Produces low-frequency moans and up-calls. Named the 'right' whale to hunt because it floated when dead. Ranges into sub-Antarctic waters to feed. Recovering from near-extinction.

Not echolocation. The southernmost breeding mammal, living on Antarctic fast ice year-round. Produces an extraordinary repertoire of underwater sounds: eerie descending trills, chirps, and sci-fi whistles that can be heard through the ice. Maintains breathing holes by grinding ice with its teeth. Dives to 600+ m.

Not echolocation. Solitary apex predator of Antarctic pack ice. Males produce haunting, pulsing underwater trills and low broadcast calls during breeding season. Feeds on penguins (ambushing them at ice edges), krill, fish, and even other seals. Sinuous and powerful, with a massive gape and lobed teeth for krill filtering.

australia.description: Widespread in eastern Australia from Queensland to Victoria. Constant-frequency CF calls at ~68–70 kHz. Cave-roosting in forests and woodlands. Uses horseshoe-shaped noseleaf to direct calls.
Restricted to tropical north Queensland. Lowest echolocation frequency of any rhinolophid (~28–34 kHz CF). Vulnerable (EPBC Act). Cave-roosting in warm humid caves and old mines.
Very high-frequency CF calls, about 147–162 kHz. Small hipposiderid of tropical woodlands and monsoon forests in northern Australia. Often beyond range of standard bat detectors.
Australia's only Rhinonicteris. High-frequency CF calls, about 116 kHz in the Kimberley and Top End and 120 kHz in the Pilbara. Obligate cave-dweller. Vulnerable (EPBC Act).

australia.name: Diadem Leaf-nosed Bat
australia.description: Largest Australian hipposiderid. CF ~58–63 kHz. Cave-roosting in tropical rainforest of far north Queensland. Striking pale shoulder markings. Long-distance forager. Near Threatened.
Australia's only megadermatid and largest carnivorous bat. Very quiet broadband FM calls (20–56 kHz). Hunts vertebrate prey including other bats, lizards, and frogs. Vulnerable (EPBC Act).
Large, fast-flying bat with glossy black fur and yellow belly. QCF ~15–22.5 kHz. Migratory; high-altitude open-air forager across northern and eastern Australia.
Widespread across northern and western Australia. QCF search calls peaking ~25 kHz. Roosts in caves, rock crevices, and abandoned mines. Fast, direct flight in open habitats.

australia.name: Bare-rumped Sheathtail Bat
australia.description: Critically Endangered (EPBC Act). Narrow-band QCF calls averaging ~20 kHz. Large sheathtail bat of tropical woodlands in far north Queensland and Top End. Extremely rarely recorded.
Flat to slightly sloped QCF calls at 23–27 kHz. Restricted to coastal caves and boulder piles along Queensland and NT coasts. Rare and poorly known.
Low-frequency QCF calls below 25 kHz. Roosts in sandstone caves and rocky escarpments in inland Queensland and western NSW. Rarely recorded; poorly known ecology.
Australia's largest insectivorous bat. Loud, low-frequency QCF calls (~11–14 kHz) audible to some humans. Fast, high-flying open-air forager across most of Australia.
Small free-tailed bat of south-eastern Australia. QCF search calls at ~25–30.5 kHz. Roosts in tree hollows and buildings. Rapid, direct flight.
Widespread across eastern Australian coasts. QCF search calls at ~28.5–36 kHz. Similar to Southern Free-tailed Bat but slightly higher frequency. Tree-hollow roosting.
Very loud, low-frequency QCF calls (16–23 kHz) often audible to humans. Large free-tailed bat of tropical northern Australia. Fast, high-altitude forager over woodland.

australia.name: Lumsden's Free-tailed Bat
australia.description: Shallow FM calls at about 24–28 kHz. Largest Ozimops species. Formerly Mormopterus beccarii (in part). Widespread across tropical and subtropical northern Australia.
QCF search calls at ~32–35 kHz. Small free-tailed bat of coastal eastern Australia from SE Queensland to southern NSW. Vulnerable (EPBC Act). Roosts in tree hollows and under bark.
Cave-roosting bat found along eastern Australia. FM calls at ~43–48.5 kHz. Fast, agile flier. Forms large maternity colonies. Vulnerable in some states.
High-frequency FM calls (57–64 kHz). Smaller than the Eastern Bent-winged Bat. Cave-roosting in eastern Australia from Cape York to northern NSW. Often in mixed-species colonies.
Critically Endangered (EPBC Act). FM calls similar to Eastern Bent-winged Bat (~44–50 kHz). Dependent on a single maternity cave near Warrnambool. Southwest Victoria only.
Australia's most commonly recorded bat. FM calls with alternating frequencies distinctive (~25–34.5 kHz). Roosts in tree hollows, buildings, and bat boxes across the continent.
Common across southern Australia. FM calls at ~46.5–56 kHz. Small, dark bat roosting in tree hollows and buildings. Higher frequency calls than Gould's Wattled Bat.
Australia's most widespread bat. Very quiet broadband FM calls (35–80 kHz); often difficult to detect acoustically. Gleaning insectivore with distinctive large ears.
One of Australia's smallest bats (~4 g). FM calls at ~42.5–53.5 kHz. Common in forests and urban areas across south-eastern Australia. High-frequency calls.
Small forest bat found across southern Australia. FM calls at ~39–57 kHz. Roosts in tree hollows. Call frequency overlaps with Little Forest Bat.
Common in forests of eastern Australia. Very quiet FM calls (35–80 kHz), similar to Lesser Long-eared Bat. Distinguished by larger size and wetter habitat preference.
Largest Vespadelus species. FM calls at ~38–48 kHz. Found in wet and dry forests of south-eastern Australia including Tasmania.
Curved FM calls with a characteristic frequency of about 36–41 kHz. Widespread across northern and eastern Australia. Medium-sized wattled bat of open woodland and forest edges. Tree-hollow roosting.
Widespread across inland Australia. FM calls at ~28–36.5 kHz. Found in drier regions. Similar frequency to Gould's Wattled Bat. Tree-hollow roosting.
Robust bat of south-eastern coastal forests. Narrow FM frequency range (~34–37 kHz) is distinctive. Roosts in tree hollows.
Australia's only fishing bat. Very quiet FM calls (28–80.5 kHz). Trawls water surfaces with large feet. Found near rivers, lakes, and dams across eastern Australia.
Large vesper bat of south-eastern forests. FM calls at ~35–40.5 kHz. Roosts in tree hollows and buildings. Vulnerable (IUCN).
Large, robust bat of eastern coastal forests. FM calls at ~32–36.5 kHz. Aggressive predator of large insects and small vertebrates. Near Threatened.
FM/QCF calls at ~49–53 kHz. Cave-roosting bat of eastern Australia. Found in sandstone overhangs, caves, and mine tunnels in woodland and dry forest.

Steep FM calls with a characteristic frequency near 53–56 kHz. Small bat of arid and semi-arid inland Australia. Roosts in caves, mines, rock crevices, and buildings. Tolerates very hot, dry conditions.
FM calls peaking ~45–50 kHz. One of Australia's smallest bats (~3 g). Found along northern coasts from WA through NT to Queensland. Mangrove and coastal woodland specialist.
Small bat of inland Australia. FM calls at ~44–47 kHz. Restricted to semi-arid regions of central and western Australia.
Very quiet broadband FM gleaning calls (35–75 kHz). Tropical woodlands and monsoon forests of Arnhem Land, Kimberley, and Cape York. Poorly known ecology.
Formerly N. timoriensis. Restricted to drier woodlands of inland eastern and southern Australia. Very quiet FM gleaning calls (35–65 kHz). Vulnerable (EPBC Act).
Very quiet broadband FM calls. Australia's smallest long-eared bat (~4 g). Found in sandstone escarpments and monsoon forests of the Top End and Kimberley. Gleaning insectivore.
Broadband FM calls (~35–48 kHz). Distinctive black and white fur pattern. Roosts in sandstone cliff overhangs near fertile areas. Eastern Australia. Vulnerable (EPBC Act).
Extremely broadband FM calls (60–155 kHz). Specialist predator of orb-weaving spiders. Roosts in abandoned bird nests. Rare along the east coast from Cape York to southern NSW.
Vulnerable (EPBC Act). Very quiet FM gleaning calls (31–80 kHz). Restricted to semi-arid woodlands of inland NSW and Queensland. Extremely rare.
Australia's largest bat (wingspan ~1 m). Does not echolocate. Camps in large colonies along waterways of eastern Australia. Vulnerable (EPBC Act). Key pollinator and seed disperser.
Does not echolocate. Large flying-fox of tropical and subtropical northern Australia. Roosts in mangroves, rainforest, and paperbark swamps. Camps can exceed 100,000 individuals.
Does not echolocate. Nomadic, following eucalypt and paperback flowering. Widespread across northern and eastern Australia. Forms massive seasonal camps.
Does not echolocate. Endangered (EPBC Act). Restricted to Wet Tropics and Cape York in far north Queensland. Key rainforest pollinator and seed disperser.
One of only two native land mammals of New Zealand. FM calls ~37–45 kHz. Nationally Critical. Forest-dwelling. Rapid decline from introduced predators.
No echolocation. Small fruit bat of NE Australian rainforests. Tubular nostrils and spotted wings. Solitary in dense foliage. Feeds on figs.
Does not echolocate. Madagascar's largest bat. Endemic; Vulnerable. Essential seed disperser. Hunted for bushmeat.
Does not echolocate. Mariana Islands endemic. Endangered; nearly extinct on Guam due to brown tree snake impacts.

canada.description: Most commonly detected bat in Canada. FM-QCF ~27 kHz. Buildings, bridges, bat boxes. Relatively resistant to White-nose Syndrome.
Historically Canada's most common bat. FM ~45 kHz. Devastated by White-nose Syndrome; Endangered (COSEWIC).

canada.name: Hoary Bat
canada.description: Canada's largest bat. Low QCF ~20–25 kHz. Solitary tree-roosting migrant. Major wind-turbine mortality concern.
Migratory tree bat. FM ~25–30 kHz. Forests and forest edges across Canada.
Migratory. FM ~40 kHz. Solitary tree-roosting. Eastern and central Canada.
Steep FM, high frequency. Gleaning forager. Endangered (COSEWIC) due to White-nose Syndrome.
FM ~45 kHz with distinctive steep sweeps. Endangered (COSEWIC). Cave hibernator.
One of Canada's smallest bats. FM ~50–55 kHz. Rock crevices and talus slopes. Appears somewhat resistant to WNS.
Western Canada. FM ~40 kHz. Mountainous forests. Tree and cliff crevice roosting.
Western montane forests. FM sweeps. Gleaning insectivore with large ears.
Very quiet FM. Southern BC only. Cave-roosting. Gleaning specialist.
Southern BC. FM ~40 kHz. Solitary tree-roosting.
Occasional records in southern BC and Ontario. QCF ~25 kHz.
Southern BC only. High QCF ~46 kHz. Desert cliffs and canyons.
Western Canada (BC, Alberta). FM ~50 kHz. Arid habitats and forests.
Western prairies and foothills. FM, characteristic frequency ~44 kHz. Rock crevices and badlands.
Southern BC. FM. Trawling bat over rivers and lakes.
Pacific Northwest temperate rainforest endemic. Broad FM sweep. Very similar to M. evotis acoustically. SE Alaska to southern BC.

costa_rica.description: Abundant in lowland forests. Roosts on tree trunks and building walls. Alternates ~45/48 kHz. Vocal learner with complex song repertoire.
Abundant in buildings and urban areas. Alternating QCF at ~34.5/39.6 kHz. One of the first species heard at dusk. Open-space aerial hawker.
Long CF at ~61 kHz with Doppler compensation—the ONLY high-duty-cycle echolocator in the New World. Unmistakable call. Huge cave colonies.
One of the most abundant Neotropical bats. Peak ~71 kHz. Low-intensity whispering calls—detectable only within a few meters. Key seed disperser.
Very common frugivore. Peak ~56 kHz. Variable intensity; not always a quiet whisperer. Important fig seed disperser throughout lowland forests.
QCF search calls with a characteristic frequency of about 25–29 kHz; FM during approach. Forms massive colonies. Fast, high-altitude forager.
Abundant nectarivore. Peak ~80 kHz. Low-intensity calls—hard to detect beyond a few meters. Uses echolocation to find flowers with acoustic reflectors.
Common near livestock. Short calls (about 2 ms). Peak about 57–61 kHz. Low-intensity. Obligate blood-feeder with infrared-sensing nose pits.
Tiny bat roosting in lines along riverbanks. Short narrowband calls near 95–100 kHz (2nd harmonic); detectors may pick up the 1st harmonic near 40–51 kHz. Cryptic bark-like camouflage.
Open-area forager near caves and buildings. Long QCF (about 9–14 ms) peaking near 41 kHz. Displays jamming avoidance in groups by shifting peak frequency.
Multiharmonic QCF at ~40 kHz (2nd harmonic). Found near caves and rock shelters. Distinctive musky odor.
CF at ~68 kHz with a sweep to a short QCF near 58 kHz. Wing membranes fused across back (naked-backed appearance). Cave-roosting; often with P. mesoamericanus.
CF at ~54–57 kHz. Largest Pteronotus. Similar to P. davyi but lower frequency. Cave-dwelling.
Bizarre leaf-chin face. Fundamental suppressed; 2nd harmonic, peak ~52 kHz, dominates recordings. Large cave colonies. Ghost-like appearance in flight.
Large fishing bat. Long CF at 53–56 kHz + FM sweep. Rakes water with large clawed feet to catch fish. Found along rivers, lakes, and coasts.
Highly plastic calls: narrowband ~7 ms in open space; broadband FM in clutter. Peak ~54–55 kHz. Common in forests and urban edges.
Large frugivore. Peak about 61–65 kHz. Low-intensity. Prominent facial stripes. Important pollinator and seed disperser.
Higher peak (~78 kHz) than C. perspicillata. Low-intensity FM. Frugivore preferring understory fruits. Common in wet lowland forests.
Peak about 69 kHz on the 2nd harmonic, like C. perspicillata. Low-intensity FM. Frugivore. Premontane and montane forests.
Nectarivore. Slightly lower peak (~75 kHz) than G. soricina. Low-intensity FM. Important pollinator of many tropical plants.
Famous frog-eating bat. Locates prey by listening to mating calls. Peak ~70 kHz. Low-intensity FM—hard to detect. Warty lips for gripping frogs.
Large omnivore. One of the lowest-frequency phyllostomids (~47 kHz peak). Low-intensity FM. Harem groups in caves and hollow trees.
Small frugivore. Peak ~75 kHz. Low-intensity FM—detectable only within a few meters. Common in lowland and premontane forests.
Gleaning insectivore. Very short broadband FM (about 0.35 ms, peak near 80 kHz). Ultra-low intensity—barely detectable beyond 2–3 m. Can find motionless prey.
Peak about 37–45 kHz. Source level ~101–106 dB SPL. FM-QCF. Frequency varies with temperature. Forest edges and open areas.
Higher frequency (~50 kHz) than S. bilineata. Similar QCF structure. Thinner dorsal stripes. Less common; found in lowland forests.
Unusual: most energy in 5th harmonic at ~68 kHz. Forest-interior forager. Multiharmonic calls.
Lower frequency (~32 kHz) than P. macrotis. 2nd harmonic dominant. Near caves and rocky outcrops in forested areas.
Highest frequency Pteronotus: initial CF ~83 kHz, terminal ~68 kHz. Doppler-shift compensation. Cave-roosting.
CF part at about 70–75 kHz, then an FM sweep down to about 40–45 kHz; higher than N. leporinus. Trawls insects and small fish from water. Less common than greater bulldog bat.
QCF at ~33 kHz. Open-space forager. Roosts in buildings. Slightly lower frequency than M. molossus.
QCF at ~35 kHz. Originally described from Coiba Island, Panama. Open-space forager. Smaller than other Molossus species.
Large molossid. Alternating calls that sweep down from about 32–36 kHz and end near 18 and 22 kHz. High, fast flight above canopy. Long-duration narrowband calls.
Very low frequency (~22–25 kHz) QCF. Large bat with long narrow wings. High-altitude forager above canopy.
Low frequency (~22 kHz) open-space forager. Flat face with forward-pointing nostrils. Roosts in buildings and hollow trees.
Distinctive upward-modulated QCF (unusual for molossids). Alternating pairs at ~30/35 kHz. Easily recognized on bat detector.
Three-frequency alternation (~26.7, 28.7, 32.4 kHz). Open-space forager. Roosts in rock crevices and buildings.
High repetition rates (15–20/s). Short FM calls (~2.5 ms). Peak ~55 kHz. Found in highlands and cloud forests.
Steep broadband FM sweep from about 100 to about 60 kHz; calls about 4–5 ms. Forages near streams and forest edges. Recorded in Costa Rica.
High-frequency FM (~55 kHz peak). Difficult to distinguish from M. nigricans acoustically. Small Myotis of lowland forests.
Lower frequency (~43 kHz) than E. brasiliensis. FM-QCF. More FM in cluttered habitats. Forest edges.
Open-air forager. Peak ~42 kHz. FM-QCF. Migratory. Roosts solitarily in foliage. Distinctive reddish fur.
Peak about 31–32 kHz, lower than L. blossevillii. FM-QCF. Roosts in palm fronds. Open-air forager around street lights.
Small vespertilionid. Broadband FM + QCF termination at ~48 kHz. Forages low in forest gaps and edges.
UNIQUE phyllostomid with CF-FM calls. Long CF at ~45 kHz (3rd harmonic). Longest phyllostomid calls (up to 8.7 ms). Extremely long nose-leaf. Cave-roosting.
Omnivore. Peak ~55 kHz. Low-intensity FM. Large colonies in hollow trees. Best hearing at 20 kHz. Low-frequency for a phyllostomid.
Gleaning insectivore that modifies termite nests into roosts. Peak ~70 kHz. Low-intensity FM—detectable only within a few meters.
High-altitude nectarivore. Peak ~70 kHz. Low-intensity FM. Cloud forests and highlands. Important pollinator.
Bizarre wrinkled face with retractable skin mask. Peak ~65 kHz. Relatively long calls for a stenodermatine (1–3 ms). Frugivore. Low-intensity.
Distinctive white fur. Narrowband QCF at ~24 kHz. Rarely encountered. High-altitude open-space forager. One of the most striking-looking bats.
Large vespertilionid. Peak ~30 kHz. FM-QCF. At southern edge of range in Costa Rica. Uncommon in highlands.
Largest bat in the Americas (wingspan ~1 m). Peak ~70 kHz. Low-intensity FM—very difficult to detect acoustically. Carnivorous: preys on birds and other bats.
Carnivorous gleaner. Peak ~77 kHz. Short FM (0.8–1.4 ms). Low-intensity—hard to detect beyond a few meters. Large ears; hunts other bats and rodents.
Unusual trawling phyllostomid. Louder than most relatives (~101 dB SPL). Peak ~85 kHz. Large feet for grabbing insects from water surfaces.
Gleaning insectivore. Lower peak (~52 kHz) than M. microtis. Low-intensity FM. Documented from Costa Rica. Forest interior.
Gleaning insectivore. Peak ~75 kHz. Low-intensity FM. Now Gardnerycteris crenulatum. Forest understory.
Gleaning insectivore/carnivore. Peak ~65 kHz. Low-intensity FM. Forest interior specialist. Roosts in hollow trees.
Rare gleaning insectivore. Peak ~75 kHz. Low-intensity FM. Poorly documented acoustically. Yellow throat patches.
Rare gleaner. Peak ~85 kHz. Ultra-short broadband FM (0.3–1 ms). Very low intensity. Forest interior.
Low-intensity gleaner. Peak ~80 kHz. Multiharmonic FM. Forest understory specialist. Rarely captured or detected.
Very small nectarivore. High frequency peak ~90 kHz. Low-intensity FM. Montane cloud forests. Poorly known acoustically.
Tiny (5–7 g) with the highest peak frequency of any phyllostomid (~100–118 kHz). Ultra-low intensity. Tent-roosting frugivore.
Iconic tiny white bat. Peak ~75 kHz. Low-intensity FM. Roosts in Heliconia leaf tents. Endemic to Central America. Specializes on one fig species.
Suction-cup disks for roosting in rolled Heliconia leaves. Extremely low intensity—barely detectable at <1 m. Distinctive social calls for roost-finding.
Among the highest frequency bats: peak ~100–130 kHz. Very low intensity—barely detectable beyond 50 cm. Delicate, cave-roosting. Formerly N. stramineus.
Very quiet calls (~35 kHz peak). Plecotus-like gleaning insectivore. Rare and poorly known. Montane forests.
Lowland forest frugivore. Multi-harmonic FM. Important Piper seed disperser. Separated from C. brevicauda by genetics.
Small frugivore of lowland forests. Tent-making roost behaviour. Multi-harmonic FM. Common in second-growth and disturbed forest.
Cloud forest and premontane frugivore. Multi-harmonic FM. Important seed disperser at higher elevations. Males have yellow shoulder epaulettes.
Widespread Neotropical molossid. Alternating QCF calls peaking near 29 and 33 kHz. Fast open-air forager. Roosts in buildings and tree hollows.
Pacific slope frugivore split from U. bilobatum. Modifies large leaves into tent roosts. Multi-harmonic FM.
Montane frugivore preferring cloud forest. Velvety brown fur. Quiet multi-harmonic FM.
Largest Lonchophylla species. Distinctive orange fur. Nectarivore of premontane and montane forests.
Small nectarivore. Visits Heliconia and tubular flowers. Multi-harmonic FM. Lowland forests.
Smallest Lophostoma. Gleaning insectivore. Roosts in termite nests and hollow trees. Multi-harmonic FM.
Very small gleaning insectivore. Broadband multi-harmonic FM, very quiet. Forest-dependent.
Forest gleaner recently split from T. saurophila. Multi-harmonic FM calls. Understory specialist.
Recently described molossid. Alternating QCF calls near 31 and 34 kHz, a third tone near 37 kHz. Acoustically and genetically distinct from M. molossus.
Large bonneted bat. Low-frequency QCF ~18–25 kHz. Fast high-altitude forager with long narrow wings.
Rare canopy-dwelling emballonurid. QCF ~40–45 kHz. Shaggy fur. Roosts singly on tree trunks and in leaf clusters.
Rare nectarivore with elongated muzzle. Very quiet FM calls. Poorly known ecology.
Recently split from M. keaysi. Steep FM sweeps from ~90–110 kHz to a tail near 59 kHz. Forest and forest-edge forager. Characteristic hairy tibia.
Caribbean endemic mormoopid. CF-FM with CF at ~70 kHz. Smallest Pteronotus. Cave-dwelling.
Large frugivore with distinctive facial stripes. Very quiet multi-harmonic FM. Feeds on figs. Canopy forager.
Small broad-nosed frugivore. Multi-harmonic FM. Common in lowland forests. Roosts in small groups under leaves and in hollow trees.
Tiny frugivore (~8 g). Multi-harmonic FM, very quiet. Tent-making behaviour. Lowland forests.
Largest stenodermatine. Multi-harmonic FM. Bold facial stripes. Roosts in modified palm leaves. Feeds primarily on figs.
Hairy-legged vampire specialising on bird blood. Very quiet FM calls. Approaches roosting birds from below. Less studied than Desmodus.
Small Myotis with silvery-tipped fur. FM sweeps. Forages near water and over clearings. Widespread Neotropics.
Montane Myotis of cloud forests and highlands. FM sweeps ~80–40 kHz. Costa Rica to Bolivia.

east_asia.name: Greater Horseshoe Bat (East Asian)
east_asia.description: Very common across China and Korea. CF ~66–77 kHz: 66–72 in Korea (higher on Jeju), about 68–77 in China. Caves and mines.
South and central China. CF varies by subspecies: ~87 kHz (Yunnan) to ~74 kHz (eastern China). Reservoir host of SARS-like coronaviruses.
Southern China and Taiwan. CF ~103–108 kHz. Caves and rock crevices.
South and central China. CF ~58–70 kHz (higher in eastern China). Hilly and montane forest.
South China (Yunnan, Guangxi, Sichuan). CF ~30–35 kHz. Primary forest. Solitary roosts in caves and tree hollows.
South and central China and Taiwan. CF ~65–75 kHz. Performs Doppler-shift compensation. Large cave colonies.
Southern China. CF ~79–88 kHz (higher in Hainan, lower in Yunnan) (cryptic species complex, two phonic types). Caves.
South China (Yunnan, Guangxi, Guangdong, Hainan). Carnivorous gleaner; locates prey by passive listening.
SW China (Guangxi, Yunnan, Hainan). FM ~25–40 kHz. Rock walls and cave ceilings.
China (Hebei, Beijing, Heilongjiang), Korea, Russia. FM-QCF ~11–19 kHz, peak ~13–15 kHz (Japanese data). Fast high-altitude forager.
Southern China (Yunnan, Guangxi, Guangdong). QCF ~25–30 kHz. Enormous cave colonies.
Widespread in China, Korea, Taiwan. FM-QCF, end ~45–50 kHz, peak ~48–55 kHz. Fast agile flier. Cave-roosting.
Widespread across China, Taiwan, and Korea. FM ~120–30 kHz, peak ~44–50 kHz. Distinctive orange-brown coloring. Forest insectivore.
China and Korea. FM ~110–50 kHz. Edge-space forager near cliffs and caves.
China, Korea, Russia. FM ~120–40 kHz, peak ~50–57 kHz. Small forest bat.
China and Korea. FM ~90–35 kHz, peak ~49–52 kHz. Trawling insectivore over water.
Extremely common across China, Korea, Taiwan. FM-QCF ~45–48 kHz peak. Most common urban bat in East Asia.
China and Korea. FM-QCF ~19–21 kHz peak. Forages up to 300 m altitude. Occasionally preys on migrating birds.
Widespread across China, Korea, Russia. FM-QCF ~24 kHz peak. Migratory. Tree hollows and buildings.
China and Korea. FM-QCF ~29–32 kHz peak. Open habitats and urban areas.

east_asia.name: Northern Bat
east_asia.description: Mongolia, northern China, Korea. FM-QCF ~30–32 kHz. The world’s most northerly bat.
Mongolia and northern China. FM-QCF calls ~25 kHz peak. Open steppe habitats.
China, Korea, Mongolia. Alternating FM: type A ~32–37 kHz, type B ~38–45 kHz. Forest-dwelling.
China and Korea. Broadband FM ~120→35 kHz, peak ~50–55 kHz. Forest gleaner.
Southern China and Taiwan. QCF ~44–47 kHz. Open-country forager; buildings and palms.
South and central China, Taiwan. Tongue-click echolocation. Cave-roosting fruit bat.
Southern China and Taiwan. Tent-roosting fruit bat. Important pollinator.
China and Vietnam. FM sweeps. Trawling forager over rivers and lakes. Large feet for gaffing prey from water.

eswatini.description: Most commonly recorded bat in Eswatini. Peak ~34–38 kHz; the similar S. mhlanganii calls at ~43 kHz. Buildings and tree hollows.
Common small bat in savanna and woodland. FM-QCF ~65–70 kHz. Buildings and tree hollows.
Common pipistrelle. FM ~43–47 kHz. Forest edges and towns.
CF ~138–144 kHz. Caves and hollow trees. Common across Eswatini.
Cave-roosting. FM-QCF ~54 kHz. Important maternity caves in Eswatini highlands.
Slit-faced bat. Very quiet broadband FM. Gleaning specialist. Hollow trees and culverts.
CF ~86–90 kHz. Caves and mine adits. Relatively common in Eswatini.
FM-QCF ~22–28 kHz. Roosting on walls and trunks. Open-air forager.
Rufous Myotis. FM sweeps. Forages over water and forest edges.
Long-tailed serotine. FM-QCF ~28–32 kHz. Savanna and forest edge.
CF ~90–92 kHz. Caves. Highland areas of Eswatini.
CF ~83–84 kHz. Savannas. Often sympatric with R. swinnyi.
High CF ~107 kHz. Dense vegetation forager.
QCF ~20–28 kHz. Cliff and building rooster. Open-air forager.
Cave-roosting fruit bat. Tongue-click echolocation. Highland caves.
Angolan free-tailed bat. QCF ~25–30 kHz. Buildings and hollow trees.
Cape serotine. FM-QCF ~37–40 kHz. Common in towns and savanna.
Green house bat. FM-QCF ~39–42 kHz. Lowveld savanna.
Blasius's horseshoe bat. CF ~94–98 kHz. Caves.
CF ~44–46 kHz. Caves and rock overhangs.
Lesser long-fingered bat. FM ~58–62 kHz. Caves.
Temminck's myotis. FM. Cave-roosting. Highland areas.
Schlieffen's twilight bat. FM ~43–48 kHz. One of the earliest bats to emerge.
Butterfly bat. FM ~38–42 kHz. Distinctive wing pattern. Woodland.
Welwitsch's myotis. FM. Forest and woodland. Long orange-tipped fur.
Rusty pipistrelle. FM-QCF ending ~53–57 kHz, peak ~56–62 kHz. Woodland and savanna.
Striped leaf-nosed bat. CF ~62 kHz. Caves. Large and distinctive.
Percival's trident bat. Highest bat echolocation frequency ~212 kHz. Requires >400 kHz sample rate detectors.
No echolocation. Wahlberg's fruit bat. Common in savanna and gardens.
African sheath-tailed bat. FM-QCF. Caves and rock overhangs.

europe.description: Fast, agile cave-dweller found across southern Europe. Long, narrow wings. Formerly one species; now split into several. Sensitive to cave disturbance.
Europe's only free-tailed bat. Loud, low-frequency calls audible to humans. Fast, high-altitude forager. Restricted to the Mediterranean; roosts in cliff crevices and tall buildings.
Widespread across Mediterranean Europe. Shallow FM sweep ending in QCF tail ~32–34 kHz. Common around buildings and cliffs.
Gleaning insectivore with distinctive notched ears. FM sweeps. Picks spiders and flies from foliage. Warm-temperate Europe; cave-roosting.
Medium horseshoe bat of southern Europe. CF peak ~94–98 kHz. Often roosts with R. euryale and R. ferrumequinum in caves.
Recently described from the M. daubentonii complex. Greece and Turkey populations. FM sweeps similar to Daubenton's bat.

greece.description: Abundant across Greece from sea level to mountains. Characteristic frequency ~45 kHz.
Common in riparian habitats and coastal areas. ~55 kHz. Often sympatric with common pipistrelle.
Abundant in urban areas and around street lights. ~40 kHz. Expanding across the Mediterranean.
Common across Greece, especially around cliffs and buildings. FM-QCF ~32–34 kHz.
Loud low-frequency calls ~10–12 kHz, audible to humans. Cliff-roosting. Common in mountainous areas.
Widespread in caves and old buildings. CF ~82–83 kHz. Large colonies in karst regions.
Common in caves and cellars. CF ~110 kHz. Found across mainland and islands.
Cave-dwelling; CF ~104 kHz. Important populations in the Peloponnese and northern Greece.
Large cave colonies across Greece. FM ~52 kHz. Important maternity colonies on Crete and mainland.
Gleaning insectivore with notched ears. FM. Common in warm-temperate areas; cave and building rooster.
Fast open-air forager. QCF ~25 kHz. Tree-roosting. Common but under-recorded.
Trawling bat over Mediterranean rivers and lakes. FM ~48 kHz. Important populations in Greek caves.
Mediterranean long-eared bat. Very quiet FM. Adriatic and Aegean coasts; recently split from P. austriacus.
CF ~94–98 kHz. Cave-dwelling; often with R. euryale and R. ferrumequinum. Mediterranean habitats.
Large ground-gleaning Myotis. FM. Cave-roosting.
Recently split from M. daubentonii complex. FM. Greek and Turkish populations.
Mountain long-eared bat. Very quiet FM. Found in mountainous regions of northern Greece.
Migratory. ~38 kHz. Passage migrant and occasional breeder in Greece.
Endemic to Crete and nearby islands. ~47–48 kHz. Recently described cryptic species.
Forest-dependent. Alternating FM ~32/34 kHz. Rare in Greece; found in montane forests.
Large noctule. QCF ~20 kHz. Migratory; more common in northern Greece.
Large Myotis. FM. Cave colonies. Hunts grasshoppers in open habitats.
CF ~106–108 kHz. Cave-dwelling. Southern and western Greece; often with R. euryale.
Migratory. FM-QCF ~25 kHz. Passage migrant and occasional breeder.
Grey long-eared bat. Very quiet FM. Lowland and Mediterranean habitats.
Very quiet broadband FM. Limited distribution in northern Greece.
FM ~45 kHz. Woodland edges. Presence confirmed in northern Greece.
Old-growth forest specialist. Very quiet broadband FM. Rare in Greece.
Cryptic Myotis. FM. Recently confirmed in Greece; montane forests.
Europe's largest bat. QCF ~16–18 kHz. Rare in Greece; migratory.

greece.name: Northern Bat
greece.description: FM ~30 kHz. Very limited in northern mountainous Greece.
Tongue-click echolocation. Limited to a few Aegean islands; non-echolocating fruit bat.

japan.description: Japan's most common urban bat. FM sweep into a long shallow tail ending near 41–45 kHz, peak ~45–48 kHz. Roosts in buildings, forages around streetlights. Found throughout the archipelago.

CF-FM calls with CF ~65–70 kHz (about 65 in Hokkaido, 67–70 in Shikoku and Kyushu). FM/CF/FM structure. Widespread from Hokkaido to Kyushu. Cave, mine, and tunnel roosts. Key species for Doppler-shift research.
CF-FM calls with peak CF ~103–111 kHz, increasing from north to south (103–104 kHz in Aomori, 108–111 kHz on Amami-Oshima). Endemic to Japan. Caves and buildings.
FM sweep into a short shallow tail, end ~45–50 kHz, peak ~48–52 kHz. Shows geographic variation in peak frequency among colonies. Fast agile flier. Large cave maternity colonies. Honshu to Ryukyus.
Steep FM sweeps ~80–35 kHz, peak ~49–52 kHz. Trawling insectivore using large feet to gaff prey from water surfaces. Rivers and streams throughout Japan.
FM-QCF calls, peak ~24–25 kHz, end ~22 kHz, start ~48 kHz (up to ~56). Steep FM into shallow QCF tail. Migratory species with seasonal movements through the archipelago. Hokkaido to Kyushu.
FM-QCF calls, peak ~21 kHz, search calls ~16–21 ms, the longest among Japanese vespertilionids. Japan's largest insectivorous bat. Forages up to 300 m altitude. Occasionally preys on migrating birds.
Low-intensity FM calls, start ~46 kHz, peak ~41 kHz, end ~23 kHz. Gleaning forager specialising in fluttering moths via passive listening. Endemic to Japan. Forest-dwelling.
Very short broadband FM sweeps from ~105–125 kHz down to ~27–44 kHz, peak ~50–55 kHz. Forest gleaner. Hokkaido to Kyushu. Roosts in tree hollows and dead curled leaves.

Very short broadband FM sweeps from ~90–135 kHz down to ~42–55 kHz, peak higher than M. hilgendorfi (~62–65 kHz in Kyushu and Shikoku, ~86 kHz in Hokkaido). Tiny bat (4–8 g). Remarkably hibernates under snow. Roosts in curled dead leaves. Hokkaido and Honshu.
Broadband FM calls typical of Murina. Distribution spans ~2000 km north–south across Japan. Sometimes considered conspecific with M. ussuriensis. Curled-leaf roosts.

CF-FM calls with CF ~105–120 kHz, higher in southern than in northern Okinawa. Shows 5–8 kHz dialect difference between northern and southern Okinawa populations, maintained by maternal transmission. Central and southern Ryukyus.
CF-FM calls with CF ~92–93 kHz on Iriomote. Yaeyama Islands (Iriomote and Kohama). Often treated as part of R. perditus.
FM calls slightly higher frequency than M. fuliginosus due to smaller body size. Ryukyu Islands and southern Kyushu. Cave-roosting.
Steep FM sweeps, peak ~50.6 kHz, start ~90 kHz, end ~43 kHz, duration ~2 ms. Small forest bat of Hokkaido and northern Honshu.
Very broadband FM calls from ~70–135 kHz down to ~20–30 kHz, peak ~36–57 kHz. Gleaning insectivore, hawks near vegetation. Forests of Kyushu and other regions.
Brief FM pulses ~110–50 kHz, duration ~3.5 ms. Edge-space forager near cliffs and caves. Honshu and Kyushu.
FM-QCF calls, peak ~30.5 kHz, duration ~6 ms, bandwidth ~32 kHz. Hokkaido and northern Honshu. The most northerly-ranging bat in the world.
CF-FM calls, peak CF ~92–98 kHz (92–93 on Iriomote, 96–98 on Ishigaki). Endemic to the Yaeyama Islands. Forest-dwelling, cave-roosting.
CF calls at ~77–84 kHz (about 82 kHz on Iriomote). Southern Ryukyu Islands (Ishigaki, Iriomote, Miyako). Limestone cave roosts. Feeds mainly on beetles.
Low-intensity FM calls, dominant ~29–33 kHz with four harmonics. Marginal occurrence in Japan (Ryukyu Islands). Roosts on rock walls and in caves.
Low FM-QCF search calls ~19–11 kHz, peak ~13–14 kHz. Fast, high-flying open-air forager. Western Japan. Roosts in rock crevices and buildings.
Echolocation ~20 kHz. High-altitude flier, very difficult to capture. Known in Japan from a single specimen on Amami-Oshima (1985). IUCN Data Deficient.
FM sweeps typical of Myotis. Endemic to Japan (Honshu, Shikoku, Kyushu). Forest-dwelling, roosts in tree hollows and buildings. Named for frosted fur.
Steep downward FM calls. Distinctive orange-brown coloring. Tsushima Island and western Japan. Forest-dwelling insectivore.
FM calls typical of Myotis. Endemic to Japan (Honshu). Cave-dwelling. Poorly studied species.
FM calls typical of small Myotis. Endemic to Japan (Honshu). Forest-dwelling. Limited published acoustic data.
FM calls typical of Myotis. Endemic to central Honshu mountains. Cave-dwelling. Very limited distribution.
FM-QCF calls similar to P. abramus but slightly lower frequency. Endemic to Japan (Honshu). Temperate forests at 100–1500 m. IUCN Near Threatened.
FM-QCF calls similar to E. nilssonii. Endemic to Japan (Honshu, Shikoku, Kyushu). Forest-dwelling, roosts in tree hollows and buildings.
FM calls in two alternating types: type A at 32–37 kHz, type B at 38–45 kHz. Very elusive. Rare in Japan (Honshu). Forest-dwelling.
Broadband FM calls typical of Murina. Endemic to the Ryukyu Islands. Recently described species from Okinawa. Forest-dwelling.
FM calls above 40 kHz. Endemic to northern Okinawa (Yanbaru forest). Described in 1997. One of the rarest bats in Japan. Subtropical forest only.
FM calls presumed similar to other Murina. Known only from a single holotype on Tsushima Island (1962). Possibly extinct due to deforestation. Alliance for Zero Extinction species.
Presumed FM-QCF calls. Known only from a specimen on the Bonin Islands (Ogasawara). Not seen since 1915—possibly extinct.
Large fruit bat of the Ryukyu Islands (4 subspecies in Japan). Does not echolocate. Feeds on fruit, flowers, and leaves. Endangered due to habitat loss and hunting.

kenya.description: Most commonly recorded bat in Kenya. Peak ~34–38 kHz; the similar S. mhlanganii calls at ~43 kHz. Roosts in buildings.

kenya.name: Little Free-tailed Bat
kenya.description: Abundant in buildings across Kenya. QCF ~21–25 kHz. Urban areas.
Common leaf-nosed bat. CF ~145–156 kHz. Caves, hollow trees, and buildings across Kenya.
Common pipistrelle across Kenya. FM ~43–47 kHz. Forest edges and towns.
FM-QCF ending ~53–57 kHz, peak ~56–62 kHz. Woodland and savanna. Tree hollows and buildings.
Tomb bat roosting on building walls and tree trunks. FM-QCF ~22–28 kHz. Open-air forager.
Cave-roosting. FM ~52 kHz. Large colonies in Rift Valley caves.
CF ~102–108 kHz. Caves and hollow trees. Widespread across Kenya.

kenya.name: Lesser Yellow Bat
kenya.description: Coastal Kenya. FM-QCF ~35 kHz. Buildings and palm trees.

kenya.name: Epauletted Fruit Bat
kenya.description: No echolocation. Loud honking fruit bat. Common in savanna and woodland.
No echolocation. Large straw-colored fruit bat forming massive camps of millions. Long-distance migrant.
Large molossid. QCF ~22–26 kHz. Western Kenya forests.
Recently split from M. natalensis. FM ~50–55 kHz. East African caves.
FM ~35–45 kHz. Dry woodland. Roosts in buildings.
Distinctive silvery wing pattern. FM ~40–50 kHz. Western Kenya forests.
Highland forest pipistrelle. FM ~45–50 kHz. Montane areas.
Large sit-and-wait predator of coastal and savanna Kenya. Heart-shaped noseleaf. Quiet broadband FM.
Large horseshoe bat. CF ~54–56 kHz. Caves and rock overhangs.
Slit-faced bat. Very quiet broadband FM. Gleaning specialist. Hollow trees and buildings.
Tongue-click echolocation in caves. Large fruit bat. Important cave populations at Mt. Elgon and Kitum Cave.
Cape serotine. FM-QCF ~37–40 kHz. Common in towns and savanna across Kenya.
Angolan free-tailed bat. QCF ~25–30 kHz. Buildings and hollow trees. Often with Chaerephon pumilus.
Geoffroy's horseshoe bat. CF ~90–92 kHz. Caves across Kenya.
Large horseshoe bat. CF ~42 kHz. Caves and rock overhangs. Widespread in Kenya.
Green house bat. FM-QCF ~40–48 kHz. Buildings and tree hollows. Savanna and woodland.
Noack's leaf-nosed bat. CF ~133–145 kHz (males about 133, females about 140–145). Caves and hollow trees. Western Kenya forests.
Giant mastiff bat. Very low QCF ~11–14 kHz, audible to humans. Cliff and cave rooster.
No echolocation. Wahlberg's fruit bat. Honking calls. Savanna and suburban gardens.
Egyptian free-tailed bat. QCF ~20–28 kHz. Cliffs and buildings.
CF ~86 kHz. Coastal and lowland caves. East African endemic.
Large horseshoe bat. CF ~50–52 kHz. Highland caves. East African endemic.
Recently split from O. martiensseni. Very low QCF ~14–24 kHz. Caves and buildings.
Dark-winged house bat. Shallow FM ending ~30–34 kHz. Savanna and woodland. Roosts in buildings.

mexico.description: Abundant across Mexico. QCF ~25 kHz. Massive cave colonies. Forms the famous column emergence at Cueva de la Boca.
Very common frugivore across lowland and mid-elevation Mexico. Quiet multi-harmonic FM.
