Abundant nectarivore across Mexico. Very quiet FM. Important cactus and agave pollinator.
Common in buildings and hollow trees. Alternating QCF, ~34–39 kHz.
Long CF at ~61 kHz. Large cave colonies. The only high-duty-cycle bat in the New World.
CF ~73 kHz, sweep to a QCF near 60 kHz. Pacific and Gulf lowlands, Sonora and Tamaulipas south. Cave-roosting.
CF ~82 kHz, sweep to a QCF near 65 kHz. Recently split from P. personatus. Cave-dwelling.
2nd harmonic dominant, peak ~52 kHz. Large cave colonies. Northern and central Mexico.
Alternating QCF peaking near 29 and 33 kHz. Fast open-air forager. Common in buildings.
QCF ~40 kHz (2nd harmonic). Lowland forests and cave entrances.
Common vampire bat. Very quiet FM. Livestock areas throughout Mexico.
Desert bat. High QCF ~46 kHz. Northern Mexico deserts.
QCF ~17–22 kHz. Rock crevices in arid regions.
FM-QCF ~27 kHz. Buildings and bridges. Highland areas.
Recently described. Alternating QCF calls near 31 and 34 kHz. Yucatan and southern Mexico.
Pacific slope of Mexico. Long QCF calls, peak ~31 kHz; high and low calls alternate about 6.5 kHz apart.
Yucatan endemic. FM ~48–53 kHz. Forest edges.
Large molossid. QCF ~20–25 kHz. Fast high-altitude forager.
FM sweeps. Forest and forest-edge forager. Southern Mexico.
Nectar bat. Quiet FM. Key pollinator of columnar cacti and agave. Migratory.
Common short-tailed frugivore. Multi-harmonic FM. Important Piper seed disperser.
Large bonneted bat. Alternating calls sweeping down from about 32–36 kHz to near 18 and 22 kHz. Open-air forager.
Gray sac-winged bat. Long QCF (about 12 ms) peaking near 41 kHz. Abundant at cave entrances and rock walls across Mexico.
Large frugivore. Quiet multi-harmonic FM. Lowland forests.
Distinctive two-lined sac-winged bat. FM-QCF. Tree trunks and buildings in lowland forests.
Big free-tailed bat. Low QCF, peak ~20–22 kHz. Canyon and cliff crevices across Mexico.
Cave myotis. FM ~45–50 kHz. Large cave colonies in central Mexico.
Mexican funnel-eared bat. Very quiet FM, peak ~100–130 kHz. Hot humid caves.
Eastern red bat. FM ~40 kHz. Solitary tree-roosting. Northern and highland Mexico.
Western red bat. FM ~40 kHz. Solitary tree-roosting.
Mexican long-nosed bat. Quiet FM. Key agave pollinator. Highland caves.
Highland yellow-shouldered bat. Quiet FM. Cloud forests.
Large carnivorous phyllostomid. Very quiet broadband FM. Caves and hollow trees.
Greater bulldog bat. FM-QCF ~55 kHz. Fish-eating specialist over coastal and freshwater.
Underwood's bonneted bat. Low QCF ~14–28 kHz. Arid and semiarid western Mexico. Loud calls.
Mexican endemic molossid. QCF ~22–38 kHz. Tropical dry forest and thorn scrub.
Highland endemic frugivore. Whispering FM. Cloud forests of Mexico.
Common lowland frugivore. Whispering FM. Recently split from S. lilium. Important seed disperser.

middle_east.description: Very common across Turkey, Levant, Iran, Central Asia. CF ~78–84 kHz. Caves and mines.
Turkey through Iran. CF ~105–115 kHz. Caves and buildings near dense vegetation.
Turkey, Levant, Iran. CF about 100–106 kHz. Cave-roosting.
Middle East caves. CF about 93–94 kHz. Often sympatric with R. euryale and R. mehelyi.
Egypt, Levant, Arabia. QCF, peak about 27–31 kHz. Arid regions; tombs, ruins, and rock faces.
Turkey, Israel, Arabia. QCF ~10–14 kHz, partially audible to humans. Cliff and building crevices.
Widespread across entire region. QCF ~18–23 kHz. High-flying open-air forager.
Turkey, Levant, Iran. FM ~47–57 kHz. Large cave colonies.
Turkey, Iran, Levant caves. FM ~22–86 kHz. Often in large cave colonies.
Dominant urban pipistrelle across the entire region. FM ~35–45 kHz peak.
Turkey, Caucasus, northern Levant. FM ~42–51 kHz peak.
Arid zones and waterways across the region. FM-QCF, ends at about 50–53 kHz.
Mediterranean Turkey, Levant, Iran. FM ~28–42 kHz peak.
Turkey, Iran, Caucasus. FM-QCF ~22–55 kHz. Open habitats.
Turkey, Iran, Central Asia. QCF ~18–25 kHz. Fast high-altitude forager.
Central Asia (Kazakhstan, Uzbekistan, Kyrgyzstan). FM-QCF ~25 kHz. Open steppe.
Levant, Sinai, Arabia to Central Asia. Alternates short calls peaking about 34 kHz with longer calls peaking about 43 kHz.
Sinai and Arabian margins. Very low intensity FM. Gleaner; almost undetectable on bat detectors.
Large cave colonies in Israel, Turkey, Egypt. Tongue-click echolocation. Key Middle Eastern cave bat.

netherlands.description: Most common bat in the Netherlands. ~45 kHz. Urban gardens and parks.
~55 kHz. Increasingly recorded; favours riparian habitats.
Common migratory species. ~38 kHz. Important stopover country for NE European populations.
Common over canals, ditches, and lakes. FM trawling.
Common in rural areas and villages. FM ~27 kHz. Roosts in buildings.
QCF ~20 kHz. Tree hollows and bat boxes. Common across the country.
QCF ~25 kHz. Tree-roosting. Common in parks and forests.
Very quiet FM. Old buildings, churches, forests. Relatively common.
Largest Dutch Myotis. Ground-gleaning beetle specialist. Cave hibernation sites in Limburg.
Netherlands is a stronghold for this species. Trawling bat over broad waterways. FM. Internationally important populations.
Villages and woodland edges. FM ~45 kHz.
Broadband FM gleaner. Forests and old buildings.
Mature forests. FM. Difficult to separate from whiskered bat.
Rare old-growth forest specialist. Very quiet broadband FM. Conservation priority.
Extremely rare in the Netherlands. Alternating FM ~32/34 kHz. Old-growth forest.
Migratory. QCF ~25 kHz. Passage migrant, occasionally breeds.
Southern Netherlands only. Very quiet FM. Warmer lowland areas.

netherlands.name: Northern Bat
netherlands.description: Occasional vagrant from Scandinavia. FM ~30 kHz.
Geoffroy's bat. FM. Rare; southern border only (Limburg).
~40 kHz. Recent arrival expanding northward with climate change. First Dutch records in 2010s.
Europe's largest bat. QCF ~16–18 kHz. Occasional vagrant; very rare records.

north_america.description: North America's most frequently encountered bat in buildings. FM-QCF calls with characteristic frequency ~30 kHz are loud and distinctive on spectrograms. Tolerates cold well; one of few species active in winter.
Forms the largest bat colonies on Earth — Bracken Cave, TX holds ~20 million. QCF search calls ~25–29 kHz, varying from flat to FM. Long narrow wings for fast, high flight.

Historically the most commonly encountered bat across northern North America. FM sweep ~80–40 kHz, characteristic frequency ~40 kHz. Populations have crashed >90% in eastern range due to White-nose Syndrome since 2006.
Solitary foliage-roosting tree bat with distinctive reddish fur. FM sweep with characteristic frequency ~40 kHz. Long-distance migrant. One of the most common bats in eastern forests and suburbs.

North America's largest bat (~30 g) with frosted brown fur. Distinctive low-frequency QCF calls ~20–25 kHz, unmistakable on spectrograms. Solitary, migratory. Most frequently killed bat at wind energy facilities.

Medium-sized bat with silver-tipped dark fur. Low-frequency QCF calls ~25–27 kHz. Slow, maneuverable flight over water and forest clearings. Solitary tree-roosting migrant. Second most common wind turbine fatality.

Tiny bat (~6 g) formerly called Eastern Pipistrelle. FM sweep, characteristic frequency ~42–43 kHz. Distinctive slow, erratic fluttery flight. Tricolored fur bands. Severely impacted by White-nose Syndrome.

Smallest North American bat (~3.5 g), formerly Western Pipistrelle. FM sweep with characteristic frequency ~46 kHz. Common in desert canyons. Often the first bat flying at dusk, sometimes before sunset.
Medium-sized bat of the eastern US. FM-QCF calls ~38 kHz characteristic frequency. Resembles a small Big Brown Bat. Roosts in tree cavities and buildings; does not use caves.

Small, adaptable western Myotis. FM sweep with characteristic frequency ~50 kHz. Often the most common bat detected at western sites. Difficult to distinguish acoustically from Western Small-footed Myotis.
Western water-foraging specialist that trawls insects from the surface with oversized feet. FM sweep with characteristic frequency ~50 kHz. Common near rivers, lakes, and stock tanks.
Western coniferous forest bat. FM sweep with characteristic frequency ~40 kHz. Keeled calcar and furred underwing membrane are diagnostic in hand. Fast, direct flight through forest canopy.
Large Myotis of the south-central US. FM sweep with characteristic frequency ~45 kHz. Forms large cave colonies. Bare patches on back between shoulder blades are diagnostic in hand.

Unique dual forager: echolocates for aerial prey and passively listens to glean scorpions and large insects from the ground. FM calls ~30 kHz. Large ears, pale fur. Immune to scorpion venom. Western deserts and grasslands.
Southeastern counterpart of the Eastern Red Bat with deep mahogany fur. FM sweep ~63 to 40 kHz, characteristic frequency ~40 kHz. Roosts in Spanish moss and pine needle clusters.

Western counterpart of the Eastern Red Bat. FM-QCF calls with characteristic frequency ~42 kHz. Solitary foliage-roosting migrant. Found from British Columbia to Argentina. Reddish fur similar to Eastern Red Bat.

Enormous ears (~35 mm). Very quiet, short FM calls ~25–40 kHz for gleaning moths. Highly sensitive to roost disturbance. Found across the western US; several isolated eastern subspecies are endangered.
Named for the distinctive fringe of stiff hairs along the tail membrane. Steep FM sweep ~66 to 20 kHz, characteristic frequency ~21–26 kHz. Western mountains; roosts in caves, mines, and buildings.
Very quiet, short FM calls typical of a gleaning forager, characteristic frequency ~34 kHz. Large ears extend well beyond the nose when laid forward. Western forests and woodlands.
Tiny bat (~5 g) of western arid lands. FM sweep with characteristic frequency ~44 kHz. Calls nearly identical to California Myotis. Roosts in rock crevices, cliff faces, and eroded badlands.
One of North America's smallest bats (~5 g). FM sweep with characteristic frequency ~50–55 kHz. Roosts in rock crevices and talus slopes. Appears somewhat resistant to White-nose Syndrome.
Southeastern US cave bat often found near water. FM sweep with characteristic frequency ~44–45 kHz. Forms large maternity colonies; Florida cave colonies can number in the tens of thousands.
Large yellowish tree bat of the southeastern coastal plain. FM-QCF calls ~30 kHz characteristic frequency. Roosts in dead palm fronds and Spanish moss along the Gulf and Atlantic coasts.
Southwestern desert species with yellowish fur. FM-QCF calls ~34 kHz characteristic frequency. Roosts in palm fronds. Range expanding northward with ornamental palm plantings in urban areas.
Southeastern big-eared bat with white belly fur. Very quiet gleaning calls ~25–40 kHz. Roosts in abandoned buildings, hollow trees, and under bridges. State-listed in many southeastern states.

Large free-tailed bat with low QCF calls (peak ~20–22 kHz, down to ~14–18 kHz), often audible to humans. Roosts in high cliff crevices in the Southwest. Loud piercing social calls carry long distances.
Medium-sized free-tailed bat of the southwestern deserts. QCF calls ~22 kHz. Named for the pocket-like fold on the tail membrane. Roosts in rock crevices in desert canyon country.
Largest bat in North America by wingspan (~56 cm). Very low QCF calls ~10–12 kHz, easily audible. Needs a vertical drop to launch into flight; roosts on tall cliff faces and high buildings.

Low-intensity gleaning FM calls (peak about 60 kHz, sweeping from about 80 to 47 kHz), hard to detect. Large ears and prominent nose leaf. Non-migratory desert species in AZ and southern CA. Cannot hibernate; depends on warm mines and caves year-round.

Lowest echolocation frequency of any North American bat (~10–12 kHz), easily audible. Unmistakable appearance: three large white spots on jet-black fur, enormous pink ears. Sparse but widespread across western arid lands.

Short FM search calls ~30 to 14 kHz; long trills at ~20–27 kHz are social calls, often audible. Distinctive lappets project from base of oversized ears. Southwestern pine-oak forests. Calls unlike any other North American bat of similar size.

Range barely enters southern Texas at a single cave. Calls peak ~52 kHz (2nd harmonic). Bizarre facial features with leaf-like skin flaps. Tropical species at the extreme northern edge of its range in the US.
Nectar-feeding bat with elongated snout. Very quiet FM calls ~75 kHz. Seasonal migrant to southern Arizona. Visits hummingbird feeders. Low-intensity echolocation typical of phyllostomids.

Major pollinator of saguaro and organ pipe cacti. Quiet FM calls sweeping from about 85 to 50 kHz. Migrates to southern Arizona in summer. Formerly endangered, delisted in 2018 — a conservation success story.

Steep broadband FM sweeps ~35–115 kHz (characteristic frequency ~43 kHz). Gleaning forager in forest understory. Populations have declined >99% in parts of the eastern range due to White-nose Syndrome. Federally endangered since 2023.
Calls nearly identical to Little Brown Myotis, characteristic frequency ~41 kHz. Hibernates in dense clusters in limestone caves; a single cave may hold thousands. Federally endangered since 1967.

Largest eastern Myotis. FM sweep ~80–42 kHz, characteristic frequency ~46 kHz. Obligate cave bat year-round. Populations recovering under federal protection; some colonies now exceed historic numbers.
Restricted to southern Florida. Low QCF calls ~14–16 kHz, occasionally audible. One of the rarest bats in North America. Roosts in tree cavities and bat houses. Federally endangered.
Nectar bat that migrates to the Big Bend region of Texas in summer. Quiet FM calls ~75 kHz. Pollinates agave. Only known US roost is a single cave in the Chisos Mountains. Federally endangered.
Medium tree bat. FM characteristic frequency ~35–40 kHz. Roosts in dead palm fronds. Southern USA (Texas, Louisiana, Florida) to South America. Formerly Lasiurus ega.
Mexican mormoopid split from P. davyi complex. CF ~73 kHz with a sweep to a QCF near 60 kHz. Cave-roosting in large colonies. Dry forests of western Mexico.
Recently split from P. personatus. CF ~82 kHz with a sweep to a QCF near 65 kHz. Mexican lowland and premontane forests. Cave-dwelling.
Widespread Neotropical molossid. Alternating QCF peaking near 29 and 33 kHz. Fast open-air forager. Common in buildings across Mexico and Central America.
Recently described from Mexico and Central America. Alternating QCF calls near 31 and 34 kHz. Acoustically distinct from M. molossus.
Emballonurid with multiharmonic QCF; most energy in 2nd harmonic at ~40 kHz. Mexican lowlands.
Large crested mastiff bat. Alternating calls: a low call rising ~26 to 28 kHz and a high call falling ~36 to 30 kHz. Fast high-altitude forager. Roosts in tree hollows. Mexico to South America.
Small vespertilionid of the Yucatan Peninsula. FM sweeps ~48–53 kHz. Forest edges and secondary growth.
Split from M. keaysi. FM sweeps. Forest and forest-edge forager across Mexico and Central America.
No echolocation. Mariana Islands endemic (Guam, Rota, Saipan). Endangered; severely impacted by brown tree snake on Guam.

south_america.description: Abundant across Amazonian and Atlantic Forest lowlands. Roosts on tree trunks and building walls. Alternates ~45/48 kHz. Complex vocal learning with regional song dialects.
Abundant in buildings and urban areas throughout South America. Alternating QCF at ~34.5/39.6 kHz. One of the first bats detected at dusk. Open-space aerial hawker.
One of the most abundant South American bats. Peak ~71 kHz. Low-intensity whispering calls—detectable only within a few meters. Key seed disperser of Piper plants.
Abundant large frugivore throughout South America. Peak about 61–65 kHz. Prominent facial stripes. Low-intensity multiharmonic FM. Important seed disperser.
Very common frugivore, replaces A. jamaicensis across much of mainland South America. Peak ~54 kHz. Low-intensity multiharmonic FM. Important seed disperser.
Abundant nectarivore throughout South America. Peak ~80 kHz. Low-intensity calls—hard to detect beyond a few meters. Uses echolocation to find flowers with acoustic reflectors. Important pollinator.
Common frugivore of eastern and southern Brazil, eastern Bolivia, Paraguay, north-east Argentina and Uruguay. Low-intensity FM. Yellow shoulder epaulettes in males. Key seed disperser of Solanum.
Common throughout South America near livestock. Short calls (about 2 ms). Peak about 57–61 kHz. Low-intensity. Obligate blood-feeder. Important rabies vector in livestock regions.
Abundant throughout South America—the type locality is in Brazil. QCF search calls ~25–29 kHz, FM during approach. Forms massive colonies. Fast, high-altitude forager.
Widespread in South American lowlands. Low-frequency QCF at ~25–26 kHz. Largest Molossus. Roosts in buildings and hollow trees. Open-space forager.
One of the most widespread South American vespertilionids. Highly plastic calls adapting to clutter. Peak ~54–55 kHz. FM sweeps. Common in forests and urban edges.
Common frugivore of open habitats and forest edges. Peak ~62 kHz. Prominent white facial and dorsal stripes. Low-intensity FM. Cerrado and Atlantic Forest.

The South American high-duty-cycle echolocator. Long CF-FM calls (about 15–21 ms) with Doppler compensation; the CF part is at about 53 kHz or 59 kHz depending on the cryptic form (the 53 kHz mainland form is P. rubiginosus). Unmistakable call structure. Huge cave colonies. Split from P. mesoamericanus.
Widespread in Amazonian lowland forests. Higher frequency (~50 kHz) than S. bilineata. Similar QCF structure. Thinner dorsal stripes. Roosts on tree trunks.

Common along Amazonian rivers, often in lines under bridges and overhanging banks. Short narrowband calls near 95–100 kHz (2nd harmonic); detectors may pick up the 1st harmonic near 40–51 kHz. Cryptic bark-like camouflage. Widespread from Mexico to Bolivia.
Common along South American rivers and coasts. Long CF at 53–56 kHz + FM sweep. Rakes water with large clawed feet to catch fish. Found throughout the continent.
Widespread along Amazonian waterways. CF part at about 70–75 kHz, then an FM sweep down to about 40–45 kHz; higher than N. leporinus. Trawls insects and small fish from water surfaces.
Widespread in South American lowlands. CF at ~54–57 kHz. Largest Pteronotus. Bare-backed in flight. Cave-dwelling. Often in mixed colonies with other mormoopids.
South American lowlands. Highest frequency Pteronotus: initial CF ~83 kHz, terminal ~68 kHz. Cave-roosting.
Widespread in South American lowlands. Multiharmonic QCF at ~40 kHz (2nd harmonic). Found near caves and rock shelters.
Common in South American lowlands. Large omnivore. Peak ~47 kHz. Low-intensity FM. Harem groups in caves and hollow trees. One of the loudest phyllostomids.
Common in South American lowland forests. Famous frog-eating bat—identifies prey by their mating calls. Peak ~70 kHz. Low-intensity FM. Warty lips.
Andean foothills and premontane forests throughout South America. Peak about 69 kHz on the 2nd harmonic, like C. perspicillata. Frugivore specializing on Piper.
Common Amazonian frugivore. Peak ~55 kHz. Intermediate size between A. jamaicensis and A. lituratus. Low-intensity FM. Indistinct facial stripes.
Tent-roosting frugivore in northern South American lowlands. Peak about 68 or 90 kHz, depending on which harmonic is loudest. Low-intensity nasal FM. Modifies palm and banana leaves into tents.
Small frugivore of northern SA lowlands. Peak ~75 kHz. Low-intensity FM. Tent-roosting. Important disperser of understory fruits.
Common in Amazonian forests. Modifies active termite nests into roosts—unique among bats. Peak ~70 kHz. Low-intensity FM. Gleaning insectivore.
Widespread in South American forests. Very short broadband FM with a peak near 80 kHz. Ultra-low intensity. Gleaning insectivore with large ears.
Andean cloud forests and highlands throughout South America. Nectarivore. Peak ~70 kHz. Low-intensity FM. Important pollinator. Tailless.
Nectarivore with short tail (unlike tailless A. geoffroyi). Peak ~72 kHz. Low-intensity FM. Atlantic Forest and lower Andean slopes. Important pollinator.
Widespread in South American lowlands. Alternating calls that sweep down from about 32–36 kHz and end near 18 and 22 kHz. High, fast flight above canopy. Large ears joined at base.
Northern South America (Colombia, Venezuela, Ecuador). QCF at ~34 kHz. Open-space forager. Roosts in buildings.
Small but widespread molossid. Search calls sweep upward from about 43 to 54 kHz, unusual among molossids. Open cerrado and forest edge forager.
Common across South American lowlands and mid-elevations. Peak about 41–45 kHz. FM-QCF. Forest edges and open areas.
Widespread in South America. Open-air forager. Peak ~42 kHz. FM-QCF. Migratory. Distinctive reddish fur. Roosts solitarily in foliage.

Common South American Myotis. Peak about 64–80 kHz in South American recordings. FM sweeps. Silver-tipped dorsal fur distinctive. Forages over water and in forest clearings. Widespread from Mexico to Argentina.
Southern South American Myotis (Chile, Argentina, Patagonia). Peak about 47 kHz; short calls (about 2–4 ms). FM sweeps. One of the southernmost-ranging bats in the Americas. Forest and edge habitats.
Amazonian forest-interior forager. Unusual: most energy in 5th harmonic at ~68 kHz. Multiharmonic calls. Roosts in hollow trees.
Amazonian lowlands. Lower frequency (~32 kHz) than P. macrotis. 2nd harmonic dominant. Near caves and rocky outcrops.
Amazonian endemic. Highest frequency Saccopteryx (~52 kHz). Similar QCF structure to congeners. Smaller than S. bilineata. Roosts on tree trunks in terra firme forest.
Rare canopy-level forager. Steep FM sweeps ~45–55 kHz. Long shaggy fur. One of the least-known Neotropical emballonurids. Amazonian forests.
Distinctive white wing membrane patches. QCF at ~42 kHz. Amazonian lowland forests.
South American populations in Venezuela, Colombia, Peru. CF at ~68 kHz with a sweep to a short QCF near 58 kHz. Cave-roosting.
Northern South America (Venezuela, Colombia). 2nd harmonic, peak ~52 kHz, dominates. Large cave colonies. At southern edge of range.
Widespread in South American lowlands. Omnivore. Peak ~55 kHz. Low-intensity FM. Large colonies in hollow trees. Important pollinator of balsa trees.
UNIQUE phyllostomid with CF-FM calls—the only leaf-nosed bat with constant-frequency echolocation. Long CF at ~45 kHz. Longest phyllostomid calls (up to 8.7 ms). Amazonian caves.
Widespread in South American forests. Gleaning insectivore. Peak ~75 kHz. Low-intensity FM. Now Gardnerycteris crenulatum. Forest understory.
Amazonian forests. Gleaning insectivore/carnivore. Peak ~65 kHz. Low-intensity FM. Roosts in hollow trees. Forest interior specialist.
South American lowland forests. Higher peak (~78 kHz) than C. perspicillata. Low-intensity FM. Smallest Carollia.
Small frugivore. Peak ~68 kHz. Low-intensity FM. Widespread in Neotropical lowland forests. Important seed disperser.
Small frugivore. Peak ~78 kHz. Low-intensity FM. Tent-roosting. Yellow ear margins. Northern South American lowlands.
Large stenodermatine frugivore. Peak ~58 kHz. Prominent white facial stripes. Low-intensity FM. Forages in canopy. Amazonian and northern SA lowlands.
Canopy frugivore with large eyes. Peak ~62 kHz. Low-intensity FM. Widespread in Neotropical lowlands. White dorsal stripe.
Small Amazonian frugivore. Peak ~80 kHz. Low-intensity FM. Related to Carollia. Important disperser of understory fruits. Common in terra firme forest.
Small nectarivore. Peak ~80 kHz. Low-intensity multiharmonic FM. Important pollinator of understory plants. Amazonian forests.
Andean frugivore of montane forests (1000–3200 m). Peak ~70 kHz. Low-intensity FM. Key seed disperser in cloud forest ecosystems.
Widespread in South America. Distinctive three-frequency alternation (~26.7, 28.7, 32.4 kHz). Open-space forager. Cliff and building roosts.
South American lowlands. Low frequency (~22 kHz) open-space forager. Roosts in hollow trees and buildings.
South American lowlands. Distinctive upward-modulated QCF. Alternating pairs at ~30/35 kHz. Open-space forager above canopy.
South American lowlands. Very low frequency (~22–25 kHz) QCF. High-altitude forager above canopy. Large bonneted bat.
Medium-sized bonneted bat. QCF at ~26–30 kHz. Open-area forager. Southern South America (Argentina, Uruguay, Brazil). Roosts in buildings.
Medium bonneted bat of the southern cone (Argentina, Paraguay, southern Brazil). QCF at ~28 kHz. Open and semi-open habitat forager.
Small to medium molossid. QCF at ~25 kHz. Flat face with forward-pointing nostrils. Open habitats across South American lowlands.
Andean highlands and cloud forests. Short FM calls (~2.5 ms). Peak ~55 kHz. Forages in cluttered forest understory.
Widespread in South American lowlands. Steep broadband FM sweep from about 100 to about 60 kHz; calls about 4–5 ms. Forages near streams and over water.
South American lowlands. Lower frequency (~43 kHz) than E. brasiliensis. FM-QCF. Forest edges and open areas.
South American Myotis. Peak ~46 kHz. FM sweeps. Southern Brazil, Uruguay, Argentina. Open areas and forest edges.
High-altitude Andean Myotis (1500–3800 m). Peak ~50 kHz. FM sweeps. Cloud forests and paramo edges. Colombia to Bolivia.
Large vespertilionid, recently split from L. cinereus. Low-frequency FM-QCF at ~22–25 kHz. Long narrow wings for fast open-air flight. Migratory. Frosted fur.
Large-eared vespertilionid. Peak ~32 kHz. FM sweeps. Brazilian cerrado and Atlantic Forest. Slightly higher frequency than H. montanus, consistent with smaller ears.
Small Eptesicus of southern Brazil, Paraguay, Argentina. Peak ~50 kHz. FM-QCF. Forest edges and open areas.
Widespread in South American lowlands. Peak about 31–32 kHz, lower than L. blossevillii. FM-QCF. Roosts solitarily in palm fronds. Yellow fur.
Northern South America (Colombia, Venezuela, Ecuador). QCF at ~33 kHz. Open-space forager. Roosts in buildings.
Northern South America. QCF at ~35 kHz. Smallest Molossus. Open-space forager.
Rare in Amazonian canopy. Distinctive all-white fur—the ghost bat. Narrowband QCF at ~24 kHz. High-altitude forager above the canopy.
Northern South America (Venezuela, Trinidad). QCF at ~43 kHz. Open-area forager near rock shelters and caves.
At the southern edge of its range in northern South America (Venezuela, Colombia). Long QCF peaking near 41 kHz. Open-area forager near caves.
Feeds on bird blood. Peak ~70 kHz. White wing tips distinctive in flight. Low-intensity FM. Rarer than D. rotundus. Lowland forests of South America.
Bird blood specialist (unlike the mammal-feeding D. rotundus). Peak ~80 kHz. Higher frequency than common vampire. Short multiharmonic FM. Low-intensity. Atlantic Forest and Amazonia.
Largest bat in the Americas (wingspan ~1 m). Peak ~70 kHz. Low-intensity FM—very difficult to detect acoustically. Carnivorous: preys on birds and other bats.
Carnivorous gleaner. Peak ~77 kHz. Short FM (0.8–1.4 ms). Low-intensity—hard to detect beyond a few meters. Large ears; hunts other bats and rodents.
Unusual trawling phyllostomid. Louder than most relatives (~101 dB SPL). Peak ~85 kHz. Large feet for grabbing insects from water surfaces.
Gleaning insectivore. Lower peak (~52 kHz) than M. microtis. Low-intensity FM. Forest interior. Amazonian forests.
Rare gleaning insectivore. Peak ~75 kHz. Low-intensity FM. Poorly documented acoustically. Yellow throat patches. Amazonian forests.
Rare gleaner. Peak ~85 kHz. Ultra-short broadband FM (0.3–1 ms). Very low intensity. Forest interior.
Low-intensity gleaner. Peak ~80 kHz. Multiharmonic FM. Forest understory specialist. Rarely captured or detected.
Tiny Amazonian tent-roosting frugivore. Highest peak frequency of any phyllostomid (~100–118 kHz). Ultra-low intensity.
Large omnivorous phyllostomid. Peak ~55 kHz. Low-intensity FM. Pale face distinctive. Roosts in hollow trees. Amazonian forests.
Highland nectarivore. Peak ~68 kHz. Low-intensity FM. Andean cloud forests 1000–2600 m. Uniquely keeled lower incisors.
High-altitude Andean frugivore (2000–3400 m). Peak ~68 kHz. Low-intensity FM. One of the few bat species found above 3000 m.
Suction-cup disks for roosting in rolled Heliconia/Calathea leaves. Extremely low intensity—barely detectable at <1 m. Distinctive social calls for roost-finding. Amazonian lowlands.
Similar to T. tricolor but slightly larger suction disks. Peak ~50 kHz. Roosts in furled Heliconia leaves. Amazonian lowland forests. Extremely low-intensity echolocation.
Medium molossid. QCF at ~28–32 kHz. Amazonian and Atlantic Forest lowlands. Roosts in tree hollows. Uncommonly recorded.
Large free-tailed bat. Low QCF, peak ~20–22 kHz, often audible. Roosts in cliff crevices and buildings. South American drylands and cerrado.
At the edge of its range in northern coastal South America. Peak ~56 kHz. Low-intensity FM. Important fig seed disperser where it occurs.
Northern South America. Small vespertilionid. Broadband FM + QCF at ~48 kHz. Forest edges.
Small Myotis endemic to eastern Brazil (Cerrado, Caatinga). Peak ~52 kHz. Steep FM sweeps. Recently described. Associated with rock outcrops.
Tiny (3–5 g) insectivore with vestigial thumb. Very high frequency FM sweeps peaking ~130–150 kHz. One of the highest-frequency New World bats. Caves and mines. Endemic family Furipteridae.
Rare, endemic to western South America (Ecuador, Peru, Chile). High-frequency FM sweeps ~80–100 kHz. Cave-dwelling. One of only two species in the endemic family Furipteridae. IUCN Vulnerable.
Very high frequency echolocator, peak ~100–120 kHz. Extremely low intensity. Cave-roosting. Endemic to eastern Brazil (Cerrado/Caatinga). IUCN Vulnerable. Cave-dependent.
Very high frequency FM, peak ~100–130 kHz. Cave-roosting. Northern South America (Venezuela, Colombia, Trinidad). Low-intensity calls barely detectable beyond 1 m. Restricted range.
Rare Amazonian disk-winged bat. Roosts in curled leaves. Poorly known acoustically. Low-intensity FM calls. Restricted range.
Very large molossid. Low-frequency QCF at ~18–20 kHz, sometimes audible. Open-space forager over savanna and cerrado. Rarely recorded. Northern Argentina to Colombia.
Largest-eared Histiotus. Very low-frequency peak ~25 kHz. FM sweeps. Chile and western Argentina. Arid and semi-arid open habitats. Restricted range.
Small Amazonian molossid. QCF at ~40 kHz. Poorly known—one of the least-studied South American bats. Forest edge and gap forager.
Large South American lasiurine. FM-QCF ~30–35 kHz. Solitary tree-roosting migratory bat. Formerly Lasiurus egregius. Rarely captured; known mainly from southern Brazil.
Enigmatic Peruvian bat; monotypic genus sometimes placed in its own family Tomopeatidae. Roosts in desert cliffs along the arid Pacific coast. One of South America's rarest bats.

south_america.name: Hoary Bat
south_america.description: Widespread in the Americas. QCF ~20–25 kHz. South American populations formerly treated as separate subspecies. Solitary tree-roosting migrant.

south_asia.description: NE India, Nepal, Bhutan. CF ~69–84 kHz (varies). Often sympatric with R. rouxii.
Forested hills of northern and NE India, Nepal, Bhutan. CF ~32–43 kHz. Cave-roosting.
Northern India, Nepal, Pakistan, Bhutan. CF ~70–83 kHz. Caves and mines; hunts large insects over open ground.
Pakistan, northern India, Nepal. CF ~108–112 kHz. Eastern edge of range. Caves and buildings near dense vegetation.
CF ~147–161 kHz in South Asia. Peninsular India and Sri Lanka. Caves and rock shelters in forests.
CF about 121–128 kHz. Western Ghats and NE India. Small bat in caves and rock crevices.
NE India, Bangladesh, Sri Lanka. Low-intensity FM. Moist lowland forests. Caves, hollow trees.
Widespread in Pakistan and NW/central India. QCF ~30–35 kHz. Arid and semi-arid zones; ruins and rock crevices.

south_asia.name: Bare-rumped Sheathtail Bat
south_asia.description: Largest sheathtail bat in South Asia. Narrowband QCF calls ~19–25 kHz; multi-harmonic. Dark fur flecked with white; bare rump. Fast above-canopy forager. Tree hollows, caves, buildings. India, Sri Lanka, Bangladesh.
FM sweeps from about 38 to 20 kHz, peak about 27–32 kHz, with several harmonics. Very widespread; often the most abundant bat at study sites in Sri Lanka. Rock walls, cliffs, cave ceilings.
Common across peninsular India and Sri Lanka. FM-QCF ~28–35 kHz. Exposed surfaces of buildings and rock faces.
Pakistan and NW India arid zones. FM ~25–35 kHz. Ruins, rock crevices, old temples.
Narrowband FM, about 17–40 kHz with a peak near 23–28 kHz. Large cave colonies across South Asia. Fast high-altitude forager.
Pakistan through India and Sri Lanka. QCF ~18–23 kHz. High-flying open-air forager in arid and urban habitats.
FM-QCF ~44–50 kHz. Common across South Asia. Smaller than S. heathii. Urban areas.
Western Ghats, Andaman Islands and Sri Lanka. FM about 100–40 kHz, peak about 54–65 kHz. Trawls for invertebrates near water.
NE India (Meghalaya). FM ~40 kHz down to ~16–18 kHz, peak ~25 kHz; sometimes two-toned. Among the world’s largest insectivorous bats. Hill forest caves.
FM ~44–55 kHz. Largest Miniopterus in South Asia. Previously misidentified as M. schreibersii. Large cave colonies across India and Sri Lanka.
Andaman Islands, India. CF ~63–68 kHz. Forest-dwelling; caves and buildings.
Endemic to the Andaman Islands. CF peak ~55–58 kHz. Low frequency for a horseshoe bat. Cave-roosting.
No echolocation. Large flying fox. Forms enormous roost camps in banyan trees. Key pollinator and seed disperser. Formerly P. giganteus.

southeast_asia.name: Bare-rumped Sheathtail Bat
southeast_asia.description: Largest sheathtail bat in the region. Narrowband QCF calls about 19–27 kHz, higher in Brunei and Melanesia than in northern Australia; multi-harmonic. Dark fur flecked with white; bare rump diagnostic. High above-canopy forager in tropical lowland forests. Widespread but rarely recorded.
Philippine endemic. CF peak ~58–62 kHz. Forest-dependent; caves. Distinctive yellowish facial skin.
Andaman Islands and parts of mainland SE Asia. CF ~63–68 kHz.

sweden.name: Northern Bat
sweden.description: Sweden's most widespread bat. Found to the Arctic Circle. FM ~30 kHz. Common in boreal forests and settlements.
Common in southern and central Sweden. ~55 kHz. Riparian habitats and towns.
Common across Sweden. Trawls over lakes and rivers. FM sweeps.
Migratory; breeds in southern Sweden. ~38 kHz. Wetlands and forest edges.
Mature forests of central and northern Sweden. FM ~40 kHz. Difficult to separate from whiskered bat acoustically.
Villages and woodland edges. FM ~45 kHz. Southern half of Sweden.
Broadband FM gleaner. Southern and central Sweden. Forests and parkland.
Large noctule. QCF ~20 kHz. Southern Sweden; tree hollows. Early emerger.
Very quiet broadband FM. Old forests and buildings. Common in southern Sweden.
Migratory. FM-QCF ~25 kHz. Eastern and coastal Sweden.
~45 kHz. Southern Sweden only; less common than soprano pipistrelle.
Rare in Sweden; restricted to old-growth forests in the south. Alternating FM ~32/34 kHz.
Southern tip of Sweden only. FM ~27 kHz. Buildings and parkland.
QCF ~25 kHz. Rare breeder in southern Sweden.
Trawling bat. FM. Very rare in Sweden; found near large lakes and rivers in the south.
Southern tip of Sweden only. Very quiet FM. Buildings and parkland.
At northern range limit. Single known site in Skåne. FM. Ground-gleaning beetle specialist.
Old-growth forest specialist. Very quiet FM. Extremely rare in southern Sweden.
Cryptic Myotis. FM. Recently discovered in Sweden; very limited range.

uk.description: Britain's most common bat. Peak frequency ~45 kHz; calls heard on almost every bat detector outing. Roosts in buildings, forages along hedgerows, woodland edges, and over water. Often the first species new bat workers learn to identify.

Split from common pipistrelle in 1999. Peak frequency ~55 kHz. Strongly associated with waterways and riparian habitats across the UK. Maternity roosts can hold over 1,000 individuals. Sometimes called the 55 kHz pipistrelle.

Widespread across Britain. Very quiet, broadband FM calls (25–50 kHz) rarely detected beyond a few metres. Gleaning feeder — picks moths and spiders from foliage. Roosts in older buildings, churches, and tree holes. Ears nearly as long as the body.

The 'water bat' — iconic low passes skimming rivers, canals, and lakes, scooping insects from the surface. Regular FM calls sweep from ~85 kHz to ~32 kHz. Roosts under bridges and in tunnels. Widespread across England, Wales, and Scotland.

Broadband FM sweeps from ~110–150 kHz down to ~15–20 kHz. Gleaner — hunts close to vegetation, sometimes hovering to pick prey off leaves. Distinctive fringe of stiff hairs along the tail membrane. Roosts in old buildings, trees, and bat boxes across Britain.

Small Myotis, widespread but under-recorded. FM calls sweep ~100–28 kHz, very similar to Brandt's bat on a detector. Reliable separation requires examination in the hand. Roosts in buildings; forages along woodland edges and over water.

Cryptic species pair with whiskered bat — only separated in 1970. Calls nearly identical (~100–28 kHz FM). Tends to be more woodland-associated than whiskered. Found across England and Wales; scarcer in Scotland.

Britain's largest common bat. Distinctive loud, narrow-band calls around 20–25 kHz, often alternating with steep FM sweeps. One of the first bats out at dusk — sometimes flies in daylight. Open-air forager, often high above the canopy. Roosts in tree holes.

Smaller cousin of the noctule. Calls at ~25–27 kHz — slightly higher than noctule. Fast, high-flying forager. More common in Ireland than in Great Britain. Roosts in tree holes and bat boxes; rarely in buildings.

Large bat of southern England. Loud FM-QCF calls with characteristic frequency around 25–28 kHz. Slow, heavy flight often along treelines and around street lights. Roosts almost exclusively in buildings. Range rarely extends north of the Midlands.

Long-distance migrant — birds ringed in Latvia have been found in the UK. Peak frequency ~38 kHz; calls can resemble common pip but slightly lower and often with distinctive social calls. Breeding colonies now established in several UK sites. Associated with waterside habitats.

Britain's largest horseshoe bat. Constant-frequency calls at ~82 kHz — unmistakable warbling tone on a heterodyne detector. Restricted to south-west England and south Wales. Hibernates in caves and mines; summer roosts in large roof spaces. UK population internationally important.

Tiny horseshoe bat weighing only 5–9 g. CF calls at ~110 kHz. Found in western Britain — south-west England, Wales, and western Ireland. Very sensitive to roost disturbance and light pollution. Hibernates underground; maternity roosts in buildings.

Distinctive flat-faced bat with alternating call frequencies — short FM pulses alternating between ~32 kHz and ~43 kHz. One of the UK's rarest bats. Hunts tympanate moths and can switch frequencies to evade moth hearing. Found in mature woodland in southern England; roosts behind loose bark.

Very similar to brown long-eared but restricted to the southern coast of England, mainly around the Channel Islands border. Slightly louder calls than brown long-eared. Fewer than 1,000 individuals estimated in the UK. Roosts in buildings.

Elusive woodland specialist of southern England. Long ears (for a Myotis) and broadband FM calls. Rarely caught in mist nets — stays within the canopy. Associated with ancient woodland with veteran trees. One of the UK's rarest resident bats.

Europe's smallest Myotis, confirmed in the UK in 2010. FM calls sweep from ~100 kHz to ~40 kHz with peak energy ~50–55 kHz — slightly higher than whiskered or Brandt's. Very few confirmed UK sites; likely under-recorded. Requires DNA or detailed morphometrics for reliable identification.

Britain's largest Myotis. Declared extinct as a UK breeding species in 1990, but a single male has hibernated in a Sussex mine since at least 2002. Loud FM calls sweep ~85–22 kHz. Gleaner — picks large beetles from the ground. Any UK sighting is nationally significant.

Continental migrant occasionally reaching eastern England and North Sea oil rigs, mostly in autumn. Shallow FM-QCF calls ending near 23–25 kHz, without the regular high-low alternation of the noctule. Loud social calls audible to the human ear.
Mediterranean species expanding northward through Europe. Peak frequency ~40 kHz. Extremely rare in the UK with only a handful of confirmed records, but range expansion may bring more sightings.

Shallow FM sweep with quasi-constant-frequency tail at ~32–34 kHz. Primarily a Mediterranean species but increasingly recorded crossing the Channel to southern England. Distinctive call shape helps separate it from pipistrelles on a spectrogram.
Northern bat of Scandinavia and continental Europe. Calls around 27–30 kHz. Very rare UK vagrant — most records are from Scotland and the Northern Isles.

united_states.description: Most commonly detected bat across much of the US. FM-QCF ~27 kHz. Buildings, bridges, bat boxes.
Forms massive colonies (millions) in caves and bridges across the southern US. QCF ~25 kHz. Bracken Cave, TX is the world's largest known bat colony.
Formerly abundant across the eastern US. FM ~45 kHz. Severely impacted by White-nose Syndrome.
Common migratory tree bat in eastern US. FM ~40 kHz. Major wind-turbine mortality.

united_states.name: Hoary Bat
united_states.description: Largest US vespertilionid. QCF ~20–25 kHz. Solitary tree-roosting migrant. Major wind-energy concern.
Migratory tree bat. FM ~25–30 kHz. Forest edges across the US.
Tiny desert bat of the Southwest. High QCF ~46 kHz. One of the first bats to emerge at dusk.
Western US. Distinctive low FM ~30 kHz. Ground-gleaning specialist taking scorpions and beetles.
Steep FM. Gleaning forager. Endangered due to WNS. Eastern US forests.
Eastern US. FM ~45 kHz. Devastating WNS decline. Cave hibernator.
Large free-tailed bat. Low QCF, peak ~20–22 kHz. Western canyons and cliffs.
Western counterpart of eastern red bat. FM ~40 kHz.
Western US. FM sweep. Mines and caves. Distinctive fringe of hairs on tail membrane.
Spectacular large ears and spotted fur. Very low FM ~10–15 kHz. Western cliffs. Unmistakable on a bat detector.
Large lappets on muzzle. FM search calls ~30 to 14 kHz. Western montane forests.
Very quiet FM. Cave-roosting gleaning specialist. Western US and scattered eastern populations.
Southeastern US. Very quiet FM. Hollow trees and old buildings. Gleaning specialist.
Desert Southwest. QCF ~17–22 kHz. Cliff crevices and rock shelters.
Mexican long-nosed bat. Quiet FM. Big Bend region of Texas. Key agave pollinator.
Indiana bat. FM ~45 kHz. Critically impacted by WNS. Cave hibernation; forest-edge foraging.
Gray bat. FM ~45 kHz. Cave obligate year-round. Large colonies in southeastern US caves.
No echolocation. Guam and Northern Mariana Islands (US territory). Critically endangered due to brown tree snake.
Small western Myotis. FM ~50 kHz. Arid habitats, mines, buildings.
Western trawling bat. FM. Rivers and reservoirs. Buildings and bridges.
Cave myotis of the Southwest. FM ~45–50 kHz. Large cave colonies. Also extends into the Southeast.
Evening bat. FM ~38 kHz. Eastern US forests and suburban areas. Tree-roosting.
Southeastern counterpart of eastern red bat. FM ~40 kHz. Spanish moss and pine forests.
Western prairies and badlands. FM, characteristic frequency ~44 kHz. Rock crevices.
Southeastern cave bat. FM ~48 kHz. Large cave and bridge colonies in Gulf states.
Western mastiff bat. Very low QCF ~12–15 kHz, audible to humans. Cliff-roosting. Largest US bat.
California leaf-nosed bat. Broadband FM. Desert Southwest. Gleaning specialist. Does not hibernate.
Ghost-faced bat. 2nd harmonic ~67 kHz. Southern Texas border. Cave-dwelling.
Northern yellow bat. FM ~30 kHz. Gulf Coast states. Spanish moss rooster.
Southern yellow bat. FM ~35 kHz. Texas and Florida. Palm tree rooster.
Keen's myotis. Broad FM sweep. Pacific Northwest temperate rainforests (WA). Very similar to M. evotis.
Underwood's bonneted bat. Low QCF ~14–28 kHz. Desert Southwest (AZ, NM). Audible to humans.

vic_australia.description: Widespread and abundant across Victoria. Roosts in tree hollows, buildings, and bat boxes. Alternating call frequencies are distinctive.
Common across southern Australia. Small, dark bat roosting in tree hollows and buildings. Higher frequency calls than Gould's Wattled Bat.
Australia's most widespread bat. Very quiet, broadband FM calls; often difficult to detect acoustically. Gleaning insectivore with large ears.
Australia's largest insectivorous bat. Loud, low-frequency calls audible to some humans. Fast, high-flying open-air forager.
One of Australia's smallest bats (~4 g). Common in forests and urban areas throughout Victoria. High-frequency calls.
Small forest bat found across southern Australia. Roosts in tree hollows. Call frequency overlaps with Little Forest Bat.
Common in forests of eastern Australia. Very quiet calls, similar to Lesser Long-eared Bat. Distinguished by larger size and habitat preference.
Largest Vespadelus species. Found in wet and dry forests of south-eastern Australia including Tasmania.
Cave-roosting bat found along eastern Australia. Fast, agile flier. Maternity cave near Bairnsdale. Vulnerable in Victoria.
Small free-tailed bat of south-eastern Australia. Roosts in tree hollows and buildings. Rapid, direct flight.
Widespread across eastern Australian coasts. Similar to Southern Free-tailed Bat but slightly higher frequency calls.
Large vesper bat of south-eastern forests. Roosts in tree hollows. Vulnerable (IUCN). Distinctive mid-range frequency calls.
Robust bat of south-eastern coastal forests. Narrow frequency range distinctive. Roosts in tree hollows.
Widespread across inland Australia. Found in drier regions of northern and western Victoria. Similar frequency to Gould's Wattled Bat.
Australia's only fishing bat. Trawls water surfaces with large feet. Found near rivers, lakes, and dams. Very quiet calls.
Large, fast-flying bat with glossy black fur and yellow belly. Migratory; visits Victoria seasonally. High-altitude forager.
Constant-frequency echolocation using distinctive horseshoe-shaped noseleaf. Cave-roosting. Found in forests of eastern and southern Victoria.
Formerly N. timoriensis. Rare in Victoria, restricted to drier woodlands. Very quiet gleaning calls. Vulnerable.
Small bat of inland Australia. In Victoria, restricted to the semi-arid northwest (Mallee region).
Large, robust bat of eastern coastal forests. Rare in Victoria, mainly in far east Gippsland. Aggressive predator of large insects and small vertebrates.
Critically Endangered (EPBC Act). Dependent on a single maternity cave near Warrnambool. Population <50 individuals. Southwest Victoria only.
Vulnerable (EPBC Act). Extremely rare in Victoria; restricted to northwest Mallee (Hattah-Kulkyne, Gunbower). Possibly <50 individuals in VIC.
Australia's largest bat (wingspan ~1 m). Does not echolocate. Camps in colonies along waterways. Vulnerable (EPBC Act). Pollinator and seed disperser.
Seasonal visitor to northern Victoria. Does not echolocate. Nomadic, following eucalypt flowering. Occasionally camps at Swan Hill and Numurkah.
